God had told Moses that Aaron was already coming (v.14), and here he is, and he kissed him. It is a small, warm, entirely human detail in a chapter full of signs and warnings, and it is the only reunion in Exodus. Whatever had passed between them in four decades of separation, whatever Aaron thought of a brother who fled and never came back, the text records a kiss.

Then: And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do. All of them. The first thing the mouth of God's prophet does is listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel. Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people. And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go together, gather the elders, Aaron speaks the words and Moses does the signs — and then the sentence that answers verse 1 of this chapter: And the people believed.

Moses had said they would not. He had said it as though it were the obvious outcome, and God had told him otherwise, and Moses had gone on arguing until God grew angry. He was wrong. The objection that felt most realistic to him, the one built on knowing his own people, was simply mistaken. How often the thing we are most certain will fail turns out to be the very thing God has already promised will not.

And what convinced them is stated precisely: when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction. The verb is paqad, the same word Joseph used on his deathbed four centuries earlier when he told his brothers that God would surely visit them and bring them up out of this land (Gen. 50:24). Joseph's bones are still in Egypt, still waiting on that verb, and a promise the last man who remembered it had been dead for four hundred years turns out to have been keeping time all along.

Then the last clause of the chapter: and they bowed their heads and worshiped.

Nothing has been delivered yet. Not a plague has fallen, not a chain has been struck off; they are still slaves, and tomorrow they will still make bricks, and within one chapter the workload will be doubled and they will curse Moses for it. All they have is a report that God has seen. And on the strength of that alone they go down on their faces. This is what God has been after since the bush, and he said so plainly — let my people go that they may serve me — because the end of the exodus was never a change of address but a people on their knees in front of the God who came down for them. Egypt was never the point. He was.

4.theology:
The sufficiency of God in human weakness. God's call rests on his power, not the servant's gifts. "Who made man's mouth?" silences every excuse.

Divine sovereignty. God claims authority over speech, disability, Pharaoh's heart, and the outcome of history. Nothing lies outside his rule.

Redemption unto worship. "Let my son go that he may serve me." Salvation's goal is not mere liberation but the worship of God.
4.examples:
Then: A reluctant shepherd, full of excuses, was sent to confront a superpower, assured only that the God who made his mouth would go with him.

Now: When God calls us beyond our competence, the question is never "Am I able?" but "Is God able?" Our weakness is the stage for his strength. And we are redeemed not for ourselves but to serve and worship our Redeemer.

5.title: When Obedience Makes Things Worse
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'"<sup>2</sup>But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."<sup>3</sup>Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword."<sup>4</sup>But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens."<sup>5</sup>And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"<sup>6</sup>The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen,<sup>7</sup>"You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves.<sup>8</sup>But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.'<sup>9</sup>Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."<sup>10</sup>So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw.<sup>11</sup>Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'"<sup>12</sup>So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.<sup>13</sup>The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw."<sup>14</sup>And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"<sup>15</sup>Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this?<sup>16</sup>No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."<sup>17</sup>But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>18</sup>Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks."<sup>19</sup>The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."<sup>20</sup>They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh;<sup>21</sup>and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?<sup>23</sup>For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
5.overview:
The first confrontation goes badly. Moses and Aaron deliver God's word — "Let my people go" — and Pharaoh responds with the defiant question that defines all human rebellion: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" Pharaoh, worshiped as a god in Egypt, will not bow to the God of slaves. So he doubles the burden: the Israelites must now gather their own straw while meeting the same quota of bricks.

The result is that obedience to God makes things, for the moment, far worse. The Israelite foremen turn on Moses; Moses turns on God: "Why did you ever send me?" This is the dark valley every believer eventually walks — when doing the right thing brings not relief but trouble, and faith is stretched to its breaking point. Ferguson reminds us that God's deliverances often deepen before they dawn; the darkest hour is just before the outstretched arm.

The chapter teaches us that God's timetable is not ours, and that the lowest point of our circumstances may be precisely the threshold of his greatest work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: The first Thus says the LORD in Scripture, and the demand is for a festival: Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness. Pharaoh answers with the question the whole book exists to settle — Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?... I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.

Verses 3-5: The demand softens to a request for a three days' journey. Pharaoh does not argue theology; he issues a work order — Get back to your burdens — and complains that Moses would make them rest from their work.

Verses 6-9: Straw is withdrawn and the quota kept. His diagnosis: They are idle; therefore they cry, "Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God." And his instruction: let them not pay regard to lying words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Question the Book Answers

Who is the LORD? is asked dismissively and answered exhaustively. By 9:27 Pharaoh says The LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong; by 12:31 he is out of bed in the night begging Israel to leave; by 14:25 his own army is shouting the LORD fights for them. Every man who has asked that question dismissively has been answered eventually. The only variable is whether the answer arrives as mercy or as ruin.

And the verb in I do not know the LORD is yada — the same word used of the king who did not know Joseph (1:8). Not a gap in his information but a refusal of any claim on him. Ingratitude and unbelief turn out to be one reflex applied to two objects.

Pharaoh Objects to Rest

You make them rest from their work uses shabath. The first sabbath language in Exodus is on a slave-master's lips, as an accusation — his complaint against God is precisely that God gives people rest. The book answers it directly: God will command a sabbath and give the reason, you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15). Slavery has no day off; that is what makes it slavery. Every kingdom that has owned people has said get back to your burdens. One master says my burden is light (Matt. 11:28-30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Something quietly discouraging happens between verse 1 and verse 3. The first demand was an imperative from God; the second is please, with a reason attached. Moses and Aaron have been in the room for one verse and are already negotiating downward. Anyone who has had to say something difficult on God's behalf will recognise it.

Now: Pharaoh looks at a people asking for a festival and concludes they have too much spare time. It is the oldest sneer available and it has never gone out of use — that devotion is a hobby for those with insufficient responsibilities, and the cure is a heavier schedule. Note too that he does not call the message false because he misunderstood it. He understood it exactly, and named it lying words, because a lie can be legislated against and a word from God cannot.

Why did God permit this, having warned Moses it was coming? Because had Pharaoh released Israel at the first request, they would have walked out grateful to a reasonable king and the story would have been a successful negotiation. Every avenue of human explanation is being closed off in advance, so that when Israel finally walks out there is no one left to thank but God.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'" But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel..." Three words there are about to be spoken ten thousand times in the Old Testament, and this is the first of them. Thus says the LORD. Every prophet from here to Malachi will open his mouth with that formula, and it begins in a throne room in Egypt, in front of a man who is about to say he has never heard of the speaker.

And notice what is actually demanded. Not freedom, not land, not wages, not an end to the beatings — that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness. The word is chag, a festival, the sort of thing Israel will keep three times a year for the rest of its history. God is not asking Pharaoh to be more humane. He is asking him to release a congregation.

Pharaoh's reply is the most naked sentence in the book: Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.

Take the verb. I do not know — yada, the same word used of the king in 1:8 who did not know Joseph. It is not a gap in his information; it is a refusal of relationship and of any claim on him. He did not acknowledge the Hebrew who saved Egypt, and he does not acknowledge the Hebrew's God. Ingratitude and atheism turn out to be the same reflex applied to different objects.

But the question is a real one, and it is the question this entire book exists to answer. Who is the LORD? Watch what happens to the man who asked it. By 9:27 he will say The LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. By 10:16 he is asking for forgiveness. By 12:31 he is out of bed in the middle of the night begging them to leave. And by 14:25 his own army is shouting Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them. Pharaoh asked who the LORD was, and he received a full and unhurried answer over eighteen chapters. Every man who has ever asked that question dismissively has been answered eventually. The only variable is whether the answer arrives as mercy or as ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword." But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens." And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something quietly discouraging happens between verse 1 and verse 3. The first demand was Thus says the LORD... Let my people go. The second is please let us go a three days' journey, with a reason attached and a note of self-protection: lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword. The imperative has become a request. Moses and Aaron have been in the room for one verse and they are already softening.

It is very human, and most people who have ever had to say something difficult on God's behalf will recognise it — the message that was clear in the preparation and gets negotiated downward in the delivery.

Pharaoh does not engage with any of it. Why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens. He does not argue theology; he issues a work order. That is how the world most often deals with the claims of God — not by refuting them but by pointing at the schedule.

Then his last sentence, and it contains a word nobody expects here: you make them rest from their work. The Hebrew is shabath. The first appearance of sabbath language in Exodus is on the lips of a slave-master, using it as an accusation. Pharaoh's complaint against God is precisely that God gives people rest.

Hold that, because the book is going to answer it directly. On a mountain not many chapters from here God will command a sabbath and give as the reason: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15). Slavery has no day off; that is what makes it slavery. The God who redeems builds rest into the week and writes it into stone. And the one who came to finish the exodus said the thing Pharaoh could never have said — Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). Every kingdom that has ever owned people has said get back to your burdens. He is the only master who says my burden is light.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen, "You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.' Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh's counter-measure is precise and vicious. They will still make the same number of bricks; they will simply no longer be given the straw. Straw is not optional in Nile-mud brick — the fibres bind the clay and stop it crumbling as it dries. So the quota stays and the raw material is withdrawn, and the labour of gathering it is added on top of a day that was already full.

And listen to his diagnosis: They are idle; therefore they cry, "Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God." He has looked at a people asking for a festival and concluded they have too much spare time. Worship, to Pharaoh, is what happens when the workforce is under-employed. It is the oldest sneer there is, and it has never gone out of use — that devotion is a hobby for people with insufficient responsibilities, and the cure is a heavier schedule.

Then: let them not pay regard to lying words. The word of God, delivered by his appointed messenger with signs to authenticate it, is called a lie by the man it was addressed to. He is not confused. He has understood exactly what was said and has decided to name it falsehood, because a lie can be legislated against and a word from God cannot.

Why did God let this happen, having told Moses in advance that it would? Had Pharaoh released Israel at the first request, they would have walked out of Egypt grateful to a reasonable king, and the story would have been about a successful negotiation. God is going to make that reading impossible. Every avenue of human explanation is being closed off in advance, so that when Israel finally walks out there will be no one left to thank but God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 10-12: The order travels down the chain in the same form Moses used — Thus says Pharaoh — and Israel is scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

Verses 13-14: The quota is unchanged and impossible, and it is the Israelite foremen, not the Egyptian taskmasters, who were beaten for the shortfall.

Verses 15-16: Those foremen appeal over their heads to Pharaoh himself: Why do you treat your servants like this?... the fault is in your own people.

Verses 17-19: You are idle, you are idle — the sneer repeated to their faces — and the appeal fails. The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble.

Verses 20-21: They come out and find Moses and Aaron waiting: The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh... and have put a sword in their hand to kill us.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Machine Built to Turn a People Against Its Deliverer

The foremen are Hebrews. Egypt appoints men from among the slaves to drive the slaves, holds them responsible for an arithmetic that cannot work, and flogs them when it fails. It is one of the cruellest arrangements oppression has devised and it is still in use: put some of the oppressed in charge of the rest, and the resentment of the many falls on the few instead of on the throne. By verse 21 those beaten men are cursing Moses. Pharaoh does not have to lift a finger.

Appealing to the Wrong Throne

There is nothing dishonourable in the foremen's petition — it is what any sensible person would try, respectfully made and factually unanswerable, and God does not condemn them for it. But the man they are petitioning is the man who wrote the order. The only relief available inside Egypt comes from a king who has already answered Who is the LORD? with I will not. They are asking the disease for a cure.

The Rejected Deliverer

This is the second time Israel has turned on Moses — the first was Who made you a prince and a judge over us? (2:14) — and he will hear it at the sea, over water, over food, and over a report about giants. It is the pattern of the greater Deliverer drawn small: He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The crowd that spread cloaks on the road on Sunday was calling for his execution by Friday, on much the same charge sheet — he had made things worse, he had provoked Rome, it was better that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Straw is not decorative in Nile-mud brick; the fibres bind the clay and stop it crumbling as it dries. Withdraw it, keep the quota, and add the gathering to a day that was already full — and not even straw, but stubble, the stumps left after harvest, the scrapings. A nation is put on its knees in other people's fields picking up chaff to make the same number of bricks it made yesterday.

Now: Scripture does not hurry verse 19. It could have moved straight from Pharaoh's refusal to God's answer in chapter 6, and instead it stops to record what it is like to try everything available and watch it fail. There are stretches of the Christian life that look exactly like that verse, and it matters that the Bible has one for them.

And the curse in verse 21 is not petulance — it is reasonable. Before Moses came they were slaves; now they are slaves being flogged for an impossible quota, and the only thing that has changed since they bowed and worshipped in 4:31 is that life is measurably worse. From where the foremen stand, Moses is not the deliverer. He is the cause.

verseByVerse.quote: So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'" So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The policy is passed down the chain, and how it travels repays attention. The taskmasters and the foremen go out and repeat it almost word for word: Thus says Pharaoh, "I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least."

Thus says Pharaoh. The same formula Moses used in verse 1, now on the other side. Two words are loose in Egypt — one from the throne of God and one from the throne of Egypt — and for the moment the second is the one with the whips behind it.

So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw. Not even straw: stubble — the stumps left in a field after harvest, the scrapings, what remains when everything usable has already been taken. A nation is put on its knees in the dirt of other people's fields, picking up chaff, to make the same number of bricks it made yesterday.

The word for scattered is the word used of dispersing an army. Israel, which has just begun to be addressed by God as a single son, is broken up across the whole country, each family scrabbling alone. It is hard to organise a people who are spread that thin, and Pharaoh knows it.

verseByVerse.quote: The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." The arithmetic is impossible and everybody involved knows it is impossible. That is not a flaw in the policy; it is the policy. A quota that cannot be met turns every day into a failure and every worker into a debtor.

And then the detail that makes this chapter hurt: the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten. The foremen are Hebrews. Egypt has appointed men from among the slaves to drive the slaves, and when the quota fails it is not the Egyptian taskmasters who are flogged but the Israelite middle-men.

It is one of the cruellest arrangements oppression has ever devised, and it is still in use: put some of the oppressed in charge of the rest, make them responsible for the impossible, and let the resentment of the many fall on the few instead of on the throne. By verse 21 those beaten men will be blaming Moses. Pharaoh will not have to lift a finger to turn Israel against its deliverer. He has built a machine that does it for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foremen do something brave. They go over the taskmasters' heads and appeal directly to Pharaoh — bruised men walking into the presence of the king who ordered the bruising — and they put their case well: Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, "Make bricks!" And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people.

It is a good argument, respectfully made, and factually unanswerable. They are not asking for freedom. They are not mentioning Moses, or the LORD, or the feast in the wilderness. They are asking a reasonable man to look at an unreasonable arrangement and correct it.

And here is the thing to notice, because it explains the whole chapter. They have appealed to the wrong throne. There is nothing dishonourable in what they have done — it is what any sensible person would try, and God is not condemning them for it. But the man they are petitioning is the man who wrote the order, and the only relief available in Egypt is from a king who has already answered Who is the LORD? with I will not. They are asking the disease for a cure.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks." The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'" He says it twice. The sneer of verse 8 is now delivered to the faces of men whose backs are bleeding from a quota they could not meet. There is no argument here and no engagement; there is a phrase repeated because repeating it is easier than thinking.

Then Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks. The appeal is over. The policy stands.

And the narrator gives us the moment it lands: The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble. That is the sentence, flat and without comment. They had one card and they played it, and it did not work, and now they have to walk back out and tell their people that nothing is going to change.

Scripture does not rush this. It could have moved straight from Pharaoh's refusal to God's answer in chapter 6, and instead it stops to record what it is like to try everything available and watch it fail. There are stretches of the Christian life that look exactly like verse 19, and the Bible has a verse for them.

verseByVerse.quote: They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh; and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come out of the palace and Moses and Aaron are standing there waiting to hear how it went.

The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us.

That is not grumbling. That is a curse, invoking God against the men God sent. And the terrible thing is how reasonable it is. Before Moses came they were slaves; now they are slaves being flogged for an impossible quota, and the only thing that has changed since the signs were performed and the people bowed their heads and worshipped (4:31) is that life has become measurably worse. From where the foremen are standing, Moses is not a deliverer. He is the cause.

This is the second time Israel has turned on him. The first was forty years ago — Who made you a prince and a judge over us? (2:14) — and it drove him into the desert. He will hear it again at the sea, and over water, and over food, and over a report about giants, until at the end of his life he is still absorbing it.

And it is the pattern of the greater Deliverer, drawn small. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). The crowd that spread cloaks on the road for him on Sunday was calling for his execution by Friday, and the charge sheet was much the same: he had made things worse, he had provoked Rome, it was better that one man should die for the people. Moses was blamed for a beating. Christ was blamed for everything, and did not defend himself, and went on delivering the people who were shouting.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-23: Moses takes it straight to God, and it is an accusation rather than a question: O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Does Not Rebuke the Complaint

Moses tells God that God has done evil and has not delivered his people at all — the bluntest speech in Exodus so far, made by the man God chose — and there is no correction, no reminder of who is addressing whom. The next verse simply begins Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh. An answer, not a reprimand.

Scripture is full of this and never treats it as a failure of faith: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps. 13:1); O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Hab. 1:2); Jeremiah telling God outright that he has been deceived (Jer. 20:7). The alternative to Moses' prayer is not a more reverent prayer; it is silence, or walking away. Note the direction — Moses turned to the LORD. Where the protest is taken is the evidence of the faith. A man who has stopped believing does not bother to argue.

The Why That Was Not Answered

There is one prayer of exactly this shape that received no reply. In a garden and then on a cross the true Deliverer asked My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — and no voice came, and no rescue arrived, and the darkness held for three hours. Moses said you have not delivered your people at all and was told to watch. The Son was not answered, because the deliverance being worked that afternoon required him to stay where he was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses obeyed exactly. He went where he was sent, said what he was given to say, performed the signs — and the measurable result was that a suffering people suffered more and began cursing him for it.

Now: Obedience made things worse. Scripture says so plainly and does not apologise for it, and it is important to see what God does not say in reply. He does not tell Moses he must have misheard the call. He does not suggest the difficulty proves a wrong turn, or that more faith would have produced a smoother result. He tells him to wait one verse.

That is the word for anyone who did the obedient thing and watched it cost them — who spoke the true word and lost the friendship, took the harder road and found it harder than advertised. The chapter ends with nothing fixed and no explanation given, and the man who prayed it was not wrong about any of his facts. He was only early.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."

Read that again and notice that it is an accusation. Not a request for understanding, not a carefully hedged question — Moses tells God that God has done evil to these people and has not delivered them at all. It is the bluntest thing anyone has said to God so far in Exodus, and it is said by the man God chose.

And God does not rebuke him for it. There is no correction, no reminder of who is speaking to whom. The very next verse begins But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh" — an answer, not a reprimand.

That should reframe how a great many people pray. Scripture is full of this kind of speech and it is never treated as a failure of faith: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps. 13:1); O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Hab. 1:2); Jeremiah telling God outright that he has been deceived (Jer. 20:7). The alternative to Moses' prayer is not a more reverent prayer. It is silence, or leaving. He does neither. Note where he goes with the complaint — Moses turned to the LORD. The direction of the protest is the evidence of the faith. A man who has stopped believing does not bother to argue.

Here is the situation in full, because it is one many readers are living in. Moses obeyed exactly. He went where he was sent, said what he was given to say, performed the signs, and the measurable result of his obedience was that a suffering people suffered more and started cursing him for it. Obedience made things worse. Scripture says so plainly and does not apologise for it, and it does not tell Moses that he must have misheard the call. It tells him to wait one more verse.

And there is one prayer of this shape that was not answered. In a garden and then on a cross, the true Deliverer asked why — My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? — and no voice came back, and no rescue arrived, and the darkness held for three hours. Moses said you have not delivered your people at all and was told to watch. The Son said why have you forsaken me and was not answered, because the deliverance being worked that afternoon required him to stay where he was. Every unanswered why since has been prayed by people whose why was answered at Golgotha, by someone whose was not.

5.theology:
The defiance of unbelief. "Who is the LORD?" exposes the heart of rebellion — a refusal to acknowledge God's right to rule.

The cost of obedience. Following God's word can bring immediate hardship. God's deliverances often deepen the darkness before the dawn.

Honest lament. Moses brings his bewilderment to God himself. Faith may wrestle in the dark, so long as it wrestles with God.
5.examples:
Then: The first obedience to God's command brought heavier chains, not freedom, and the deliverer was blamed by the very people he came to save.

Now: When obedience seems to make life harder and prayers seem to go unanswered, we are exactly where Moses stood. The lowest point is often the threshold of God's mightiest work. Bring your "why" to the LORD.

6.title: I Will Redeem You with an Outstretched Arm
6.text: <sup>1</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land."<sup>2</sup>God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.<sup>4</sup>I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.<sup>6</sup>Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.<sup>7</sup>I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.<sup>8</sup>I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"<sup>9</sup>Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.<sup>10</sup>So the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land."<sup>12</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?"<sup>13</sup>But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon.<sup>16</sup>These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.<sup>18</sup>The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.<sup>20</sup>Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.<sup>23</sup>Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites.<sup>25</sup>Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans.<sup>26</sup>These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts."<sup>27</sup>It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.<sup>28</sup>On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,<sup>29</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you."<sup>30</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
6.overview:
In answer to Moses' despair, God responds not with a new plan but with a renewed revelation of himself. "I am the LORD" frames the passage like a refrain. God recalls his covenant with the patriarchs and then unfurls a magnificent chain of "I will" promises — the so-called seven "I wills" of redemption: I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, I will take you, I will be your God, I will bring you in, I will give you the land. Salvation is spelled out entirely in the first person of God. Every verb belongs to him.

Here the great word redeem enters in force: "I will redeem you with an outstretched arm." To redeem is to buy back, to free at cost, to claim as one's own. The outstretched arm — a recurring image of God's saving power — will reach its fullest stretch on a Roman cross, where the Redeemer's arms are stretched out to purchase a people at the cost of his blood.

Yet the chapter ends realistically: the people, broken in spirit by their slavery, do not listen. God's promises are not finally validated by the faith of his people but by the faithfulness of God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-3: God answers Moses' accusation with a timetable — Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh — and then with his name: I am the LORD. He appeared to the patriarchs as El Shaddai, but by this name I did not make myself known to them.

Verses 4-5: I have also heard the groaning... and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Name Brackets Everything

I am the LORD opens verse 2 and closes verse 8, and every promise in between rests on it. When his people are at the end of themselves, God says his name.

Verse 3's old difficulty — Genesis has Abraham using the name freely — turns on what Scripture means by knowing a name: to know it is to have experienced what it stands for. Abraham heard the syllables and died with one son and no country. The patriarchs had the promise; these slaves are about to get the performance.

God "Remembered"

It never means he had forgotten. It is the word for acting on what he has always held — covenant moving from promise into motion. When God remembers Noah the waters go down; when he remembers Hannah she conceives; when a dying criminal says remember me, he is in Paradise that afternoon. God is not responding to the volume of the groaning; he is keeping an appointment made four centuries earlier with a man who owned nothing in Canaan but the field he was buried in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses had just told God he had done evil and delivered nobody (5:22-23). The reply is not an explanation. It is an appointment.

Now: God rarely answers the question we asked. Moses asked why; he was told now you shall see. That is not evasion — it is the difference between an argument and a promise, and only one of them can be leaned on while the trouble lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land." God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses had just accused God of doing evil and delivering nobody (5:22-23). God's reply is not an explanation but a timetable: Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh. Not later, and not maybe. The complaint was answered by an appointment.

Then God does what he always does when his people are at the end of themselves — he says his name. I am the LORD. That sentence brackets this whole passage, opening verse 2 and closing verse 8, and everything promised in between stands or falls on it.

Verse 3 raises an old question: God says he appeared to the patriarchs as God Almighty — El Shaddai — but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them. Yet Genesis has Abraham using that name freely. The resolution lies in what the Bible means by knowing a name. To know a name is to have experienced what it stands for. Abraham heard the syllables; he never saw the covenant-keeping God actually keep this covenant, because he died with one son and no country. Israel is about to watch the name do what the name means. The patriarchs had the promise. These slaves are going to get the performance.

verseByVerse.quote: I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners. Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have also heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.

That word remembered has caused needless trouble. It never means God had forgotten and something jogged his memory. In Hebrew it is the word for acting on what you have always held — covenant moving from promise into motion. When God remembers Noah the waters go down; when he remembers Hannah she conceives; when a dying criminal asks remember me, he is in Paradise that afternoon.

And the covenant being remembered is four hundred years old, made with a man who owned nothing in Canaan but the field he was buried in. God is not responding to the volume of the groaning. He is keeping an appointment made with a dead man, and the groaning has simply reached the hour that was set.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 6-7: Seven promises, each beginning I will — bring out, deliver, redeem, take you as my people, be your God — carried out with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.

Verse 8: The seventh: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob — sealed, as it opened, with I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
Redeem Is a Family Word

Ga'al is not a general term for rescue. The go'el was the near relative whose duty it was to buy back what a poor kinsman had lost — his land, his freedom, his name; it is what Boaz does for Ruth. God does not promise to free Israel by force of arms but the way a relative clears a debt, and that requires him to count himself family. He did it properly in the end: since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things (Heb. 2:14).

The Sentence the Bible Is Walking Toward

I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God recurs at Sinai, in the prophets, in the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 — and is still being spoken on the last page of Scripture over a city coming down out of heaven (Rev. 21:3). Rescue was never the destination. Rescue was how he got them to the place where that sentence could be said.

The Outstretched Arm

The phrase becomes shorthand for God's saving power throughout the Old Testament — until Isaiah asks To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? and points not at a raised fist over Egypt but at a man despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions (Isa. 53:1-5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seven verbs, one subject. Israel contributes nothing to the list.

Now: Every one of those promises was impossible from where Israel stood that afternoon, and the guarantee attached is not a strategy, a timetable, or a show of force. It is three words — I am the LORD. He staked them on nothing except who he is, which is the only security that has never once failed.

verseByVerse.quote: Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the promises, and there are seven of them, each beginning I will: bring you out, deliver you, redeem you, take you to be my people, be your God, bring you in, give it to you. Seven verbs, one subject. Israel is not asked to contribute anything to the list.

The third is the one to slow down on. I will redeem you — ga'al, which is not a general word for rescue but a family word. The go'el was the near relative whose duty it was to buy back what a poor kinsman had lost: his land, his freedom, his name. It is what Boaz does for Ruth. God does not say he will free Israel by force of arms. He says he will free them the way a relative pays off a debt — and that requires him to count himself family.

The manner is named too: with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. That phrase becomes shorthand for God's saving power all through the Old Testament, until Isaiah asks the question that turns it inside out — To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? — and then points, not at a raised fist over Egypt, but at a man with no form or majesty, despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions (Isa. 53:1-5). The arm of the LORD was finally revealed stretched out, and it was nailed there.

Then verse 7, which is the sentence the whole Bible is walking toward: I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God. That formula recurs at Sinai, in the prophets, in the new covenant of Jeremiah 31, and it is still being spoken on the last page of Scripture over a city coming down out of heaven — Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man... they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Rev. 21:3). Rescue was never the destination. Rescue was how he got them to the place where that sentence could be said.

And the Redeemer who counted himself family did it properly. Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things (Heb. 2:14) — not a liberator arriving from outside the family, but the nearest of kin taking on the flesh of the people he came to buy back, and paying in the only currency that was ever going to clear the debt.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.

The seventh promise closes the circle: not merely out of Egypt but into somewhere. Redemption in Scripture is never only an escape; it always has an address. God does not save people from something and leave them standing in a desert.

And the passage ends where it began, with the name. Six promises have been laid out, every one of them impossible from where Israel is standing this afternoon, and the guarantee attached is not a strategy or a timetable or a demonstration of force. It is three words. I am the LORD. He has staked the promises on nothing except who he is, which is the only security that has never once failed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-30 — Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9-13: They did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. Moses concludes that Pharaoh will not listen either, and calls himself of uncircumcised lips.

Verses 14-27: The narrative stops for a genealogy establishing who Moses and Aaron are — Levi, Kohath, Amram — including Aaron's marriage and the naming of Korah.

Verses 28-30: The account circles back and Moses repeats his objection word for word.
verseByVerse.theology:
Too Crushed to Hear a Promise

Seven unbreakable promises were delivered and could not be taken in. The text does not call this rebellion or unbelief. Kotzer ruach is shortness of spirit, the breath squeezed out — not people refusing a promise but people crushed past the point of holding one. Scripture records the condition without a word of reproach, and God's plan does not pause for it. He does not withdraw the seven I wills because the audience was too tired to receive them.

A Genealogy With Nothing Edited Out

The honour falls on Levi — whose father's dying words about him were Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce (Gen. 49:7). The tribe with the worst blessing in Genesis is the one God builds his priesthood from. And the list is not tidied: among Kohath's descendants it names Korah, who will lead a rebellion and be swallowed by the ground. God writes the genealogy of his deliverers without removing the disgraces — as he would again, at greater length, in Matthew 1.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses has now pleaded inadequacy five times, and the chapter deliberately ends on the fifth rather than covering for him.

Now: There are people who cannot hear good news, and they are usually not being difficult — grief, exhaustion and long pain do this, and a promise arrives and will not go in. What God has undertaken to do never depended on anyone's ability to feel encouraged about it. Everything about to happen in Egypt was promised in verses 6 to 8 by someone who needed no one's competence, and the last word before the plagues begin is a reluctant man's excuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. So the LORD said to Moses, "Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?" But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.

Seven unbreakable promises had just been delivered to them, and they could not take them in. Note carefully what the text does not say. It does not call this rebellion, or hardness, or unbelief. The Hebrew is kotzer ruach — shortness of spirit, the breath squeezed out. These people were not refusing the promise; they had been crushed past the point where they could hold one.

Say that plainly, because there are people who cannot hear good news and are not being difficult. Grief, exhaustion and long pain do this. A promise arrives and simply will not go in. Scripture records that condition without a word of reproach — and, importantly, God's plan does not pause for it. He does not withdraw the seven I wills because the audience was too tired to receive them. He goes on to verse 10 and keeps working. What God has undertaken to do never did depend on Israel's ability to feel encouraged about it.

Moses draws the obvious conclusion — if my own people will not listen, why would Pharaoh? — and adds a new phrase for his old objection: I am of uncircumcised lips. He has now raised inadequacy five times. God's reply is not to argue with him but to issue orders and move him along.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon. These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years. The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations. Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years. The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites. Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans. These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts." It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, mid-crisis, the narrative stops dead for a family tree.

It reads like an interruption and it is doing real work. Moses and Aaron have just been ordered to confront the most powerful man alive, and the text pauses to establish exactly who these two men are: Levi's line, through Kohath, through Amram. They are documented. Israel's deliverance is not being entrusted to a pair of strangers with a story about a bush.

But notice which family gets the honour. Levi's — and everyone reading knew what Levi had done, because his father's dying words about him were Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce (Gen. 49:7). The tribe with the worst blessing in Genesis is the tribe God builds his priesthood from. Nor is the list tidied up: it records Aaron marrying Elisheba, and among the descendants of Kohath it names Korah, who will lead a rebellion and be swallowed by the ground.

God writes the genealogy of his deliverers without editing out the disgraces. He would do it again, at greater length, in the first chapter of Matthew, where the line of the Messiah runs through Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba, and nobody's history is quietly dropped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by circling back to where verse 12 left off, and Moses says it one more time: Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?

He is not a hero. That is the point of ending here. Between the seven I wills and the first plague stands a man still telling God he cannot speak, and Scripture puts his objection in twice, in his own words, rather than covering for him.

Which leaves the chapter resting exactly where it should. Everything that is about to happen in Egypt was promised in verses 6 to 8 by someone who needed no one's competence, and the last word before the plagues begin is a reluctant man's excuse — set against seven sentences that all start with I will and one that says I am the LORD.

6.theology:
Redemption is God's work. The seven "I wills" make every verb of salvation God's own. We are brought, delivered, redeemed, and taken — monergism written into the exodus.

The covenant relationship. "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" is the goal of redemption — not just rescue from bondage but belonging to God.

God's faithfulness over our unbelief. The people cannot believe, yet God will save. His promises rest on his character, not our capacity to receive them.
6.examples:
Then: To a people too broken by slavery to listen, God spoke seven sovereign "I wills," pledging to redeem them with an outstretched arm purely on the basis of his covenant.

Now: When our spirits are too crushed to believe the gospel, the ground of our hope is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of our Redeemer. His outstretched arm — Christ on the cross — has already secured the "I wills" of our salvation.

7.title: The Battle of the Gods Begins
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet.<sup>2</sup>You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land.<sup>3</sup>But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,<sup>4</sup>Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment.<sup>5</sup>The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."<sup>6</sup>Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them.<sup>7</sup>Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.<sup>8</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,<sup>9</sup>"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'"<sup>10</sup>So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.<sup>11</sup>Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts.<sup>12</sup>For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.<sup>13</sup>Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go.<sup>15</sup>Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent.<sup>16</sup>And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed.<sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood.<sup>18</sup>The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'"<sup>20</sup>Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood.<sup>21</sup>And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>23</sup>Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.<sup>24</sup>And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile.<sup>25</sup>Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
7.overview:
The plagues begin, and we must understand what they truly are: not random disasters but a systematic dismantling of the gods of Egypt. "On all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments," God says (12:12). Each plague topples a deity — the Nile that Egypt worshiped, the sun, the livestock, life itself. This is cosmic warfare: YHWH versus the entire pantheon of the world's greatest superpower, and it is no contest.

The chapter sets the terms. Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs — a sign that God's power consumes all counterfeits. Then the Nile, the very lifeblood of Egypt and an object of worship, turns to blood. The river that ran red with Hebrew infants' blood (1:22) now runs red in judgment. God repays in kind.

Threaded through it all is the refrain of Pharaoh's hardening and the divine purpose: "that the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." The plagues are not merely punitive; they are revelatory. Even in judgment, God is making himself known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Moses as God to Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. The hardening is named again, and the purpose of everything that follows is stated before a single plague falls: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.

Verses 6-7: They did just as the LORD commanded them — and the ages are given: Moses eighty, Aaron eighty-three.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Plagues Are an Answer to a Question

In 5:2 Pharaoh sneered, Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice? I do not know the LORD. Ten plagues are the reply. They are not a bargaining tactic escalating because the early rounds failed; they are a sustained and terrible answer to a man who said he did not know who he was talking to. And note who is meant to end up knowing — not Israel but the Egyptians. Even the judgment is aimed at making God known to the people it falls on.

Like God to Pharaoh

Elohim here is not flattery and does not make Moses divine. It places him in the position God occupies in a conversation: the one whose word simply stands, relayed by a prophet and meant to be obeyed. Pharaoh is a god by Egypt's reckoning, and he is about to deal with someone who outranks him in the only reckoning there is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After five objections across three chapters, the narrator disposes of Moses' reluctance in a single sentence. He went.

Now: Eighty years old, and everything he is remembered for is still ahead of him. Forty years in Egypt produced a fugitive and forty in Midian produced a shepherd, and the work he was actually called to starts at an age when most men have finished. God's timing is not embarrassed by ours, and a life can be mostly over and entirely unspent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land. But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment. The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. The word is elohim, and it is not flattery. Moses is not being told he is divine; he is being placed in the position God occupies in a conversation — the one whose word simply stands, to be relayed by a prophet and obeyed. Pharaoh is a god in Egypt's reckoning. He is about to deal with someone who outranks him in the only reckoning that matters.

Then the purpose of everything that follows, stated before a single plague falls: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.

That is the answer to a question. In 5:2 Pharaoh had sneered, Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice? I do not know the LORD. Ten plagues are the reply. They are not a bargaining tactic that escalates because the early rounds failed; they are a sustained, patient, terrible answer to a man who said he did not know who he was talking to. And note who is supposed to end up knowing — not Israel, but the Egyptians. Even the judgment is aimed at making God known to the people it falls on.

The hardening is named again here, as it was at 4:21, and Scripture will go on saying it both ways throughout — Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and God hardens Pharaoh's heart — without resolving the tension for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them. Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them. After five objections across three chapters — who am I, what is your name, they will not believe me, I cannot speak, please send someone else — the narrator disposes of Moses' reluctance in one sentence. He went.

And then the detail the storyteller has been saving: Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh.

Eighty. Everything Moses is remembered for is still ahead of him. The forty years in Egypt produced a fugitive; the forty in Midian produced a shepherd; and the work God actually called him to begins at an age when most men have finished. Whatever else the arithmetic of this verse means, it means that God's timing is not embarrassed by ours, and that a life can be mostly over and entirely unspent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 8-10: Pharaoh will demand a credential, and Aaron's staff becomes a serpent — this time a tannin, not the nachash of chapter 4.

Verses 11-13: The magicians duplicate the sign by their secret arts — but Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs, and Pharaoh's heart was hardened.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Dragon on the Throne-Room Floor

The change of word carries the scene. Tannin is a darker term than the ordinary word for snake — used of sea-monsters and the chaos-creatures God is said to have crushed, and used by Ezekiel of this very king: Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, "My Nile is my own" (Ezek. 29:3). The sign performed in front of the throne is a picture of the throne.

The Counterfeit Can Copy and Cannot Survive

Egypt's magicians match the sign — and Aaron's staff eats theirs. That is the whole contest in one image before a plague has fallen. They manage two more rounds, then tell Pharaoh this is the finger of God (8:19), and finally cannot even stand in his presence for the boils on their own skin (9:11). Paul knew their names: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth... But they will not get very far (2 Tim. 3:8-9). Opposition to God can often reproduce the effect. It has never held the ground.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scripture does not pause to explain what the magicians were doing — sleight of hand, real dark power, or both. It simply declines to be impressed.

Now: A thing can be genuinely supernatural and still be worthless. The test Exodus applies to the magicians is not whether they can produce an effect but whether what they produce can stand. It is the same test the New Testament applies, and it is why they will not get very far is the whole of Paul's anxiety about them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'" So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh will ask for a credential — Prove yourselves by working a miracle — and God supplies the answer before the question is put. Aaron throws down the staff and it becomes a serpent.

One word has changed since chapter 4, and it carries the scene. There the staff became a nachash, the ordinary word for a snake. Here it becomes a tannin — a bigger, darker word, used in the Old Testament for sea-monsters and dragons, the chaos-creatures God is said to have crushed. It is also, pointedly, the word Ezekiel puts on the king of Egypt himself: Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams, that says, "My Nile is my own" (Ezek. 29:3).

So the sign performed on the throne-room floor is a picture of the throne. A dragon appears in front of Pharaoh, and everyone in the room is about to see what happens to it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts. For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs. Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magicians match it. They also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same by their secret arts. For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. Whatever is going on here — sleight of hand, real dark power, or both — Scripture does not pause to explain it, and it does not treat the imitation as impressive.

Because of what happens next: But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.

That is the whole contest in one image, before the plagues have even begun. Egypt's power can copy the sign. It cannot survive it. The counterfeit is real enough to produce a serpent and useless enough to be eaten, and the magicians will manage two more rounds before they are reduced to telling Pharaoh this is the finger of God (8:19) and then dropping out of the story altogether, unable even to stand in his presence because of the boils on their own skin (9:11).

Paul knew their names. Writing to Timothy about men who oppose the truth with a counterfeit version of it, he reaches for this scene: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth... But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men (2 Tim. 3:8-9). It is a fair summary of Exodus 7. Opposition to God is often able to reproduce the effect. It has never once been able to hold the ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-25 — The Nile Turned to Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14-18: Moses meets Pharaoh at the water's edge in the morning. The first plague is announced before it lands, with the demand attached: Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness.

Verses 19-21: Every water in Egypt turns to blood. The fish die, the Nile stank, and the Egyptians could not drink from it.

Verses 22-25: The magicians did the same by their secret arts; Pharaoh did not take even this to heart; the people dig along the riverbank for water; and seven full days passed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Nile First

Because Egypt is the Nile. The country has almost no rainfall; the annual flood lays down black silt, and that is the entire basis of Egyptian agriculture, wealth and empire. They worshipped the river as the god Hapi. To strike it is to go for the throat of everything Egypt trusts.

And an old account is being settled. It was into this river that Pharaoh commanded every Hebrew boy be thrown (1:22). Egypt filled the Nile with the blood of children; the first thing God does is turn the Nile to blood. The punishment is shaped like the crime, which is how God's judgments generally are.

Two First Signs

The greater Deliverer also began with water in jars, at a village wedding — and turned it into wine so the celebration could continue and a poor family would not be shamed (John 2:1-11). Both are opening signs, both transform ordinary water, and together they measure the distance between the covenants: the first sign of the exodus turns water to blood and a nation cannot drink; the first sign of Christ turns water to wine and the feast is saved. He came to the same element and did the opposite with it, because he had come to bear the judgment rather than pour it out.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Consider what the magicians' achievement actually amounts to. The country's water is already undrinkable; the one thing Egypt needs is someone who can turn blood back into water; and its finest religious technicians produce a demonstration that they too can ruin a bucket. They made the disaster marginally worse to save face.

Now: Seven full days passed. Scripture times it, and the timing is mercy — a week in which Pharaoh could have changed his mind, with the offer of verse 16 standing the whole time. God's judgments have gaps in them, and the gaps are not lapses in his attention. They are room to repent. Nine more will come, each announced in advance, each with a door left open, until a king asked politely in chapter 5 has been asked ten times and said no ten times.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent. And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed. Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood. The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Moses to intercept Pharaoh at the water's edge in the morning, and the first plague is announced before it lands. Nothing here is a surprise attack; every plague comes with a warning and a demand attached — Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness.

Why the Nile first? Because Egypt is the Nile. The country has almost no rainfall; the river floods each year, lays down black silt, and that is the entire basis of Egyptian agriculture, wealth and empire. They worshipped it as the god Hapi and called the inundation his gift. To strike the Nile is not to inconvenience Egypt. It is to go for the throat of everything Egypt trusts.

And there is an older account being settled. It was into this river that Pharaoh commanded every Hebrew boy to be thrown (1:22). Egypt filled the Nile with the blood of children, and the first thing God does is turn the Nile to blood. The punishment is shaped like the crime, which is how God's judgments generally are.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'" Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood. And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plague is total. Not just the river but their canals, their ponds, and all their pools of water — even, the text says, the water already drawn and standing in wooden and stone vessels indoors.

Then the consequences, and the narrator records them in the order a person standing there would notice them. The fish in the Nile died. A staple food supply gone in a day. And the Nile stank. The great river of the world, the pride of the empire, reduced to a stench that carried across the whole country. And the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile.

Set that beside another first sign.
