When the greater Deliverer began his public work he also started with water in jars, at a village celebration, and what he did with it was turn it into wine so that a wedding could keep going and the poor family hosting it would not be shamed (John 2:1-11). Both are opening signs; both take ordinary water and transform it; and the two together map the distance between the covenants. The first sign of the exodus turns water to blood, and a nation cannot drink. The first sign of the Lord Jesus turns water to wine, and the party is saved. He came to the same element and did the opposite thing with it, because he had come to bear the judgment rather than to pour it out.

verseByVerse.quote: But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart. And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile. Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magicians rise to the occasion one last time, and what they do is quietly absurd: the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts.

Think about what that achievement consists of. The country's water is already undrinkable. The one thing Egypt needs is someone who can turn blood back into water, and what its finest religious technicians produce is a demonstration that they too can ruin a bucket. They have made the disaster marginally worse in order to save face. That is the exact reach of every power set against God: it can add to the misery, and it has never been able to undo any of it.

So Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart, while his people dug along the riverbank for drinking water — the ordinary Egyptians on their knees in the mud, paying for their king's pride, as ordinary people generally do.

And then: Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile. A whole week. Scripture times it, and the timing is mercy — a week in which Pharaoh could have changed his mind, and the offer of verse 16 still stood the entire time. God's judgments have gaps in them, and the gaps are not gaps in his attention. They are room to repent. Nine more plagues will come, each one announced in advance, each one with a door left open, until a king who was asked politely in chapter 5 has been asked ten times and has said no ten times, and no one in Egypt or Israel or anywhere since can claim he was not given the chance.

7.theology:
The LORD over all gods. The plagues are judgments on the gods of Egypt (12:12). YHWH alone is God; every idol is exposed as powerless.

The hardening of the heart. Pharaoh hardens himself, and God hardens Pharaoh — a mystery Scripture holds together (Rom. 9). Human rebellion and divine sovereignty are both fully true.

Judgment as revelation. "That they may know that I am the LORD." Even God's acts of judgment serve to make his glory known.
7.examples:
Then: God began systematically to dismantle the gods of the world's greatest empire, turning its worshiped river to blood and swallowing the magicians' counterfeits, while Pharaoh hardened his heart.

Now: Our culture's idols — wealth, power, self — are no more able to save than Egypt's Nile. God still exposes every counterfeit and calls every heart to know that he alone is the LORD. The question is whether we will be softened or, like Pharaoh, hardened.

8.title: Escalating Judgment and a Line Drawn
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>2</sup>But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs.<sup>3</sup>The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls.<sup>4</sup>The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'"<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'"<sup>6</sup>So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.<sup>8</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.<sup>11</sup>The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."<sup>12</sup>So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh.<sup>13</sup>And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.<sup>14</sup>And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank.<sup>15</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'"<sup>17</sup>And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.<sup>18</sup>The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast.<sup>19</sup>Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>21</sup>Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand.<sup>22</sup>But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.<sup>23</sup>Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.<sup>25</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land."<sup>26</sup>But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?<sup>27</sup>We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us."<sup>28</sup>So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me."<sup>29</sup>Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained.<sup>32</sup>But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
8.overview:
The plagues escalate — frogs, gnats, flies — and two great themes come into focus. First, the incomparability of God: "that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God." Pharaoh's magicians can produce frogs but cannot remove them; soon they cannot even reproduce the plague of gnats and are forced to confess, "This is the finger of God." The counterfeit power of darkness reaches its limit and collapses before the living God.

Second, the distinction God makes between his people and the world. With the plague of flies, God sets apart Goshen, where Israel dwells, so that no swarms come there. This "making a difference" between Israel and Egypt is one of the great themes of the exodus: God knows his own and protects them in the day of judgment. As Ferguson observes, the God who pours out wrath also shelters his people from it — a foreshadowing of the Passover and, beyond it, of the cross where Christ bore the judgment so that none should fall on us.

Pharaoh begins to bargain — "sacrifice within the land," "do not go very far" — the classic half-repentance of a hard heart that wants relief without surrender.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-15 — Frogs and a Hollow Repentance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-7: Frogs come up over the whole land — into houses, bedrooms, beds, ovens and kneading bowls — and the magicians duplicate the sign.

Verses 8-11: Pharaoh asks for prayer for the first time. Moses lets him name the hour, and he says Tomorrow.

Verses 12-15: The frogs die and are heaped up, and the land stank. But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second God Struck

Frogs swarmed out of the Nile as the flood receded, and Egypt had a goddess for it — Heqet, frog-headed, invoked at childbirth and for the fertility of the land. She was a comfort. God gives Egypt so much of her that they cannot cross a room.

Relief Is Not Rescue

The word respite does precise work. Pharaoh never asked for God; he asked for the frogs to stop, and the moment the pressure lifted so did the promise. That is the commonest form of false repentance and the easiest to mistake for the real thing: trouble makes a man pray, and the prayer is genuine while the trouble lasts. The test is never what is said under the pressure. It is what is done in the respite.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses lets Pharaoh set the time so that when the frogs die on schedule nobody can call it coincidence — that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.

Now: Tomorrow. He could have said now; the frogs are in his bed; he is offered an end at a time of his own choosing and picks one more night in it. That answer does not need explaining so much as recognising. People do prefer a familiar misery to a deliverance that will cost them something. Pharaoh's tomorrow is the whole psychology of delayed repentance in one word, and Scripture has been answering it ever since — behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs. The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls. The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'" And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'" So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second plague comes with the same demand and the same warning, and it strikes the second thing Egypt worshipped. Frogs emerged from the Nile in vast numbers as the flood receded, and Egypt had a goddess for it — Heqet, shown with a frog's head, invoked at childbirth and for the fertility of the land. She was a comfort. God gives Egypt so much of her that they cannot walk across a room.

Notice where they go. Not merely into the fields: into your house, into your bedroom, on your bed, into the houses of your servants and your people, into your ovens and your kneading bowls. The list moves relentlessly inward, from the country to the house to the bedroom to the bed — and then into the food. There is nowhere in Egypt left to be clean, and nowhere for Pharaoh himself to sleep undisturbed.

And the magicians rise to it again: the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt. For the second time their contribution to a national emergency is to produce more of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD." Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile." And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then something happens that has not happened before. Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go."

The man who asked Who is the LORD? is now asking for prayer to him by name. It is the first crack, and Moses presses it in a curious way: Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you... that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. He lets Pharaoh set the time, so that when the frogs die on schedule nobody can call it coincidence.

And Pharaoh answers with the strangest word in the chapter. Tomorrow.

He could have said now. The frogs are in his bed. He is offered an end to it at a time of his own choosing and he chooses to spend one more night in it. Nobody has ever fully explained that answer, and it does not need explaining so much as recognising, because it is not rare. People do prefer a familiar misery to a deliverance that will cost them something, and they will take one more night of it rather than face what the morning would require. Pharaoh's tomorrow is the whole psychology of delayed repentance in a single word, and Scripture has been answering it ever since: Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh. And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields. And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank. But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses prays, and the frogs die exactly as arranged — and the narrator will not spare us the aftermath: And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank. Deliverance in Egypt smells terrible. The plague ends and the country spends days shovelling up the evidence.

Then the verse the chapter turns on: But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.

He kept his word about nothing. The moment the pressure lifted, so did the promise. And the word respite is doing precise work — it was relief, not rescue, and relief was all he had ever wanted. He never asked for God; he asked for the frogs to stop.

That is the most common form of false repentance and the easiest to mistake for the real thing. Trouble makes a man pray, and the prayer is genuine while the trouble lasts. The test is never what is said under the pressure. It is what is done in the respite.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-19: The third plague arrives with no warning: the dust of the earth becomes gnats on man and beast. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not, and they tell Pharaoh, This is the finger of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Finger of God

Three times the magicians matched Moses. This time they fail, and it is the last useful thing they do — by chapter 9 they cannot stand in Pharaoh's presence for the boils on their own skin.

Their phrase has one striking afterlife. Accused of casting out demons by the prince of demons, Jesus said: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Luke 11:20). He is quoting Egypt's beaten sorcerers. The finger that made gnats out of dust, and later wrote the commandments on stone (31:18), was at work in a Galilean village setting people free — and the sign that the kingdom had arrived was the same sign that once told a court of professionals they were out of their depth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Egypt was a scrupulously clean culture — its priests shaved their whole bodies and washed repeatedly to stay fit to approach the gods. Now the ground itself produces vermin that settle on man and beast, and every priest in the country is disqualified.

Now: The magicians are honest professionals. They try, they fail, and they go straight to the king with the verdict. There is something almost admirable in it, and it makes Pharaoh's response worse: his own experts tell him what he is dealing with, and he does not listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'" And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast. Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third plague comes with no warning at all — the first of the series to arrive unannounced — and it comes out of the dust. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt. Egypt was a scrupulously clean culture, its priests shaving their entire bodies and washing repeatedly to remain fit to approach the gods. Now the ground itself is producing vermin that settle on man and beast, and every priest in the country is disqualified.

And here the contest turns. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. Three times they have matched Moses. This time they fail, and being honest professionals they go straight to the king with the verdict: This is the finger of God.

They are more right than they know, and it is the last useful thing they do; by chapter 9 they cannot even stand up in Pharaoh's presence because of the boils on their own skin.

That phrase has one striking afterlife. Standing among people who accused him of casting out demons by the prince of demons, Jesus said: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (Luke 11:20). He is quoting Egypt's beaten magicians. The finger that produced gnats out of the dust of the earth, and that later wrote the commandments on stone (31:18), was at work in a Galilean village setting people free — and the sign that the kingdom had arrived was the same sign that had once told a court of professional sorcerers they were out of their depth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-32 — Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 20-24: Swarms of flies, and something new — I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell. A division is put between the two peoples.

Verses 25-29: Pharaoh begins to negotiate: sacrifice within the land; then only you must not go very far. Moses refuses the first and warns against another cheat.

Verses 30-32: Moses prays, not one remained — and Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Line Drawn Through a Country

Until now the plagues fell on everybody. From here God distinguishes, and states why: so that Pharaoh may know he is the LORD in the midst of the earth — not a local god of the Hebrews confined to their quarter, but sovereign over the whole map, choosing where his hand falls. It is uncomfortable to read and Scripture does not soften it. The division is not arbitrary and not ethnic: it is the mark of a people God has claimed, and Egypt is shown by geography what it refused to hear in words.

Mercy That Keeps Being Offered

God knows exactly what Pharaoh will do with the relief — he has said so in advance — and he lifts the flies anyway, completely, because Moses asked. Mercy is not a negotiating position withdrawn when it fails to work. It goes on being offered to a man who has already shown what he does with it, which is what mercy has always been like: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses refuses to sacrifice inside Egypt for a shrewd reason — the Hebrews would be killing animals the Egyptians held sacred, in full view: will they not stone us? Worship a surrounding culture finds abominable cannot be conducted in the middle of it as though nothing were at stake.

Now: List Pharaoh's offers, because the shape repeats through chapter 10 with leave your children and leave your flocks. Go, but not out. Go, but not far. Go, but leave something behind as security that you are coming back. It is never a flat refusal, which could be recognised and resisted. It is always a slight adjustment to terms that were God's to set.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand. But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth. Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'" And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth plague introduces something new, and it is the detail to hold on to: But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth. Thus I will put a division between my people and your people.

Until now the plagues have fallen on everybody. From here God draws a line through the country. The word for set apart is the language of distinction — and the point is stated: so that Pharaoh may know that the LORD is not a local god of the Hebrews confined to their quarter, but the LORD in the midst of the earth, sovereign over the whole map, choosing where his hand falls and where it does not.

It should be said honestly that this is uncomfortable to read, and Scripture does not soften it. Two peoples in one country, and the swarms go to one house and not the next. But the division is not arbitrary and it is not ethnic: it is the mark of a people God has claimed, and Egypt is being shown by geography what it refused to hear in words. The land was ruined by the flies — and four miles away, nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land." But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us? We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us." So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me." Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Pharaoh begins to negotiate, and his offers are worth listing because they set the pattern for the rest of the contest. First: Go, sacrifice to your God within the land. Stay in Egypt and worship here.

Moses refuses, and his reason is practical and shrewd. The Hebrews would be sacrificing animals the Egyptians held sacred — the bull, the ram — and doing it in front of them: if we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us? Worship that the surrounding culture finds abominable cannot be conducted in the middle of that culture as though nothing were at stake.

So Pharaoh moves to his second offer: I will let you go... only you must not go very far. Then a third condition — Plead for me. And Moses, agreeing, adds the warning that has already proved necessary: only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go.

The shape of these compromises is the same every time, and it will continue in chapter 10 with leave your children and leave your flocks. Go, but not out. Go, but not far. Go, but leave something behind as security that you are coming back. It is never a refusal, which could be recognised and resisted. It is always a slight adjustment to the terms — and the terms were God's.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD. And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained. But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses prays, God does exactly what Moses asked — not one remained — and the chapter closes on the sentence we have already read once: But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.

This time also. The narrator is counting. Twice now Pharaoh has asked for prayer, been answered precisely, and gone back on his word the moment he could breathe. He is not being worn down; he is being revealed, and each round shows the same thing more clearly than the last.

And God keeps answering the prayers. That is the part worth stopping on. He knows exactly what Pharaoh will do with the relief — he has said so in advance — and he lifts the flies anyway, in full, not one remaining, because Moses asked him to. Mercy here is not a negotiating position that gets withdrawn when it fails to work. It goes on being offered to a man who has already established what he does with it, which is what mercy has always been like, and why God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8).

8.theology:
The incomparability of God. "There is no one like the LORD our God." The plagues expose every rival as powerless; even the magicians confess "the finger of God."

Distinguishing grace. God sets apart Goshen, sheltering his people in the day of judgment — a foreshadowing of Passover and the cross.

The hardened heart and false repentance. Pharaoh repents only of consequences, bargains for partial obedience, and hardens again when relief comes.
8.examples:
Then: As plagues escalated, Egypt's magicians confessed defeat, God shielded his people in Goshen, and Pharaoh offered the half-repentance and compromised obedience typical of a hardened heart.

Now: The world still offers God a partial obedience — "don't go too far." But God draws a line between his people and the world, and in Christ he shelters us wholly from the judgment to come. He calls not for bargaining but for surrender.

9.title: That My Name May Be Proclaimed in All the Earth

All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh.<sup>9</sup>It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast.<sup>11</sup>And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>14</sup>For this time I and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth.<sup>16</sup>But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'"<sup>20</sup>Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses,<sup>21</sup>but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt."<sup>23</sup>Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt.<sup>24</sup>There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.<sup>25</sup>The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field.<sup>26</sup>Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.<sup>27</sup>Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong.<sup>28</sup>Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer."<sup>29</sup>Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's.<sup>30</sup>But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."<sup>31</sup>(The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.<sup>32</sup>But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.)<sup>33</sup>So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth.<sup>34</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants.<sup>35</sup>So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
9.overview:
The plagues intensify toward life and death: livestock die, boils break out on man and beast, and then comes the devastating hail, the worst storm Egypt has ever seen. Again God distinguishes — no plague touches Goshen, and those Egyptians who fear the word of the LORD are spared by bringing their cattle indoors. Even among the Egyptians, the fear of God begins to bear fruit.

At the center of the chapter stands one of the most theologically weighty verses in all Scripture, quoted by Paul in Romans 9:17: "For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth." Here is the ultimate purpose of Pharaoh's existence and the plagues' fury — the worldwide proclamation of God's name and power. Pharaoh is a vessel through whom God displays his glory. Sproul taught that this verse forces us to reckon with the absolute sovereignty of God over even the most hardened rebel.

Pharaoh utters his fullest confession yet — "I have sinned; the LORD is in the right" — but it dissolves the moment the hail stops. Words of repentance without a changed heart are worthless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-7: A plague on the livestock, with a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt. Pharaoh investigates, finds not one Israelite animal dead — and hardens his heart.

Verses 8-12: Soot from a kiln thrown into the air becomes boils on man and beast. The magicians could not stand before Moses, and for the first time the text says the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Striking the Pantheon

Egypt's gods were largely animal — Apis the sacred bull of Memphis, Hathor the cow-goddess, Khnum the ram. A plague on cattle is an economic blow, but it is first a strike through the middle of the pantheon, killing the creatures the gods were thought to inhabit.

The Order of the Hardening

Through five plagues the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart. From the sixth, God is named as the one who does it. Scripture is careful about the order and it matters: a man spent five rounds making himself into something, and then God confirmed him in what he had made himself. That is not God overriding a will that wanted to repent. It is a settled character being sealed, and it is the most frightening thing in the book.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A kiln is where the bricks were fired. Moses takes a handful of the ash of Israel's slavery and throws it into the wind in front of the king who ordered it — the instrument of their suffering becoming the instrument of his judgment.

Now: Pharaoh checks. He sends investigators, gets an unambiguous result, and hardens anyway. That is worse than ignorance, and the narrator means it to be. He is not a man lacking evidence; he is a man for whom evidence has stopped being the deciding factor — a condition no further evidence can cure.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them, behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock that are in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks. But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing of all that belongs to the people of Israel shall die."'" And the LORD set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land." And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died. And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth plague falls on the herds, and it is aimed with the same precision as the others. Egypt's gods were largely animal: Apis the sacred bull of Memphis, Hathor the cow-goddess, Khnum the ram. A plague on cattle is not merely an economic blow, though it is that. It is a strike through the middle of the Egyptian pantheon, killing the creatures in which the gods were thought to be present.

Twice now the text has flagged the separation, and here it is exact: the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt. Pharaoh, to his credit, checks — And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. He conducts an investigation, receives an unambiguous result, and hardens his heart anyway.

That is worse than ignorance and the narrator means it to be. He is not a man who lacks evidence. He is a man for whom evidence has stopped being the deciding factor, which is a condition no further evidence can cure.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh. It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt." So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast. And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians. But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sixth plague is the first to strike Egyptian bodies, and the way it is delivered is deliberate theatre. Moses takes soot from a kiln and throws it into the air in front of Pharaoh.

A kiln is where the bricks were fired. Moses takes a handful of the ash of Israel's slavery, and the instrument of their suffering becomes the instrument of Egypt's judgment, scattered on the wind in front of the king who ordered it.

Then the sentence that finishes the magicians: And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians. They opened the contest by matching him staff for staff. They end it unable to remain upright in the same room, and they are never mentioned again.

And here, for the first time in the narrative, the phrasing turns: But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh. Through five plagues the text has said Pharaoh hardened his own heart. From the sixth, God is named as the one who does it. The order matters and Scripture is careful about it. A man spent five rounds making himself into something, and then God confirmed him in what he had made himself. That is not God overriding a will that wanted to repent. It is a settled character being sealed — and it is the most frightening thing in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — The Warning and the God-Fearers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: Before the hail, God explains himself: For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. He warns Egypt to shelter its livestock, and whoever feared the word of the LORD among Pharaoh's servants did so.
verseByVerse.theology:
Raised Up for a Purpose

Paul quotes verse 16 directly (Rom. 9:17). Note what God says he is doing: not merely defeating Pharaoh but making him a demonstration so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. It worked. Rahab knew this story a generation later and it was why she hid the spies (Josh. 2:10); Philistines were still talking about it centuries on (1 Sam. 4:8). The most famous unbeliever in the Old Testament became the world's advertisement for the God he refused.

Every Plague Short of the Tenth Is a Restraint

By now I could have put out my hand and struck you... and you would have been cut off from the earth. Egypt is not being destroyed as fast as it could be.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God tells his enemies how to survive the next plague — send, get your livestock... into safe shelter — and some of them listen.

Now: Keep those God-fearing Egyptians in view, because they do not disappear. When Israel finally leaves, a mixed multitude also went up with them (12:38): people who were not Israelites by birth, walking out under the same blood. The line God draws through this country does not finally run between nations. It runs between those who feared his word and those who did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. You are still exalting yourself against my people and will not let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the seventh plague God makes a speech, and it is the theological centre of the whole contest. For this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.

Paul quotes that verse directly (Rom. 9:17) when he is arguing that God's mercy does not depend on human willing or running. And note what God says he is doing with Pharaoh: not merely defeating him but making him a demonstration — so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. It worked. Rahab in Jericho knew this story a generation later and it was why she hid the spies (Josh. 2:10); Philistines were still talking about it centuries afterwards (1 Sam. 4:8). The most famous unbeliever in the Old Testament became the world's advertisement for the God he refused.

And God says something else here that should not be missed: By now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. Egypt is not being destroyed as fast as it could be. Every plague short of the tenth is a restraint, not an escalation.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, about this time tomorrow I will cause very heavy hail to fall, such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now. Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'" Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses, but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the mercy inside the warning. God announces heavy hail for the next day and adds: Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter. He tells his enemies how to survive the next plague. And some of them listen — whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses. Egyptians, inside Pharaoh's own administration, who had begun to take God at his word.

Keep those men in view, because they do not disappear. When Israel finally walks out, the text is careful to say that a mixed multitude also went up with them (12:38) — people who were not Israelites by birth leaving Egypt under the same blood. The line God draws through this country turns out not to run simply between nations. It runs between those who feared the word of the LORD and those who did not, and it was always going to end with people from every nation walking out under a Passover they had no ancestral claim to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — Hail and a Confession That Melts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 22-26: Hail with fire flashing continually in it — the worst storm in Egypt's history — striking everything in the open. Only in the land of Goshen... was there no hail.

Verses 27-35: Pharaoh's fullest confession: I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Moses answers that he still does not fear God — and when the storm stops, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart. The flax and barley are destroyed; the wheat and emmer, being late, survive.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Earth Is the LORD's

Moses will pray so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's — not the Nile, not Goshen, but the earth. Pharaoh's theology assumed a world carved into jurisdictions with a god over each patch. The hail teaches him there are no patches, and Paul reaches for the same conviction: the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof (1 Cor. 10:26).

Two Kinds of Sorrow

Pharaoh uses the name, confesses sin, declares God righteous and himself guilty. If words were the measure it would be a conversion. But look at his sentence: there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. He wants the noise to stop. This is worldly grief, which produces death, against godly grief that produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor. 7:10). The difference is not sincerity in the moment — he probably meant it while the hail fell. The difference is what remains when the weather clears.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Nut was the sky goddess, Set the god of storms, Osiris the god of crop and vegetation. All of them are silent while the sky opens, and weather obeys a border no natural explanation can account for.

Now: One detail is easy to pass over and quietly devastating: the flax and barley are destroyed, but the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up. Egypt still has a harvest standing. The narrator mentions it because the locusts will eat it in the next chapter — so Pharaoh was handed both a warning and an inventory of exactly what he still had to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt." Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt. There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field. Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hail comes with fire running down inside it — the narrator says it twice, fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail — and it is the worst storm in Egypt's recorded history: such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.

It strikes what is standing in the open: man, beast, every plant, every tree. Nut was the sky goddess, Set the god of storms, Osiris the god of crop and vegetation. All of them are silent while the sky opens.

And again the exemption: Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail. The country is being systematically dismantled in one place and not touched in the other, and no natural explanation is available for weather that obeys a border.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer." Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's. But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh's response is his fullest yet, and on the face of it, it is repentance: This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail.

He uses the name. He confesses sin. He declares God righteous and himself guilty. If words were the measure, that is a conversion.

Moses is not fooled for a moment: But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God. And he is right — the confession will last exactly as long as the storm.

Read his sentence again and the flaw is visible in it: there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. He wants the noise to stop. He is not seeking God; he is seeking quiet, and he will say whatever the moment requires to get it. This is worldly grief, which produces death, as against the godly grief that produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Cor. 7:10). The difference is not the sincerity of the feeling in the moment — Pharaoh probably meant it while the hail was falling. The difference is what remains when the weather clears.

Moses' own answer contains the sentence the chapter has been building toward. He will pray, he says, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's. Not the Nile, not Goshen, not the territory the Hebrews occupy — the earth. Pharaoh's whole theology assumed a world carved into jurisdictions with a god over each patch. What the hail is teaching him is that there are no patches. Paul reaches for the same conviction when he tells the Corinthians they may eat what is set before them, for the earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof (1 Cor. 10:26). There is no ground anywhere that belongs to anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: (The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud. But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.) So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth. But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants. So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so it proves: when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart — he and his servants together.

There is one more detail, easy to pass over and quietly devastating: the flax and the barley were struck down... but the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up. Egypt still has a wheat harvest standing in the fields. The narrator mentions it because in the very next chapter the locusts will eat it. God struck the early crop and left the late one, and Pharaoh was given both a warning and an inventory of exactly what he still had to lose.

9.theology:
The sovereignty of God in hardening. The LORD himself now hardens Pharaoh (v. 12), and declares Pharaoh exists for the display of God's power (v. 16; Rom. 9:17).

The glory of God as the goal of all things. "That my name may be proclaimed in all the earth" is the supreme purpose behind the plagues and behind history itself.

The futility of false repentance. Pharaoh's perfect confession melts when the pressure lifts. Words without a changed heart save no one.
9.examples:
Then: God brought Egypt to its knees with disease and the worst hailstorm in its history, declaring that even Pharaoh existed to display God's power and proclaim his name in all the earth.

Now: God still governs even the hardest hearts toward the proclamation of his glory. And we are warned: it is possible to confess sin with flawless words in a crisis and remain unchanged. True repentance bears fruit when the storm has passed.

10.title: Darkness Over the Land
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them,<sup>2</sup>and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD."<sup>3</sup>So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>4</sup>For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country,<sup>5</sup>and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field,<sup>6</sup>and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.<sup>7</sup>Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?"<sup>8</sup>So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?"<sup>9</sup>Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD."<sup>10</sup>But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind.<sup>11</sup>No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left."<sup>13</sup>So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts.<sup>14</sup>The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again.<sup>15</sup>They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt.<sup>16</sup>Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me."<sup>18</sup>So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.<sup>21</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt."<sup>22</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.<sup>23</sup>They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.<sup>24</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind."<sup>25</sup>But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.<sup>26</sup>Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there."<sup>27</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go.<sup>28</sup>Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die."<sup>29</sup>Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
10.overview:
The eighth and ninth plagues — locusts and darkness — push Egypt toward the brink of un-creation. The locusts devour everything the hail left, stripping the land bare; then comes a darkness "to be felt," three days of thick blackness that strikes at Ra, the sun-god, the chief deity of Egypt. The God who said "Let there be light" now says, in effect, let there be darkness — and the cosmos of Egypt unravels.

This darkness is profoundly significant. As Keller notes, it anticipates the darkness that would cover the land at Calvary, when from the sixth hour to the ninth, darkness fell as the true Firstborn bore the judgment of God. At Calvary the darkness fell not on God's enemies but on God's own Son, in our place. The plague of darkness in Egypt is a shadow of the deeper darkness Christ entered for us, so that we might have light — for "all the people of Israel had light where they lived."

Pharaoh's bargaining grows more desperate: leave the children, leave the livestock. But God will accept no partial exodus. He claims his people whole.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-6: God gives his reason — that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson — and threatens locusts beyond anything in living memory.

Verses 7-11: Pharaoh's own officials break: Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined? He offers the third compromise — the men may go, the children stay.

Verses 12-20: The locusts eat everything the hail left. Pharaoh makes his most religious confession yet, God removes them entirely, and he hardens again.
verseByVerse.theology:
Staged for an Audience Not Yet Born

The plagues are not only for breaking Egypt but for giving Israel a story to tell — to your son and your grandson, two generations down, people who will never see a plague or a Pharaoh. Israel's whole faith is about to become something handed across a dinner table.

The Pronoun That Gives Him Away

Pharaoh's confession in verse 16 is word-perfect: he names the sin, asks forgiveness, uses the covenant name. The tell is one small pronoun, twice — the LORD your God. After eight plagues he still will not say my. He wants the God of the Hebrews to lift the locusts and then go back to belonging to the Hebrews. And only this once gives away the rest: not repentance but a request for one more exemption.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The court is telling the king what the magicians told him in chapter 8 and what his own investigation told him in chapter 9. He is now the only man in Egypt still arguing.

Now: The third compromise looks generous and is a trap. A people whose children are held in Egypt will always come back to Egypt. Pharaoh understands something about worship that many miss — he does not need to abolish it, only to detach it from the next generation. Leave the children out of it, and within one lifetime there is nothing left to abolish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them, and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD." So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country, and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field, and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God states his reason for the whole sequence, and it is not what a reader expects. Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart... that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD.

The plagues are being staged for an audience not yet born. The point is not only to break Egypt but to give Israel a story to tell — and the command is to tell it to your son and your grandson, two generations down, to people who will never have seen a plague or a Pharaoh. Israel's whole faith is about to become something handed across a dinner table.

Then the threat: locusts, in a quantity such as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen. Egypt still has the wheat and emmer standing after the hail (9:32), and God has already told Pharaoh so. He knows exactly what is at stake and exactly what will take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?" So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?" Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind. No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh's own officials break first. How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined? The court is telling the king what the magicians told him in chapter 8 and what the investigation told him in chapter 9. He is now the only man in Egypt still arguing.

So Moses is called back, and Pharaoh opens with a question that sounds accommodating: Who are the ones going? Moses answers without an inch of margin: We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD.

And Pharaoh refuses precisely there: Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking. The third compromise, and the cleverest. Let the adults go and worship; leave the children behind.

It looks generous and it is a trap, because a people whose children are held hostage in Egypt will always come back to Egypt. Pharaoh understands something about worship that many people miss: he does not need to abolish it, only to detach it from the next generation. Leave the children out of it, and within one lifetime there is nothing left to abolish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left." So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts. The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again. They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt. Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you. Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me." So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD. And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt. But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts come on an east wind and the description is total: they covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained. What the hail spared, this finishes. Egypt now has nothing growing anywhere.

Pharaoh's confession this time is his most religious yet: I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you. Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me.

Every word is right. He names the sin, asks forgiveness, uses the covenant name. And the tell is one small pronoun repeated twice — the LORD your God. After eight plagues he still will not say my. He wants the God of the Hebrews to lift the locusts and then go back to belonging to the Hebrews. And the phrase only this once gives away the rest: this is not repentance but a request for one more exemption.

God removes the locusts by a wind so thorough that not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt, and Pharaoh hardens again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-29 — A Darkness to Be Felt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 21-23: A darkness to be felt covers Egypt for three days. They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place — but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.

Verses 24-29: The fourth compromise — the children may go, the livestock stay. Moses answers not a hoof shall be left behind. Pharaoh threatens him with death if he returns, and Moses agrees: I will not see your face again.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Plague Aimed at the Head of the Pantheon

Ra, the sun god, was Egypt's supreme deity, and Pharaoh was held to be his son and living image. For three days the sun does not rise, and the god the king claims to embody is simply absent.

Two Darknesses

Egypt sat in a blackness it could feel while Israel kept the light. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). And when the true exodus was accomplished, darkness came again — from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour (Matt. 27:45) — but it did not fall on Egypt while Israel stayed lit. It fell on the Son, so that the people dwelling in darkness could see a great light. Egypt sat in the dark because it would not have God; he entered a dark he did not deserve so that we would not have to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A darkness to be felt is worth taking literally — dense enough to have texture, to press on the skin. And the effect is one dreadful sentence: not a country in crisis but a country immobilised, every person alone where they stood when the light went out, for three days, unable to see whoever was beside them.

Now: Two things sit in Moses' refusal. Not a hoof — nothing of God's people stays behind, no deposit, no retainer held against the possibility of return. And we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there — obedience that has not yet been told what it will cost cannot sign anything away in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt." So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ninth plague needs no locust and no frog. Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt.

This is the one aimed straight at the head of the pantheon. Ra, the sun god, was Egypt's supreme deity, and Pharaoh was held to be his son and living image on earth. For three days the sun does not rise on Egypt, and the god the king claims to embody is simply absent.

The phrase a darkness to be felt is unusual and worth taking literally — a dark so dense it has texture, that presses on the skin. And the effect is given in one dreadful sentence: They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days. Not a country in crisis but a country immobilised, every person alone where they happened to be standing when the light went out, for three days, unable to see the person beside them.

But all the people of Israel had light where they lived. Same country, same sky, and across the border in Goshen the sun is up.

The book will not let the image go, and neither does the New Testament. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). And when the true exodus was accomplished, darkness came again — from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour (Matt. 27:45) — but this time it did not fall on Egypt while Israel kept the light. It fell on the Son, so that the people dwelling in darkness could see a great light. Egypt sat in a blackness it could feel because it would not have God. He entered a blackness he did not deserve so that we would not have to.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind." But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God. Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there." But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go. Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die." Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last negotiation, and Pharaoh has come a long way. Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind. The children may go. Just leave the animals.

It is the fourth compromise and the same principle as the third: keep something of theirs in Egypt and they must come back for it. Moses will not have it, and his refusal is one of the great lines in the book: Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there.

Two things are in that answer. The first is total: not a hoof. Nothing of God's people stays in Egypt — no deposit, no retainer, no small holding left behind against the possibility of return. The second is more searching: we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there. Moses cannot negotiate away resources whose use has not yet been disclosed to him. Obedience that has not yet been told what it will cost cannot sign away anything in advance.

Pharaoh ends the conversation with a threat — the day you see my face you shall die — and Moses accepts it: As you say! I will not see your face again. The negotiations are over. Nine plagues have failed and there is one left, and the next words Pharaoh speaks to Moses will be in the middle of the night with his own son dead.

10.theology:
The undoing of creation. Locusts and a tangible darkness reverse the order God established, dethroning Egypt's sun-god and showing the LORD's mastery over creation itself.

The darkness that prefigures Calvary. The three days of darkness anticipate the darkness over Golgotha, where the true Firstborn bore judgment so his people might have light.

Generational testimony. God designs the exodus to be retold to children and grandchildren, that every generation may know he is the LORD.
10.examples:
Then: God stripped Egypt bare with locusts and plunged it into a darkness that could be felt, dethroning the sun-god, while his people dwelt in light — yet Pharaoh still bargained and hardened.

Now: The darkness over Egypt points to the darkness over the cross, where Christ entered judgment for us. Those in him are children of light. And we, like Israel, are called to tell our children how the LORD has saved — that they too may know him.

11.title: The Announcement of the Last Plague
11.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely.<sup>2</sup>Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.<sup>4</sup>So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt,<sup>5</sup>and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle.<sup>6</sup>There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again.<sup>7</sup>But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.'<sup>8</sup>And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
11.overview:
This brief chapter is the hush before the storm — the solemn announcement of the tenth and final plague: the death of every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh's throne to the slave at the mill. It is the climactic judgment, the one that will finally break Pharaoh's grip. "Israel is my firstborn son," God had said (4:22); Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn, and now the firstborn of Egypt will fall.

This is the most sobering plague because it confronts us with the wages of sin: death. The judgment that falls on Egypt is the judgment that justice requires of all. And the only thing that will make a difference between Israel and Egypt on that terrible night is not Israel's merit — for Israel deserves death as much as Egypt — but the blood of a lamb. The next chapter will reveal the means of escape. Here we are simply told that the LORD "makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel."

As Ferguson reflects, this distinction is the heart of grace: not that some are better, but that some are covered. The firstborn of Egypt die; the firstborn of Israel live — because a substitute will die in their place. The shadow of the cross falls across this whole chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-3 — Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-3: Yet one plague more, after which Pharaoh will drive you away completely. Israel is to ask for silver and gold, and the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moses himself is now very great in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology:
Permission Becomes Expulsion

Nine times Pharaoh has been asked to release them. When it happens he will not grant permission but drive them out — a king who would not let them walk ends by throwing into the street the people he spent ten chapters refusing to lose.

The Back Wages

The silver and gold is the promise of 3:21-22 coming due, and it works because the LORD gave the people favor — God turns the hearts of the givers. Four centuries of unpaid labour, settled late, by a nation that could afford it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The man is named at the height of his standing: Moses was very great in the land of Egypt.

Now: Set that beside chapter 4. This is the fugitive with a price on his head who argued that nobody would believe him and that he could not speak — now the most respected man in the country outside the palace. God does not always answer an objection by refuting it. Sometimes he simply outlives it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely. Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry." And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
