Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely.

Note the escalation in that last phrase. Nine times Pharaoh has been asked to release them. When it finally happens he will not grant permission — he will drive them out, expelling the people he spent ten chapters refusing to lose. A king who would not let them walk will end up throwing them into the street.

Then the instruction about silver and gold, and the sentence that explains how it works: And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. This is the promise of 3:21-22 coming due — the back wages for four centuries of unpaid labour — and it happens because God turns the hearts of the givers, not because Israel is persuasive.

The chapter adds one more remarkable line: Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people. The fugitive with a price on his head, who protested that nobody would listen to him and that he could not speak, is now the most respected man in the country outside the palace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-8 — The Death of the Firstborn Announced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 4-8: The final warning: About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die — from Pharaoh's heir to the firstborn of the slave girl at the handmill. In Goshen, not a dog shall growl. Moses leaves in hot anger.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Two Ends of the Sentence

The firstborn of the man on the throne and the firstborn of the girl grinding grain in a back room are named together, deliberately. This judgment is not aimed at a class. It falls on a nation without regard to rank, and the slave girl's loss is recorded in the same breath as the king's.

It Should Not Be Softened

This is God announcing the death of children, and Scripture does not soften it. Two things belong alongside, and neither is an excuse. Egypt began this — the boys of Israel were thrown into the Nile by royal decree (1:22), and the account is settled in the coin Egypt chose. And a way of escape is about to be published to every household in the land, Egyptian or Hebrew, and anyone who takes it will live. That is precisely why a mixed multitude walks out with Israel (12:38).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: On the worst night in Egypt's history, in Goshen even the dogs are quiet.

Now: Moses leaves in hot anger — the only time his anger is recorded in the whole contest. It is not provoked by Pharaoh's cruelty to Israel but by his refusal of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle. There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again. But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.' And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses delivers the final warning, and it is the most terrible sentence in Exodus: About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle.

Take the two ends of that sentence seriously, because they are chosen deliberately. The firstborn of the man on the throne, and the firstborn of the girl grinding grain in a back room — the top and the bottom of Egyptian society, named together. Judgment here is not aimed at the rich or the powerful as a class. It falls on a whole nation without regard to rank, and the slave girl's loss is recorded in the same breath as the king's.

It should not be softened, and Scripture does not soften it. This is God announcing the death of children. Two things belong alongside it and neither is an excuse. The first is that Egypt began this: the boys of Israel were thrown into the Nile by royal decree (1:22), and the account is being settled in the coin Egypt chose. The second is that a way of escape is about to be published to every household in the land, Egyptian or Hebrew, and anyone who takes it will live — which is exactly why a mixed multitude walks out with Israel (12:38).

And then the distinction stated at its sharpest: But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel. On the worst night in Egypt's history, in Goshen even the dogs are quiet.

Moses leaves in hot anger — the only time his anger is recorded in this whole contest, and it is not at Pharaoh's cruelty to Israel but at his refusal of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-10: The chapter closes by restating the pattern: Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt — and the summary of nine chapters, the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Refusals Are the Mechanism

The word that in verse 9 is both the difficulty and the point. Pharaoh's refusal is not merely foreseen; it is put to use. God is not salvaging something from a setback — the refusals are how the wonders multiply, and the wonders are what will be told to the son and the grandson (10:2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything asked, every sign given, every door left open, every warning issued in advance — and the answer, ten times, was no.

Now: The narrative stops on the edge of the worst night in Egypt's history and does not go straight to it. What comes next is not the plague. It is a chapter about a lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt." Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes by restating what God said would happen and what did: Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt.

That word that is the difficulty and the point. Pharaoh's refusal is not merely foreseen; it is put to use. God is not salvaging something from a setback — the refusals are the mechanism by which the wonders multiply, and the wonders are what will be told to the son and the grandson (10:2).

And the last verse totals it up: Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land. That is the summary of nine chapters. Everything asked, every sign given, every door left open, every warning issued in advance — and the answer, ten times, was no.

The narrative stops here, on the edge of the worst night in Egypt's history, and does not go straight to it. What comes next is not the plague. It is a chapter about a lamb.

11.theology:
The wages of sin is death. The final plague confronts us with judgment in its starkest form. The death of the firstborn shows that sin's just penalty is death.

Distinguishing grace. God makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel — not by merit but, as ch. 12 reveals, by the blood of a substitute.

God's faithfulness to ancient promises. The plundering of Egypt fulfills the word given to Abraham four centuries earlier (Gen. 15:14).
11.examples:
Then: God announced the climactic judgment — the death of every firstborn — a judgment that exposed all Egypt, palace and hovel alike, and could be escaped only by the distinction God himself would make.

Now: The death of the firstborn confronts us with the truth that sin's wage is death and that none can escape on the basis of merit. The only distinction that saves is the blood of the Lamb — Christ, the true Firstborn, who died that we might live.

12.title: Christ Our Passover
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,<sup>2</sup>"This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.<sup>3</sup>Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household.<sup>4</sup>And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb.<sup>5</sup>Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats,<sup>6</sup>and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.<sup>7</sup>"Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.<sup>8</sup>They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it.<sup>9</sup>Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts.<sup>10</sup>And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn.<sup>11</sup>In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.<sup>12</sup>For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>"This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast.<sup>15</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.<sup>16</sup>On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you.<sup>17</sup>And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever.<sup>18</sup>In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.<sup>19</sup>For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land.<sup>20</sup>You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."<sup>21</sup>Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb.<sup>22</sup>Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning.<sup>23</sup>For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you.<sup>24</sup>You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.<sup>25</sup>And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service.<sup>26</sup>And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?'<sup>27</sup>you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped.<sup>28</sup>Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.<sup>29</sup>At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock.<sup>30</sup>And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead.<sup>31</sup>Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said.<sup>32</sup>Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"<sup>33</sup>The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead."<sup>34</sup>So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing.<sup>36</sup>And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children.<sup>38</sup>A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds.<sup>39</sup>And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves.<sup>40</sup>The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years.<sup>41</sup>At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.<sup>42</sup>It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.<sup>43</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it,<sup>44</sup>but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him.<sup>45</sup>No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it.<sup>46</sup>It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.<sup>47</sup>All the congregation of Israel shall keep it.<sup>48</sup>If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.<sup>49</sup>There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you."<sup>50</sup>All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron.<sup>51</sup>And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
12.overview:
We come now to the beating heart of the book — the Passover. Here the gospel is preached in shadow with such clarity that the apostle Paul can simply say, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7). On this night God delivers his people not by their strength, their worthiness, or their works, but by the blood of a lamb.

Consider the lamb: it must be without blemish, a male in its prime, set apart, slain at twilight, its blood applied to the doorposts, not a bone broken. Every detail points to Christ. He is the Lamb of God without spot or blemish (1 Pet. 1:19); his blood, applied to us by faith, turns away the wrath of God; "not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:36). The destroyer passes over every house marked by the blood. The Israelites inside were not safer than the Egyptians because they were better; they were safe because they were covered. Salvation is by substitution — a life for a life, the lamb for the firstborn.

As Sproul preached with trembling, the most important question that night was not "Are you an Israelite?" but "Is there blood on your door?" And the most important question now is not "Are you religious?" but "Are you covered by the blood of Christ?" This is the chapter that explains the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Lamb and the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: God resets the calendar — This month shall be for you the beginning of months.

Verses 3-6: A lamb per household, joined with a neighbour if the family is too small; without blemish, a male a year old; taken on the tenth day, kept until the fourteenth, and killed by the whole assembly at twilight.

Verses 7-11: The blood on the two doorposts and the lintel; the meal roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, eaten dressed to travel.

Verses 12-13: On all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments — and when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
verseByVerse.theology:
Counting From the Rescue

A nation's calendar tells it what its life is measured from. Israel had a year already; God moves its start to the night they were redeemed, so everything before is dated backwards from the lamb.

Four Days of Inspection

The animal lives with the family in full view, and any flaw has four days to show itself. Nothing is offered that has not been looked over. Centuries later a man rode into Jerusalem on the tenth of that month and was examined for four days by every authority in the nation — and the verdicts are on record: I find no guilt in him (John 18:38); this man has done nothing wrong (Luke 23:41); Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47).

When I See the Blood

The blood is a sign for you, but the seeing that matters is God's. Israel is not saved by looking at it, or feeling rightly about it, or understanding it. They are saved because God looks at it. Every family that night was as safe as the blood on its doorframe and no safer, and none could improve the position by being braver or more devout.

And pasach may carry the sense of covering or shielding as much as skipping past — God standing over the doorway. Either way this is not God overlooking sin. The house was passed over because a death had already happened at it. Judgement did not swerve; it landed on the lamb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The first act of Israel's worship has no temple, no priesthood and no altar. It is a lamb for a household, calibrated to appetite, arranged around a kitchen table.

Now: Note where the blood goes — on the outside of the house, where every neighbour could see it. A marked door was a public statement that the people inside believed a warning and had killed an animal on the strength of it. And note where it does not go: not on the threshold. The one part of the frame a foot would land on is left unmarked, because blood that saves a household is not walked on. Hebrews reaches for that exact horror — trampled underfoot the Son of God, and profaned the blood of the covenant (Heb. 10:29).

Everything the New Testament says about the cross is lying here in outline: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7); Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29); ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:19). It is the most sustained image in Scripture, and it starts in a doorway in Egypt with a bowl of blood and a bunch of hyssop.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, "This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first thing God does is reset the calendar. This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you. Israel had a year already, running from the autumn. God moves the start of it to the night they were redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household. And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb. Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is not administrative housekeeping. A nation's calendar tells it what its life is measured from, and from now on Israel counts from the rescue. Everything that happened before is dated backwards from the lamb.

Then the instructions, and they are strikingly domestic. Not a temple, not a priesthood, not an altar — a lamb for a household. If the household is too small for a whole animal, the family next door joins in, according to what each can eat. The first act of Israel's worship is arranged around a kitchen table and calibrated to appetite.

The lamb must be without blemish, a male a year old, and taken on the tenth day and kept until the fourteenth. Four days in the house. Long enough for everyone, including the children, to know exactly which animal it is — and it must be perfect, because what is offered for a life has to be worth a life.

Those four days are an inspection. The animal lives with the family, in full view, and any flaw would have four days to show itself. Nothing may be offered that has not been looked over.

Fifteen centuries later a man rode into Jerusalem on the tenth of that same month, and for the four days that followed he was examined in public by every authority in the nation — the chief priests, the Pharisees, the Sadducees, the Herodians — each group in turn trying to find something in him that would do as a charge. Every one of them failed, and the verdicts are on record. Pilate: I find no guilt in him (John 18:38). Herod sent him back the same. The thief beside him: this man has done nothing wrong (Luke 23:41). The centurion at the foot of the cross: Certainly this man was innocent (Luke 23:47). The lamb was inspected for four days and no blemish was found, exactly as the law required.

Then: the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight. The whole assembly. Every household kills its own; nobody has it done for them. In the same city at the same festival many centuries on, a crowd would find itself answering a governor about a different lamb, and the responsibility would again belong to everyone present.

The Hebrew behind at twilight is literally between the two evenings, and by the first century it was reckoned as the middle of the afternoon — the hour when the Passover lambs were killed in the temple, in their thousands, while the city waited to eat. It was at that hour, with the knives at work a few hundred yards away, that a man outside the wall cried out with a loud voice and gave up his spirit. Nobody planned the timing but God, and nobody in Jerusalem noticed it at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it. They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it. Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts. And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn. In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the heart of it. Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.

Notice where the blood goes. Not on the family, not on the food, not on an altar — on the outside of the house, where every neighbour walking past could see it. A marked door was a public statement that the people inside believed a warning and had killed an animal on the strength of it.

And notice what the blood is not. It is not a magic charm and it is not a reward for Israelite ancestry. God says exactly what it does: The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you. The blood is a sign for you — but the seeing that matters is God's. Israel is not saved by looking at the blood, or by feeling the right way about it, or by understanding the theology of it. They are saved because God looks at it. Every Hebrew family that night was as safe as the blood on its doorframe and no safer, and none of them could improve the position by being braver or more devout.

There is one more thing about the placement, and it is in the text rather than imported. The blood goes on the two doorposts and the lintel — the sides and the top. It does not go on the threshold. The one part of the frame a person's foot would land on is the one part left unmarked, because blood that saves a household is not something to be walked on. The writer to the Hebrews reaches for exactly that horror when he describes apostasy: someone who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified (Heb. 10:29).

The meal itself is eaten in haste: roasted, not raw or boiled, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. This is not a feast to linger over. They eat dressed to leave. And the bitter herbs are there so that nobody enjoys the evening too much to remember what it cost — a mouthful of the taste of slavery served alongside the meat of the rescue.

The verb itself deserves a moment. Pasach, to pass over, may carry the sense of covering or shielding as much as skipping past — not merely a destroyer declining to enter, but God standing over that doorway. Either way the picture is not of God overlooking sin. The house was passed over because a death had already occurred at it. Judgement did not swerve; it landed on the lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD. The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there is a phrase in verse 12 that puts the whole night in its true frame: on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments. The ten plagues have never been a contest between a king and a prophet. They were God against the entire religious apparatus of the greatest civilisation on earth, and the last stroke falls on the gods themselves.

Everything the New Testament says about the cross is already lying here in outline. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7) — Paul states it as a fact the Corinthians already know. John the Baptist looks at a man walking toward him and says Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). Peter writes that we were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet. 1:19) — the very requirement of verse 5. And in the Revelation, the one on the throne is a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain. It is the single most sustained image in Scripture, and it starts in a doorway in Egypt with a bowl of blood and a bunch of hyssop.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 14-20: The night is legislated into a memorial before it happens — a feast throughout your generations, as a statute forever — with seven days of unleavened bread and all leaven put out of the houses.

Verses 21-24: Moses instructs the elders, adding the hyssop and the basin.

Verses 25-28: And when your children say to you, "What do you mean by this service?" — and the people bowed their heads and worshiped, then went and did it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Leaven

The practical reason comes later — there was no time for dough to rise (v.39) — so the bread of haste becomes the standing sign of a rescue that could not wait. But leaven gains a second meaning from how it works: a very little changes the whole batch, quietly, from inside. Hence the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. 16:6), and hence Paul, immediately after calling Christ our Passover lamb, telling the Corinthians to cleanse out the old leaven and keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:6-8). Searching the house for every trace of it is a picture of what the redeemed do with sin: not manage it, hunt it out of the building.

Hyssop

A common straggly plant that grows out of walls — the instrument of the most important act in Israel's history is a weed. David remembered it: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean (Ps. 51:7). And at the crucifixion, when Jesus said I thirst, they lifted a sponge to him on a hyssop branch (John 19:29). Of all the plants in Judea, John names that one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: After ten chapters of grumbling, doubt and complaint, the people simply obey — they bowed their heads and worshiped.

Now: The meal is built to provoke a question. It is deliberately strange — the odd bread, the bitter herbs, the roasted lamb, everyone dressed for a journey they are not taking — because strangeness makes children ask, and the asking is the point. God's chosen method for carrying the faith across the centuries is not a monument or an archive. It is a child interrupting a meal to ask why the food is odd.

verseByVerse.quote: "This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel. On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you. And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever. In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening. For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the night has even happened, God legislates how it will be remembered. This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast.

Seven days of unleavened bread follow, and leaven is put out of the houses entirely. The practical reason is given later — there was no time to let dough rise (v.39) — so the bread of haste becomes the permanent sign of a rescue that could not wait.

But leaven acquires a second meaning, because of how it works: a very small amount changes the whole batch, quietly, from the inside. That is why Jesus warns about the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. 16:6), and why Paul, immediately after calling Christ our Passover lamb, tells the Corinthians to cleanse out the old leaven and keep the festival with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:6-8). The instruction to search the house and remove every trace of it turns out to be a picture of what the redeemed are to do with sin — not manage it, not reduce it, but hunt it out of the building.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning. For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you. You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses passes it to the elders, and adds a detail God had not spelled out: Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin. Hyssop is a common straggly plant that grows out of walls. The instrument of the most important act in Israel's history is a weed.

David will remember it — Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean (Ps. 51:7). And at the crucifixion, when Jesus said I thirst, they put a sponge of sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth (John 19:29). Of all the plants in Judea, John names that one.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service. And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped. Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a command that shapes Jewish family life to this day: And when your children say to you, "What do you mean by this service?" you shall say, "It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover." The meal is built to provoke a question. It is deliberately strange — the odd bread, the bitter herbs, the roasted lamb, everyone dressed for a journey they are not taking — because strangeness makes children ask, and the asking is the point. God's chosen method for carrying the faith across the centuries is not a monument or an archive. It is a child interrupting a meal to ask why the food is odd.

And the people's response is recorded in two words that have been rare in this book: the people bowed their heads and worshiped. Then the people of Israel went and did so. After ten chapters of grumbling, doubt and complaint, they simply obey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 29-32: At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn. Pharaoh rises in the night and surrenders every condition he ever set — ending with and bless me also.

Verses 33-36: Egypt drives them out; they leave with unleavened dough and with silver and gold, and a mixed multitude goes up with them.

Verses 37-42: The count, the 430 years fulfilled on that very day, and a night of watching by the LORD.

Verses 43-51: Who may eat: not by race but by covenant sign — and you shall not break any of its bones.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Firstborn Sons

God had said it in chapter 4: Israel is my firstborn son... if you refuse, I will kill your firstborn son (4:22-23). Egypt kept God's son in chains and lost its own. And there came a night when the Father's own firstborn was not spared, and no lamb was found for him because he was the lamb. Every Hebrew child alive in Goshen that morning owed it to an animal that died in his place — a picture, drawn small and in blood on a doorframe, of the Son who would take the place of everyone.

A Door With a Condition, Not a Bloodline

No foreigner may eat — but a circumcised foreigner shall be as a native of the land. An Egyptian who took the sign belonged; an Israelite who refused it did not. From the night the nation was born, membership was defined by a mark rather than ancestry, which is precisely Paul's argument that the true Jew is one inwardly (Rom. 2:28-29).

Not One of His Bones

A rule about butchering a lamb, kept for fifteen centuries by people who had no idea what it was for. Then soldiers came to break the legs of three crucified men, broke the first and the second, but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs — and John, who was standing there, says why he recorded it: that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:32-36). He is quoting this verse.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The narrator gives the night no build-up and no adjectives. What he gives is the sound — a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead. A whole country awake in the dark at once, and one noise rising off it.

Now: On that very day. Not approximately — to the day. Four hundred and thirty years earlier God told Abraham this would happen and roughly how long it would take (Gen. 15:13-14), and the exodus lands on the exact date. Every one of those years had felt like God doing nothing; every generation in that span was born, worked and buried inside what looked like silence. A calendar was running the whole time.

And the people walking out under the blood are not a pure bloodline. A mixed multitude goes with them — people of other nations who heard what was coming and marked a door. The qualification was never ancestry. From that first night the redeemed community has never been ethnically clean, which is why the promise lands where it does: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, standing before the Lamb (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock. And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead. Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt.

The narrator gives it no build-up and no adjectives. What he does give is the sound: there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead. The whole country awake in the dark at the same moment, and one noise rising off it.

And the thing God said in chapter 4 has come true in the most terrible way available. Israel is my firstborn son... Let my son go that he may serve me. If you refuse, behold, I will kill your firstborn son (4:22-23). Egypt kept God's son in chains and lost its own.

Hold the two firstborns together and then hold a third with them. There came a night when the Father's own firstborn was not spared, and no lamb was found for him because he was the lamb, and the cry that went up was not Egypt's but his. Every Hebrew child who woke up alive that morning in Goshen owed it to an animal that had died in his place, and every one of them was a picture, drawn small and in blood on a doorframe, of the Son who would take the place of everyone.

Then Pharaoh, and it is the total collapse of the man. He rose up in the night, he and all his servants — the king out of bed, summoning the men he threatened with death if they showed their faces again. Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone.

Every condition he ever attached is gone. Not within the land, not a short distance, not without the children, not without the livestock — everything, on Moses' terms, immediately. And then the last four words, from the man who opened this contest with Who is the LORD?: and bless me also.

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead." So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders. The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt drives them out — for they said, "We shall all be dead" — and they go with dough still unleavened on their shoulders, and with the silver and gold, and with a mixed multitude alongside them.

Hold on to that phrase. The people walking out of Egypt under the blood are not a pure bloodline. Some of them are Egyptians, or of other nations, who heard what was coming and marked a door. The qualification that night was never ancestry; it was the blood on the frame. And from that first moment the redeemed community has never been ethnically clean — which is why the promise finally lands where it does: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds. And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves. The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt. It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator then does something a reader should not hurry past. He counts the time: The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.

On that very day. Not approximately, not in that era — to the day. Four hundred and thirty years earlier God had told Abraham this would happen and roughly how long it would take (Gen. 15:13-14), and the exodus lands on the exact date. Every one of those years had felt like God doing nothing. Every generation in that span was born, worked and buried inside what looked like silence. And a calendar was running the whole time.

The numbers are given too — about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children — a figure that has been debated for as long as people have read it, since the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan or a military unit. What the narrator is certain of is the scale: the family of seventy that went down into Egypt in Genesis has come out as a nation, exactly as God told Abraham it would.

So the verse calls it a night of watching by the LORD — and then says Israel must keep it as a night of watching in return. God kept vigil over them; they keep vigil over the memory of it. That is the shape of all Christian remembering: we watch because he watched first.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it, but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him. No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it. It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones. All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you." All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the rules about who may eat, and they look like an anticlimax until you see what they are doing. No foreigner may eat of it — but any foreigner who is circumcised shall be as a native of the land and may eat. A hired worker, no. A slave bought with money, yes, once circumcised.

So the door is not shut and it is not wide open either. It is a door with a condition, and the condition is not race but covenant. An Egyptian who took the sign belonged; an Israelite who refused it did not. From the very night the nation was born, membership was defined by a mark rather than a bloodline — which is exactly Paul's argument when he insists that the true Jew is one inwardly (Rom. 2:28-29), and that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek.

And then one small regulation with a long reach: you shall not break any of its bones. It is easy to read past. It is a rule about butchering a lamb.

On a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, soldiers came to break the legs of three crucified men to hasten their deaths before the Sabbath. They broke the legs of the first and the second. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. And John, who was standing there and watching, tells us why he has bothered to record such a detail: For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken" (John 19:32-36). He is quoting this verse.

A rule was given in Egypt about how to handle the carcass of a lamb, and it was kept for fifteen centuries by people who had no idea what it was for, and then a Roman soldier with a hammer made a professional judgement about a corpse and unknowingly obeyed it. The Lamb was without blemish, and he was not broken, and the blood was on the door, and God saw it and passed over.

12.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The lamb dies in the place of the firstborn. "When I see the blood, I will pass over you." Salvation is by a substitute's blood, not by merit.

Christ our Passover. The spotless lamb, the applied blood, the unbroken bones — all fulfilled in Jesus (1 Cor. 5:7; 1 Pet. 1:19; John 19:36).

Redemption remembered. The Passover becomes a perpetual memorial, fulfilled in the Lord's Supper, by which the church proclaims Christ's death until he comes.
12.examples:
Then: On the night of judgment, every household covered by the blood of a spotless lamb was passed over, while Egypt's firstborn died — and God's people went free, not by their worth but by the blood.

Now: Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. The decisive question is not how good we are but whether we are covered by his blood. By faith we apply his blood to our hearts, and the judgment passes over us forever. Every Lord's Supper recalls this redemption until he comes.

13.title: Consecration and the Guiding Presence
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten.<sup>4</sup>Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out.<sup>5</sup>And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month.<sup>6</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory.<sup>8</sup>You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'<sup>9</sup>And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.<sup>11</sup>"When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you,<sup>12</sup>you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's.<sup>13</sup>Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.<sup>14</sup>And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.<sup>15</sup>For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.'<sup>16</sup>It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."<sup>17</sup>When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt."<sup>18</sup>But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle.<sup>19</sup>Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here."<sup>20</sup>And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night.<sup>22</sup>The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
13.overview:
Redeemed people belong wholly to God. So the first command after the exodus is the consecration of the firstborn: "Whatever is the first to open the womb... is mine." Because God spared Israel's firstborn on Passover night, every firstborn now belongs to him — either given to his service or redeemed by a substitute. The principle is profound: those whom God has redeemed, he claims as his own possession. We are not our own; we were bought with a price.

The chapter also institutes the Feast of Unleavened Bread and the practice of teaching children — again the rhythm of remembering and recounting. Then comes one of the most tender images in all of Scripture: the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. God does not redeem his people and then leave them to find their own way. He goes before them, leading every step, never departing. The God who came down to deliver now travels with his people.

This guiding presence is the great comfort of the redeemed life. As Ferguson observes, the same God who saves us also leads us, and his presence — fulfilled in Christ who promised "I am with you always" and in the Spirit who indwells us — never departs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: Consecrate to me all the firstborn... is mine.

Verses 3-10: Remember this day; keep the seven days of unleavened bread; tell the children; bind it as a sign on the hand and between the eyes.

Verses 11-13: Every firstborn of the herd is God's; a donkey must be redeemed with a lamb or have its neck broken; every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.

Verses 14-16: And when in time to come your son asks you, "What does this mean?" — with the whole answer supplied, including the deaths and the price paid.
verseByVerse.theology:
Redemption Creates Ownership

The claim on the firstborn is made the morning after the tenth plague and follows from it. Every firstborn son in Israel is alive because a lamb died in his place, so God's claim is not a tax but a receipt. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price (1 Cor. 6:19-20) is the same logic carried forward; only the price has changed.

The Donkey

The donkey was unclean — it could not be sacrificed and had no place on an altar. Its firstborn therefore faces a straight alternative: a lamb dies in its place, or it dies itself. There is no third option and no question of it qualifying on its own merits. And then the son is put in exactly the same category: not fit to be offered, not able to stand on his own account, alive only because something acceptable died instead. It is the plainest picture in Exodus of substitution — the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Why so much machinery for remembering — the annual week, the odd food, the sign on the hand? Because they will forget. Within six weeks these people will say they were better off in Egypt (16:3). God is building a defence against an amnesia he knows is coming, and the defence is a rhythm.

Now: The answer God supplies for the child's question is not a formula but a story, told in the first person plural: the LORD brought us out. The father telling it was not there, and is to say us anyway. And he is not allowed to leave out the hard half — the refusal, the deaths, the price paid for this particular child. Israel's children were not given an edited version.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine.

The claim is made the morning after the tenth plague, and it follows directly from it. Every firstborn son in Israel is alive because a lamb died in his place. God's claim on him is therefore not a tax but a receipt: this life was bought, and the buyer says so.

It is the principle that will run through the whole of Scripture. Redemption creates ownership. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price (1 Cor. 6:19-20) is this verse carried forward — the logic is identical, and only the price has changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten. Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out. And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD. Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory. You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.' And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt. You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place.

The word remember is the load-bearing word of the chapter, and what follows is a set of practical arrangements for making sure a nation does not forget: seven days of unleavened bread each year, an annual telling to the children, and the memory bound as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes.

Why so much machinery? Because they will forget. Within six weeks these people will be saying they were better off in Egypt (16:3). God is not being sentimental about the past; he is building a defence against the specific amnesia he knows is coming, and the defence is a rhythm — the same week every year, the same odd food, the same question from the children, for as long as the nation lasts.

And notice what the telling is for: that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. Obedience is not the price of the rescue. It is the consequence of remembering it, and when the remembering goes, the obedience goes with it.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you, you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the rule is spelled out, and it contains something startling. Every firstborn of the herd belongs to God. But every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck.

The donkey is the point. It was an unclean animal — it could not be sacrificed, and it had no place on an altar. So its firstborn faces a straight alternative: either a lamb dies in its place, or it dies itself. There is no third option, and there is no question of the donkey qualifying on its own merits. It never could.

Then the sentence that puts every Israelite reader in the donkey's position: Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem. The son is in exactly the same category. Not fit to be offered, not able to stand on his own account, and alive only because something acceptable died instead.

That is an uncomfortable place for a father to be told his child stands, and it is meant to be. It is also the plainest picture in Exodus of what the New Testament means by substitution: For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18). The unclean animal lives because a clean one died. There has never been any other arrangement available.

verseByVerse.quote: And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.' It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when in time to come your son asks you, "What does this mean?" you shall say to him, "By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery."

This is the second time in two chapters that God has built the faith around a child's question, and the answer he supplies is worth examining. It is not a doctrinal formula and not a definition. It is a story, told in the first person plural: the LORD brought us out. The father telling it was not there. He is to say us anyway, because what happened that night happened to his people and therefore to him.

Then the hard half of the answer, which the parent is not allowed to leave out: When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt... Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem. The child is told the whole thing — the refusal, the deaths, and the price paid for him personally. Israel's children were not given an edited version.

And the whole of it is to be worn: as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes — on the hand that works and in front of the eyes that look. What you do and what you see are both to be governed by a night when a lamb died instead of a son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17-22 — The Pillar of Cloud and Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 17-22: God avoids the short coastal road lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt. Moses carries Joseph's bones. And the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, which did not depart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Long Way Round Is Chosen, Not Accidental

There was a direct road — the coastal route, perhaps two weeks. God deliberately does not use it, and the reason is not strategic but psychological: they would meet armed resistance, panic, and go home. The detour is a route chosen by someone who knows exactly what these people can bear this month, and who would rather take them the slow way than lose them on the fast one.

Guidance Is a Presence, Not a Map

God's answer to the question of how to be led is not instructions but himself, visible and moving, in front of them. And the text is careful to say the pillar did not depart — not for forty years, not while they grumbled or made a calf or refused to enter. The same fire that burned in a bush without consuming it would fill a tent, and at last take flesh: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him. Four centuries earlier Joseph made Israel swear it, and somebody kept that coffin and the promise attached to it through four hundred years of slavery. Joseph died believing in an exodus he would not see. He is now attending it.

Now: Anyone who has wondered why a straightforward thing in their life has been routed through years of wilderness has verse 17 to sit with. God's detours are not evidence that he has mislaid the map.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt." But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle. Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here." And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now one of the most quietly pastoral verses in the Bible. When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt."

There was a direct road. The coastal route to Canaan was the obvious way and would have taken perhaps two weeks. God deliberately does not use it, and the reason given is not strategic but psychological: they are not ready. They would meet armed resistance, panic, and go home.

So the longer way is not a punishment and not an accident. It is a route chosen by someone who knows exactly what these people can bear this month, and who would rather take them the slow way than lose them on the fast one. Anyone who has wondered why a straightforward thing in their own life has been routed through years of wilderness has this verse to sit with. God's detours are not evidence that he has mislaid the map.

They also do something remarkable on the way out: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him. Four hundred years earlier Joseph had made Israel swear it — God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here (Gen. 50:25) — and somebody has kept that coffin, and kept the promise attached to it, through four centuries of slavery. Joseph died believing an exodus he would not see. He is now attending it.

And then the pillar. The LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night. This is God's answer to the question of guidance, and it is not a map or a set of instructions. It is his presence, visible, moving, in front of them.

The last line says he did not depart from before the people. Not for forty years. Not while they grumbled, or made a calf, or refused to enter the land. The cloud that led them out stayed with them the whole way, and it was the same fire that had burned in a bush without consuming it, and it would one day fill a tent, and finally take flesh and walk about among them — and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

13.theology:
Redemption and consecration. Those whom God redeems, he claims. The firstborn are his; we who are redeemed by Christ are not our own.

The wisdom of God's leading. God chooses the longer road for his people's good, sparing them what they cannot yet bear. His detours are mercies.

The guiding presence of God. The pillar of cloud and fire reveals a God who never departs from his people — fulfilled in Christ and the indwelling Spirit.
13.examples:
Then: Having redeemed his people, God claimed their firstborn as his own and led them out by a visible pillar of cloud and fire that never departed, choosing even the harder road for their good.

Now: Redeemed by Christ, we belong wholly to God and consecrate our lives to him. And we are never left to find our own way: he leads us by his Word and Spirit, choosing wise paths, promising never to leave us nor forsake us.

14.title: The LORD Will Fight for You
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea.<sup>3</sup>For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.'<sup>4</sup>And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so.<sup>5</sup>When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?"<sup>6</sup>So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him,<sup>7</sup>and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly.<sup>9</sup>The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.<sup>10</sup>When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt?<sup>12</sup>Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness."<sup>13</sup>And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again.<sup>14</sup>The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."<sup>15</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward.<sup>16</sup>Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground.<sup>17</sup>And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>18</sup>And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."<sup>19</sup>Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them,<sup>20</sup>coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.<sup>21</sup>Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.<sup>22</sup>And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>23</sup>The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>24</sup>And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic,<sup>25</sup>clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."<sup>26</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen."<sup>27</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.<sup>28</sup>The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained.<sup>29</sup>But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>30</sup>Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.<sup>31</sup>Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
14.overview:
Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, Israel panics. There is no way forward, no way back, no human possibility of escape. And precisely there, in the place of utter helplessness, God works his greatest salvation. "Stand firm," Moses says, "and see the salvation of the LORD... The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." This is the gospel posture: salvation is something we receive, not achieve. We do not contribute to it; we behold it.

God divides the sea, and Israel passes through on dry ground from death to life, while the same waters that saved them destroy their enemies. Paul tells us this crossing was a baptism: "all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Cor. 10:2). The Red Sea is the pattern of every believer's salvation — passing through the waters of judgment safely because we are united to our deliverer, our old enemies drowned behind us, emerging into new life on the other shore.

As Keller preached, the Red Sea teaches us that God's deliverance often comes only when we have run out of options — when we finally stop striving and stand still to see the salvation of the LORD. The enemy that terrified us at dawn lies dead on the shore by morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 — Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-9: God tells Israel to turn back and camp against the water, so that Pharaoh will think the wilderness has shut them in. Pharaoh's grief wears off and six hundred chosen chariots pursue.

Verses 10-14: Israel panics — Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? Moses answers: Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD... The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trap Is Deliberate

God arranges for his people to look trapped, and says why twice: I will get glory over Pharaoh... and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD. Israel is about to spend a very bad night believing they have been led into a death-trap by an incompetent God, and they are in exactly the position he intended, for reasons already explained to Moses. Their panic is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is evidence that they cannot see the whole board.

Three of the Four Commands Are to Do Nothing

Stand firm. See. Be silent. There is a kind of deliverance in which the only available human contribution is to stop thrashing and let God do it, and Israel at the sea is the pattern of it. They contribute nothing to their own rescue except their presence at it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pharaoh has buried his own son and returns to the same decision within days, on economic grounds — What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us? There is no depth of loss that automatically produces repentance.

Now: Six days out of slavery and Israel is already revising Egypt upward. That should be recognised rather than sneered at. Fear does this. A known misery feels safer than an unknown deliverance, and rescued people will often ask to be taken back — not because the slavery was good but because it was familiar, and the desert in front of them is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea. For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.' And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so. When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?" So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him, and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them. And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly. The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first instruction after the exodus is to tell Israel to turn back and camp with their backs to the water. It is a militarily indefensible position and it is chosen on purpose: For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, "They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in."

God arranges for his people to look trapped. The manoeuvre is bait, and the reason is stated twice — I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD.

Hold on to that through the rest of the chapter, and beyond it. Israel is about to spend a very bad night believing they have been led into a death-trap by an incompetent God. They are in exactly the position he intended, for reasons he had already explained to Moses. The panic in verse 11 is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is evidence that they cannot see the whole board.

And Pharaoh does exactly what God said. The grief of the tenth plague wears off, the economics reassert themselves — What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us? — and six hundred chosen chariots go out after them. A man who has buried his own son returns to the same decision within days. There is no depth of loss that automatically produces repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD. They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt? Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness." And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again. The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel sees the army coming and does two things in the same breath, and the order is instructive. They feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.
