Then they turn on Moses with what may be the bitterest sarcasm in the Old Testament: Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness?

And then the sentence that gives the game away: Is not this what we said to you in Egypt, "Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians"? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness.

Six days out of slavery and they are already revising it upward. This is the first of many times Israel will look back at Egypt and remember it as better than it was, and it should be recognised rather than sneered at. Fear does this. A known misery feels safer than an unknown deliverance, and people who have been rescued will often ask to be taken back — not because the slavery was good but because it was familiar, and because the desert in front of them is not.

Moses' answer is one of the great sentences of Scripture: Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today... The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.

Four commands, and three of them are to do nothing. Stand still. Watch. Be quiet. There is a kind of deliverance in which the only available human contribution is to stop thrashing and let God do it, and Israel at the sea is the pattern of it. They contribute nothing to their own rescue except their presence at it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 15-20: Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward — straight at the water. The pillar moves from the front to the rear, and gives darkness on one side and light on the other all night.

Verses 21-25: A strong east wind divides the sea all night. Egypt follows; their chariot wheels clog; and they conclude, too late, the LORD fights for them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Pillar, Two Effects

One object — and on one side darkness thick enough to stop an army, on the other light enough to walk by all night. The presence of God is not experienced identically by everyone standing near it. The same Christ is a fragrance from life to life and from death to death (2 Cor. 2:16); the same stone is a foundation to some and the rock others trip over.

Stand Still, Then Go Forward

Moses tells the people to stand still and God tells Moses to get them walking. Both are right, and the sequence matters: first stop trying to save yourself, then move when you are told. The standing still was never meant to be permanent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God uses a mechanism and takes hours over it — a strong east wind all night. This is not a conjuring trick in an instant but a wind blowing in the dark while a nation waits to see whether the ground will be walkable by morning. And the mechanism explains nothing: no wind arranges water into walls on the right hand and the left, or dries a seabed hard enough for carts.

Now: There is something almost weary about verse 25. No thunderbolt — the wheels simply stop turning properly. And Egypt's army becomes the last group in the book to answer Pharaoh's question from 5:2. They answer it correctly, in the dark, in the middle of a sea, far too late.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward. Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground. And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen." Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them, coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a surprising rebuke: Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward. Moses has just told the people to stand still, and God tells Moses to get them walking. Both are right, and the sequence matters — first stop trying to save yourself, then move when you are told. The standing still was never meant to be permanent.

And where they are told to go forward is straight at the water, before it has parted.

Then the pillar moves. It had been in front, leading; now the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, coming between the Egyptian camp and Israel's. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.

The same pillar. One object, and on one side of it there is darkness so thick an army cannot move, and on the other side there is light enough to walk by all night. The presence of God is not experienced identically by everyone standing near it — the same Christ is a fragrance from life to life and from death to death (2 Cor. 2:16), and the same stone is a foundation to some and the rock they trip over to others.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic, clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.

Note the detail: all night, and a strong east wind. God uses a mechanism, and he takes hours over it. This is not a conjuring trick performed in an instant; it is a wind blowing in the dark for a whole night while a nation waits to see whether the ground will be walkable by morning. And the text is equally clear that the mechanism explains nothing — no wind arranges water into walls on the right hand and on the left, and no wind dries a seabed hard enough for a nation with carts and livestock to cross.

The Egyptians follow them in — the sheer momentum of the pursuit carrying them onto a seabed between two walls of water — and then God clogged their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. There is something almost weary about that verse. No thunderbolt. The wheels simply stop turning properly.

And Egypt's army works it out at last, in the dark, in the middle of a sea: Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians. They are the last people in the book to answer Pharaoh's question from 5:2, and they answer it correctly, and it is far too late.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 26-31: The waters return and not one of them remained. Israel sees the Egyptians dead on the shore, and the chapter ends: the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sea as Baptism

Paul looked back at this crossing and saw one: our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10:1-2). Water on both sides and cloud overhead; they went down as slaves and came up on the far bank a free nation, with the thing that had owned them drowned behind them. That is the shape of every baptism since — down into the water with the old master, up out of it belonging to someone else.

A Greater Crossing

Israel walked through on dry ground because the waters were held back from them. There came a day when the waters were not held back at all, and the one going through prayed all your waves and your billows have gone over me, and was not spared a drop of it. He went down into the depths so that his people could walk over dry — and the army that had held them, sin and death and the accusation of the law, is lying still on the shore behind them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Three results, each carrying its own weight: the LORD saved — not Moses and not the wind; Israel saw — they were not told about it; and they feared the LORD, and they believed.

Now: That last verse is the whole purpose of the trap in verses 1 to 4. God led them into an impossible position so that they would watch him get them out of it, because a people who have seen that will believe in a way that a people who took the coastal road never could.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen." So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea. The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained. But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore. Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waters return. Not one of them remained. And in the morning Israel sees the Egyptians dead on the shore — the army that had held them for four hundred years, finished in a night, and the survivors did not have to lift a hand.

The chapter ends with three results, and each carries its own weight. Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians — the LORD saved, not Moses, not the wind. And Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians — they saw it, they were not told about it. So the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.

That last verse is the whole point of the trap in verses 1 to 4. God led them into an impossible position so that they would watch him get them out of it, because a people who have seen that will believe in a way that a people who took the coastal road never could.

Paul looked back at this crossing and saw a baptism. Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10:1-2). Water on both sides and the cloud overhead; they went down into it as slaves and came up on the far bank as a free nation, and the thing that had owned them was drowned behind them. That is the shape Paul saw, and it is the shape of every baptism since: down into the water with the old master, up out of it belonging to someone else.

And there is a greater crossing still. Israel walked through on dry ground because the waters were held back from them. There came a day when the waters were not held back at all, and the one going through prayed all your waves and your billows have gone over me, and was not spared a drop of it. He went down into the depths so that his people could walk over dry, and the army that had held them — sin, and death, and the accusation of the law — is lying still on the shore behind them.

14.theology:
Salvation belongs to the LORD. "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." Israel beholds; God acts. Redemption is received, not achieved.

The Red Sea as baptism. Passing through the waters from death to life, united to the deliverer, with the old enemy drowned behind — the pattern of Christian baptism (1 Cor. 10:1-2).

The same waters save and judge. God's deliverance of his people is simultaneously the destruction of his enemies. Salvation and judgment flow from one hand.
14.examples:
Then: Trapped between army and sea, Israel was told to stand still and see God save. He split the waters, brought them through from death to life, and drowned their enemies behind them.

Now: When we are cornered with no way out, the gospel call is the same: stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. At the cross our true enemies were drowned, and in Christ we have passed through the waters of judgment into new life. The battle belongs to the LORD.

15.title: The Song of the Redeemed
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.<sup>2</sup>The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him.<sup>3</sup>The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.<sup>4</sup>"Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea.<sup>5</sup>The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.<sup>6</sup>Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy.<sup>7</sup>In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble.<sup>8</sup>At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.<sup>9</sup>The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.'<sup>10</sup>You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.<sup>11</sup>"Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?<sup>12</sup>You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.<sup>13</sup>"You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode.<sup>14</sup>The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia.<sup>15</sup>Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away.<sup>16</sup>Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased.<sup>17</sup>You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established.<sup>18</sup>The LORD will reign forever and ever."<sup>19</sup>For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea.<sup>20</sup>Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.<sup>21</sup>And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.<sup>23</sup>When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah.<sup>24</sup>And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"<sup>25</sup>And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them,<sup>26</sup>saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer."<sup>27</sup>Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
15.overview:
Redeemed people sing. The first thing Israel does on the far shore of the sea is break into song — the Song of the Sea, the oldest hymn of salvation in Scripture. This is no dirge but an explosion of doxology: "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously!" Salvation accomplished leads inevitably to praise lifted up. As Sproul observed, theology that does not end in doxology is dead theology. Here the saved cannot keep silent.

The song celebrates the character of God: "The LORD is a man of war" — the warrior who fights for his people; "majestic in holiness" — incomparable in purity; "the LORD will reign forever and ever" — the everlasting King. It looks back at the sea and forward to the promised land, to the place God will plant his people, the sanctuary his hands will establish. The exodus is not an end but a beginning, leading to worship in God's dwelling place.

Revelation 15 tells us that the redeemed in glory sing "the song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb." The song begun on the shore of the Red Sea will be completed before the throne. And Miriam takes up her tambourine and leads the women in dancing — the joy of salvation overflowing into the whole community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The LORD Is a Warrior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-8: The first recorded song in the Bible: I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously — and at its centre, This is my God, and I will praise him.

Verses 9-18: The enemy's six boasts answered by one breath; Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods?; a look forward to the nations and to God's sanctuary; and The LORD will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Song Is About Rescue

Not creation, not harvest, not a wedding — redemption. And the song is not about Israel. Read the pronouns: the people just delivered say almost nothing about themselves. And verse 2 supplies the possessive Pharaoh could never manage (10:17): my God, the first word out of a freed slave's mouth.

Six Boasts and One Breath

Verse 9 quotes the enemy — I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil... — six sentences all beginning with I. Verse 10 answers in full: You blew with your wind; the sea covered them. The song sets them side by side deliberately, and the disproportion is the point.

A Song Still Being Sung

In the Revelation, John sees those who have conquered standing beside a sea of glass singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb (Rev. 15:2-4). The same words, at the far end of history, at the edge of another sea, sung by a redeemed people looking back at a defeated enemy. It began on a shore in Egypt with wet sand underfoot and has never stopped.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The song does not stop at the sea. It looks ahead to Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, and finally to God's sanctuary — a temple that will not exist for four centuries. Redemption is understood on the very day it happens to be heading toward a place where God dwells with his people.

Now: Modern readers sometimes flinch at the warrior imagery, and it should simply be said plainly: a God unwilling to destroy Pharaoh's army would be a God who left Israel in the brickyards. Mercy toward slaves and judgement on slavers are not two moods. They are one act seen from two ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea. The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him. The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name. "Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea. The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD. This is the first recorded song in the Bible, and what prompted it matters. Not creation, not a harvest, not a wedding — redemption. The first thing God's people are recorded singing about is being rescued, and they have been free for approximately one day.

The song is not about Israel. Read the pronouns: I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously... The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation... The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name. The people who have just been delivered say almost nothing about themselves. They talk about him.

And at the centre of it, verse 2: This is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him. Not merely the God who acted, but my God — the possessive Pharaoh could never bring himself to use (10:17) is the first word out of the mouth of a freed slave.

verseByVerse.quote: Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy. In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble. At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary: The imagery is of a warrior: Pharaoh's chariots cast into the sea, his officers sunk like a stone, your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power. Modern readers sometimes flinch at this, and it should simply be said plainly that a God who was not willing to destroy Pharaoh's army would be a God who left Israel in the brickyards. Mercy toward slaves and judgement on slavers are not two moods. They are one act seen from two ends.

verseByVerse.quote: The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.' You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters. "Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 9 does something clever: it quotes the enemy. The enemy said, "I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them." Six boasts, all beginning with I.

And then verse 10, in its entirety: You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters. Six sentences of human intention answered by one breath. The song sets them side by side deliberately, and the disproportion is the point.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-18: The song looks past the sea — to Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, and finally to the sanctuary, O LORD, which your hands have established, ending The LORD will reign forever and ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Singing About a Temple That Does Not Exist

They are four centuries early. Redemption from Egypt is understood, on the day it happens, to be heading toward a place where God dwells with his people — which is where the whole Bible is going (Rev. 21:3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? is the answer to Pharaoh's Who is the LORD? — asked at the start of the contest as a sneer, returned at the end as worship.

Now: The song ends not with Israel's freedom but with God's reign. A rescued people's instinct, given one day's practice at it, is to talk about him rather than themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode. The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away. Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased. You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established. The LORD will reign forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the question at the heart of the song: Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? It is the answer to Pharaoh's Who is the LORD? — asked at the beginning of the contest as a sneer, and returned at the end as worship.

And the song does not stop at the sea. It looks forward — to Philistia, Edom, Moab, Canaan, and finally to the mountain of your own inheritance, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O LORD, which your hands have established. They are singing about a temple that will not exist for four centuries. Redemption from Egypt is understood, on the very day it happens, to be heading toward a place where God dwells with his people.

It ends: The LORD will reign forever and ever.

That song is still being sung. In the Revelation, John sees those who have conquered standing beside a sea of glass, holding harps, and what they sing is the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb: Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty!... Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? (Rev. 15:2-4). The same words, at the far end of history, at the edge of another sea, sung by a redeemed people looking back at a defeated enemy. It began on a shore in Egypt with wet sand under their feet, and it has never stopped.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 19-21: Miriam takes a tambourine and leads the women in the song's refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Log in the Water

A piece of wood thrown into bitterness, and the bitterness goes. Readers from the earliest centuries have found it hard to look at that without thinking of another piece of wood thrown into the bitterest thing there is. The text does not make the connection and it should not be pressed as though it did — but the shape is unmistakable, and it is the shape of the whole gospel: what was bitter is not removed, it is sweetened, by wood.

A New Name at a Well

Yahweh Rophe, the LORD who heals — given not on a mountain in fire but beside a spring in a desert, to people who had been complaining an hour earlier.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Miriam is almost certainly the girl of chapter 2 who watched a basket in the reeds and had the nerve to speak to Pharaoh's daughter. She is old now. She watched a river fail to take her brother; she has now watched a sea take an army. And her song is not a new composition — it is the first two lines of the long one, sung back as a refrain, which is what congregational worship has been ever since. Not everyone writes the song, and everyone sings it.

Now: Three days separate the singing of verse 1 from the grumbling of verse 24, and the same mouths do both. It is easy to be scornful and worth resisting: that is a distance most people cover regularly. Praise on a good day proves less about a heart than what it says on the third day of thirst.

And Elim was there all along, a short walk past Marah — twelve springs, one for every tribe. God could have routed them straight to it. He does not always take his people around the bitter place. Often he takes them through it, and camps them by the springs on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea. Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing. And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Miriam. Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.

This is almost certainly the girl from chapter 2 who stood at a distance watching a basket in the reeds and had the nerve to speak to Pharaoh's daughter. She is old now. She watched the river fail to take her brother; she has now watched a sea take an army.

And her song is the first two lines of the long one, sung back as a refrain: Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea. Not a new composition — the same truth, repeated, with a drum. Which is what congregational worship has been ever since: not everyone writes the song, and everyone sings it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 22-24: Three days without water, then water at Marah too bitter to drink, and the people grumble: What shall we drink?

Verses 25-27: A log thrown into the water makes it sweet; God gives a new name, the LORD, your healer; and they come to Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palms.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Log in the Water

A piece of wood thrown into bitterness, and the bitterness goes. Readers from the earliest centuries have found it hard to look at that without thinking of another piece of wood thrown into the bitterest thing there is. The text does not make the connection and it should not be pressed as though it did — but the shape is unmistakable, and it is the shape of the gospel: what was bitter is not removed, it is sweetened, by wood.

A New Name at a Well

Yahweh Rophe, the LORD who heals — given not on a mountain in fire but beside a spring in a desert, to people who had been complaining an hour earlier.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Three days separate the singing of verse 1 from the grumbling of verse 24, and the same mouths do both. It is easy to be scornful and worth resisting: that is a distance most people cover regularly. Praise on a good day proves less about a heart than what it says on the third day of thirst.

Now: Elim was there all along, a short walk past Marah — twelve springs, one for every tribe. God could have routed them straight to it. He does not always take his people around the bitter place. Often he takes them through it, and camps them by the springs on the other side.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah. And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days later they cannot find water, and when they do find it, it is undrinkable. So the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"

Three days. The song of verse 1 and the grumbling of verse 24 are separated by seventy-two hours, and the same mouths do both. It would be easy to be scornful, and worth resisting, because the distance between singing on the shore and complaining in the desert is a distance most people cover regularly. Praise on a good day proves less about a heart than what it says on the third day of thirst.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them, saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer." Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's remedy is strange: the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. A piece of wood, thrown into bitterness, and the bitterness goes. Christian readers from the earliest centuries have found it difficult to look at that and not think of another piece of wood thrown into the bitterest thing there is. The connection is not made by the text and should not be pressed as though it were — but the shape is unmistakable, and it is the shape of the whole gospel: what was bitter is not removed, it is sweetened, by wood.

Then God says something that governs everything from here to Sinai: If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God... I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer. A new name, and it is given at a well in a desert rather than on a mountain in fire. Yahweh Rophe, the LORD who heals.

And then, immediately: Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water. Twelve springs — one for every tribe. The place was there all along, a short walk beyond Marah. God let them reach the bitter water first, and there is no getting round the fact that he could have routed them to Elim directly. He does not always take his people around the bitter place. Often he takes them through it, and then camps them by the springs on the other side.

15.theology:
Doxology as the response to redemption. The redeemed sing. Salvation accomplished overflows into worship. Theology rightly ends in praise.

The incomparability and holiness of God. "Who is like you, majestic in holiness?" The song magnifies the unique, holy, warrior-King.

The everlasting reign of God. "The LORD will reign forever and ever." The exodus opens onto the eternal kingdom, fulfilled in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: Standing on the far shore with their enemies dead behind them, the redeemed people broke into the oldest song of salvation, exalting the warrior-God, majestic in holiness, who reigns forever.

Now: The proper response to redemption is song. We who have been brought through the waters in Christ join the song of Moses and the Lamb. Our worship now is the rehearsal of the eternal praise we will sing before the throne.

16.title: Bread from Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness,<sup>3</sup>and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.<sup>5</sup>On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily."<sup>6</sup>So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,<sup>7</sup>and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'"<sup>10</sup>And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>12</sup>"I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"<sup>13</sup>In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp.<sup>14</sup>And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground.<sup>15</sup>When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.<sup>16</sup>This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'"<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less.<sup>18</sup>But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.<sup>19</sup>And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning."<sup>20</sup>But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.<sup>21</sup>Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.<sup>22</sup>On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses,<sup>23</sup>he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'"<sup>24</sup>So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it.<sup>25</sup>Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field.<sup>26</sup>Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none."<sup>27</sup>On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none.<sup>28</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?<sup>29</sup>See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day."<sup>30</sup>So the people rested on the seventh day.<sup>31</sup>Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.<sup>32</sup>Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'"<sup>33</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations."<sup>34</sup>As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan.<sup>36</sup>(An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
16.overview:
Barely a month out of Egypt, the redeemed people grumble — not against Pharaoh now, but against God, even wishing they had died in Egypt where at least there was bread. The human heart, even the redeemed heart, is prone to forget grace and crave the security of its old slavery. Yet God responds not with judgment but with mercy: he rains "bread from heaven."

The manna is a daily miracle of provision and a daily lesson in dependence. It must be gathered each morning; it cannot be hoarded; what is kept overnight breeds worms — except on the day before the Sabbath, when a double portion keeps. God teaches his people to trust him one day at a time, to rest on the Sabbath, and to learn that "man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deut. 8:3).

And then Jesus takes up this very manna in John 6: "I am the bread of life... your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died... I am the living bread that came down from heaven." The manna was a shadow; Christ is the substance. As Ferguson reflects, the daily bread of the wilderness points to the One who alone can satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. We feed on him by faith, and we shall never hunger again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-3: One month out, the food runs down and the congregation grumbles, remembering Egypt's meat pots and bread to the full.

Verses 4-12: I am about to rain bread from heaven for you — gathered a day at a time, that I may test them. Moses tells them their grumbling is against the LORD, and the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
Memory Edits Under Pressure

Egypt was infant boys in the river, foremen beaten for a quota with no straw, and a groaning that reached heaven. One month of hunger rewrites four hundred years of that into a fond memory of good catering. People going through a hard obedience often find themselves recalling the thing God rescued them from as though it had been better — and Israel is not lying on purpose. They believe it, which is what makes it dangerous.

The Test Is the Daily-ness

God could as easily have provided a month at a time and deliberately does not. Every household gathers one day's food and no more, so every evening for forty years Israel goes to bed with no visible supply for tomorrow. They are being trained out of the instinct to secure themselves, one day at a time, for a generation. Anyone who has prayed give us this day our daily bread has prayed the manna — reliable provision that cannot be stockpiled, which is what produces trust rather than merely relief (Matt. 6:34).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God's response to a slander is bread. No rebuke and no lecture about ingratitude; he simply feeds them.

Now: Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD. Moses says it twice, and it had not occurred to them. Complaint about circumstance is rarely only that. Behind a grumble about the desert is a verdict on the one who chose the route. And the chapter's answer to it is not a defence but a sight: the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.

verseByVerse.quote: They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One month out. On the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt — the food they carried out has run down, and the whole congregation grumbles.

Listen to what they actually say, because it is one of the most revealing sentences in the book: Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.

Meat pots. Bread to the full. That is not what Egypt was. Egypt was infant boys in the river, foremen beaten for a quota with no straw, and a groaning that reached heaven. One month of hunger has rewritten four hundred years of slavery into a fond memory of good catering.

Memory is not a neutral faculty. Under pressure it edits, and it edits in favour of whatever we have left behind — which is why people going through a hard obedience so often find themselves recalling the thing God rescued them from as though it had been better. Israel is not lying on purpose here. They believe it. That is what makes it dangerous.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily." So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?" And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's response to a slander is bread. Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you. No rebuke, no lecture about ingratitude — he simply feeds them.

But the arrangement has a purpose attached, and it is stated openly: the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.

The test is the daily-ness. God could as easily have provided a month at a time, and deliberately does not. Every household must go out every morning and collect that day's food and no more, which means that every single evening for forty years Israel goes to bed with no visible supply for tomorrow. They are being trained out of the instinct to secure themselves, one day at a time, for a generation.

Anyone who has prayed give us this day our daily bread has prayed the manna. Jesus put the same word in the middle of the Lord's Prayer — this day, daily — and taught the same lesson underneath it: do not be anxious about tomorrow (Matt. 6:34). The provision is reliable and it is not stockpilable, and that combination is what produces trust rather than merely relief.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'" And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud. And the LORD said to Moses, "I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses says something the people had not considered: Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD. He says it twice. They thought they were complaining about the catering arrangements and about the management. Complaint about circumstance is rarely only that. Behind a grumble about the desert is a verdict on the one who chose the route.

And the chapter's answer to the grumbling is not a defence. It is a sight: they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: Quail in the evening, manna in the morning. What is it? becomes its name. An omer a head, and whoever gathered much had nothing left over. Some keep it overnight against orders, and it bred worms and stank.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Name Is a Question

The Hebrew man hu — "what is it?" — became the word. For forty years Israel ate a food called What-is-it? and never found a better name. Their daily bread was permanently labelled with their own bewilderment.

Paul's Argument for Generosity

The strong gatherers and the weak ended each morning with the same amount, and Paul quotes verse 18 directly when asking the Corinthians for money for the poor: Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (2 Cor. 8:15). God's economy has always tended toward the levelling of plenty and need, and the church is meant to reproduce it on purpose.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They hoarded against a God who had never once failed to deliver — on the first morning after he started.

Now: What they kept did not merely fail to help. It rotted, in the tent, overnight. There is a whole doctrine of anxiety in that verse: what is grasped past the day it was given for does not keep. It goes bad in the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp. And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'" And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less. But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The quail come in the evening and the manna in the morning, and the description is careful: a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground.

Then a lovely detail. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. The Hebrew is man hu — and that question became the name. For forty years Israel ate a food called What-is-it?, every morning, and never got a better word for it. Their daily bread was permanently labelled with their own bewilderment.

Then the ration: an omer a head, and the result recorded in verse 18 — whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. The strong gatherers and the weak ones ended the morning with the same amount. Paul quotes that verse directly when he is asking the Corinthians for money for the poor in Jerusalem: as it is written, "Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack" (2 Cor. 8:15). The manna is his argument for Christian generosity — God's economy has always tended toward the levelling of plenty and need, and the church is supposed to reproduce it on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning." But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them. Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the rule that was disobeyed immediately: let no one leave any of it over till the morning. Some did. It bred worms and stank.

They were hoarding against a God who had never once failed to deliver, on the first morning after he started. And what they kept did not merely fail to help — it rotted, in the tent, overnight. There is a whole doctrine of anxiety in that verse. What is grasped past the day it was given for does not keep. It goes bad in the hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-36 — The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 22-30: A double portion on the sixth day, and Israel's first Sabbath — weeks before Sinai. Some hoard when they should not and some gather when there is nothing. See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath.

Verses 31-36: The manna described, an omer preserved throughout your generations, and the closing note: they ate it forty years, till they came to a habitable land.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gift Before It Is a Rule

Israel keeps a sabbath here weeks before the commandment exists, and it arrives by means of the double portion — God does not command a day off and leave them to work out the arithmetic; he supplies Friday with enough for Saturday. Which is exactly the argument Jesus made to men who had turned it back into a burden: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The True Bread

A crowd once raised this chapter against Jesus — our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness — and he corrected them twice over. It was not Moses who gave it, and the manna was never the real thing: I am the bread of life. Then the sentence that emptied the hillside: Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die (John 6:31-51).

That is the measure of it. The manna was miraculous and it arrived every morning for forty years, and every person who ate it is dead. It carried a nation across a desert and could not carry one of them past their own lifetime. Then bread came down that a man could eat and not die, and it was a person — standing in front of people whose great-grandfathers had gathered flakes off the ground and asked what is it? The question Israel could never answer had an answer all along.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel breaks the rule in both directions inside a fortnight — hoarding when told to trust, working when told to rest. And the sixth-day portion, kept overnight on God's instruction, did not stink. Same food, same night, opposite result: what rots when grasped keeps perfectly when it is obeyed.

Now: The jar of manna ends up in the ark, beside the tablets and Aaron's staff (Heb. 9:4) — Israel's holiest object contains a sample of breakfast. And the closing note is flat and enormous: forty years, every morning, never once failing, including every morning after the golden calf and after Kadesh. God went on putting breakfast on the ground for a nation that spent four decades complaining about it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses, he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'" So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it. Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none." On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none. And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day." So the people rested on the seventh day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the sixth day twice as much falls, and Moses explains why: Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.

This is the first time Israel keeps a sabbath, and the date matters: it is weeks before Sinai. The commandment has not yet been given, and the practice is already in place. Rest is not first a law imposed on Israel; it is a provision arranged for them — and it arrives, note, by means of the double portion. God does not command a day off and leave them to work out the arithmetic. He supplies Friday with enough for Saturday.

Two failures follow immediately, and they are opposite. Some kept manna overnight when they should not have (v.20) and it rotted; now some go out to gather on the seventh day when there is none, and find nothing. Israel manages to break the rule in both directions inside a fortnight — hoarding when told to trust, and working when told to rest.

And the sixth-day portion, kept overnight on God's instruction, did not stink, and there were no worms in it. The same food, the same night, the opposite result. What rots when grasped keeps perfectly when it is obeyed.

Then God's exasperated question: How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? — and the summary that Jesus would later stand on: See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath. Given. It is a gift before it is a rule, which is exactly the argument Jesus made to men who had turned it back into a burden: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey. Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'" And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations." As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the details and one striking instruction. The manna was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey. And an omer of it is to be kept throughout your generations, that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness.

That jar ends up in the ark of the covenant, beside the tablets of the law and Aaron's staff (Heb. 9:4). Israel's holiest object contains a sample of breakfast. Along with the covenant and the priesthood, the nation preserved physical evidence that God had fed them when there was nothing — because they would need reminding, and because forty years of daily provision is precisely the sort of thing a people forgets.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan. (An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the flat closing note: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. Forty years. Every morning. It never once failed, including on all the mornings after the golden calf, after Kadesh, after every rebellion in the book of Numbers. God went on putting breakfast on the ground for a nation that spent four decades complaining about it.

Fifteen centuries later a crowd that had just been fed on a hillside came looking for more, and raised this chapter as a challenge: Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, "He gave them bread from heaven to eat." And Jesus corrected them on two points at once. It was not Moses who gave it, and the manna was never the real thing: my Father gives you the true bread from heaven... I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger. Then the sentence that emptied the hillside: Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die (John 6:31-51).

That is the measure of it. The manna was excellent, it was miraculous, it arrived every morning for forty years — and every single person who ate it is dead. It kept a nation alive across a desert and it could not keep one of them alive past their own lifetime. Then bread came down that a man could eat and not die, and it was a person, and he said so standing in front of people whose great-grandfathers had gathered flakes off the ground and asked what is it? The question Israel could never answer had an answer all along, and he was walking about in Galilee.

16.theology:
The grumbling heart and patient grace. The redeemed forget grace and idealize bondage, yet God answers murmuring with merciful provision.

Daily dependence. The manna teaches trust for each day, contentment, Sabbath rest, and the truth that man lives by every word of God.

Christ the bread of life. The manna is fulfilled in Jesus (John 6), the living bread from heaven who alone satisfies the soul's hunger forever.
16.examples:
Then: When the redeemed grumbled and longed for Egypt's bread, God rained manna from heaven, feeding them daily for forty years and teaching them to depend on him one day at a time.

Now: We still crave the security of our old slaveries and forget past mercies. God still calls us to daily dependence — "give us this day our daily bread" — and offers us himself, the true bread from heaven. Feeding on Christ by faith, we shall never hunger.

17.title: The Rock and the Uplifted Hands
17.text: <sup>1</sup>All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.<sup>2</sup>Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?"<sup>3</sup>But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?"<sup>4</sup>So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"<sup>8</sup>Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.<sup>9</sup>So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."<sup>10</sup>So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.<sup>11</sup>Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.<sup>12</sup>But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.<sup>13</sup>And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven."<sup>15</sup>And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner,<sup>16</sup>saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
17.overview:
Two scenes, both pointing to Christ. First, the people thirst and quarrel, testing God: "Is the LORD among us or not?" God commands Moses to strike a rock at Horeb, and water gushes out to give the people life. Paul interprets it unmistakably: "they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:4). The Rock must be struck for the water of life to flow — and at Calvary, Christ our Rock was struck by the rod of God's judgment, that the living water of the Spirit might pour out to a thirsting people. Strikingly, God says, "I will stand before you there on the rock" — God himself takes the place of judgment as the rock is struck.

Second, Amalek attacks, and as long as Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails; when his hands grow weary, Israel falters — so Aaron and Hur hold up his hands until sunset. Here is a picture of intercession: the battle below is won by the uplifted hands above. Moses the mediator, with arms outstretched, prevails for his people — prefiguring the greater Mediator whose arms were outstretched on a cross and who "always lives to make intercession" for us (Heb. 7:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Water from the Struck Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-4: No water at Rephidim, and this time the people quarreled with Moses — a legal word: they are bringing a case. Moses prays that they are almost ready to stone me.

Verses 5-7: God stands on the rock at Horeb and tells Moses to strike it with the staff that struck the Nile, before witnesses. Water comes out, and the place is named Massah and Meribah for their question, Is the LORD among us or not?
verseByVerse.theology:
God Puts Himself on the Rock

Three things sit in verse 5-6. The staff is named specifically as the staff with which you struck the Nile — the instrument of judgement on Egypt. The elders are brought as official witnesses. And God says I will stand before you there on the rock, and then tells Moses to strike it. The staff of judgement comes down where God has said he will be standing, and what comes out is not fire but water, and a nation that deserved nothing drinks and lives. Paul says it plainly: they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4).

Why the Second Rock Cost Moses the Land

Decades later Moses struck a rock in anger after being told to speak to it, and lost Canaan over it (Num. 20:8-12). The rock is struck once; after that it is spoken to. He broke a picture, and the picture was of the one offered once to bear the sins of many (Heb. 9:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The leader of the exodus is a few minutes from being stoned by the people he delivered, over water, six weeks after the sea.

Now: Is the LORD among us or not? They asked it standing under the pillar of cloud, six weeks after walking through a sea on dry ground, with bread from heaven lying on the ground around their feet. Evidence is not what settles that question, which is why more of it is so rarely the answer to it.

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?" But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No water again, and this time the language hardens. In chapter 15 they grumbled; here the people quarreled with Moses, and the word is a legal one — they are bringing a case against him. Give us water to drink.

Moses' answer names what is really happening: Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD? And their reply is the old accusation with the volume up: Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?

Then Moses prays a prayer that is almost comic in its desperation: What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me. The leader of the exodus is a few minutes from being killed by the people he delivered, over water, six weeks after the sea.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's instruction is extraordinary, and it repays reading slowly.

Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink.

Three things are in that sentence. First, the staff named specifically as the staff with which you struck the Nile — the instrument of judgement on Egypt. Second, the elders are to come and watch, so there are official witnesses. And third, and this is the astonishing part: I will stand before you there on the rock.

God places himself on the rock, and then tells Moses to strike it.

The staff of judgement comes down in the presence of witnesses on the place where God has said he will be standing, and what comes out is not fire but water, and a nation that deserved nothing drinks and lives. Whatever Moses understood at the time, the shape of it is unmistakable — and Paul, looking back, says it plainly: they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4).

That is why it mattered so much, decades later, when Moses struck a second rock in anger after being told to speak to it (Num. 20:8-12), and lost the promised land over it. The rock is struck once. After that it is spoken to. He broke a picture, and the picture was of the one who was offered once to bear the sins of many (Heb. 9:28).

The place is named for the quarrel — Massah, testing, and Meribah, quarrelling — and the question they asked is preserved with it: Is the LORD among us or not? They asked it standing under the pillar of cloud, six weeks after walking through a sea on dry ground, with bread from heaven on the ground around their feet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-13: Amalek attacks. Joshua fights; Moses climbs the hill with the staff; and when his hands grow weary Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Halves That Belong Together

In the first half a rock is struck and water pours out for people who had just accused God of bringing them out to kill them. In the second, that same people is attacked at its weakest point and defended. God gives his enemies water and then fights for them — and the arms that had to be held up on that hill were a temporary version of hands that would one day be stretched out and held in place by nails, with nobody needing to prop them, for a people still quarrelling at the foot of the hill.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Deuteronomy fills in what Exodus leaves out — Amalek attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind (Deut. 25:17-18). They picked off the stragglers: the old, the sick, the mothers with small children at the back of the column.

Now: The man on the hill cannot hold his own arms up. Two men prop him, and one sits him on a stone first because he cannot stand either. Israel's victory that day depended on a tired old man being physically held together by his friends — a picture the church has never needed to improve on. The work goes on because somebody is holding up the arms of the person who cannot hold them up himself, and nobody down in the valley can see it happening.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim. So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, without transition, war. Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.

Deuteronomy fills in the detail Exodus leaves out: Amalek attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind (Deut. 25:17-18). They picked off the stragglers — the old, the sick, the mothers with small children at the back of the column.

Moses sends Joshua to fight — the first appearance of the man who will finish this journey — and climbs a hill with the staff. Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.

Then the detail that keeps this from being a story about a hero: Moses' hands grew weary... and Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. The man on the hill cannot hold his own arms up. Two men have to prop him, and one of them sits him on a stone first because he cannot stand either.

Israel's victory that day depended on a tired old man being physically held together by his friends. It is a picture the church has never needed to improve on: the work goes on because somebody is holding up the arms of the person who cannot hold them up himself, and nobody down in the valley can see it happening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-16 — The LORD Is My Banner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-16: God tells Moses to write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua. Moses builds an altar named The LORD Is My Banner, and war is declared against Amalek from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Command to Write

This is the first time in the Bible that God tells anyone to write something down. The faith carried by telling — the child's question at Passover, the father's answer — is now also to be carried in a book, because tellings drift and Joshua will need this after Moses is dead.

The LORD Is My Banner

A banner is the standard a scattered army rallies to when it can no longer see its commander. Israel has just fought its first battle, and Moses names the altar not after Joshua's tactics or his own raised arms but after the one thing on that field the enemy could not touch.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The war announced on this hill outlasted everyone who fought in it. Amalek runs like a dark thread through the rest of the Old Testament — Saul loses his kingdom over them, and centuries later Haman the Agagite, of Amalekite descent, tries to exterminate every Jew in the Persian empire and is stopped by a young queen.

Now: A faith that depends entirely on accurate memory is one generation from being lost. God's remedy is a book, given at the moment the first leader is visibly ageing and the next one is standing beside him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner, saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things close the chapter, and both look forward a long way.

The first is a command to write: Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua. It is the first time in the Bible that God tells someone to write something down. The faith that has been carried by telling — the child's question at Passover, the father's answer — is now also to be carried in a book, because tellings drift and Joshua will need this after Moses is dead.

The second is the altar, and the name Moses gives it: The LORD Is My Banner — Yahweh Nissi. A banner is the standard a scattered army rallies to when it can no longer see its commander. Israel has just fought its first battle, and Moses does not name the altar after Joshua's tactics or his own raised arms. He names it after the one thing on that field the enemy could not touch.

Then the last line: A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation. And he did. Amalek runs like a dark thread through the rest of the Old Testament — Saul loses his kingdom over them, and centuries later a man named Haman the Agagite, of Amalekite descent, tries to exterminate every Jew in the Persian empire and is stopped by a young queen. The war announced on this hill outlasted everyone who fought in it.

But hold the two halves of the chapter together, because they belong together. In the first half a rock is struck and water pours out for people who had just accused God of bringing them out to kill them. In the second, that same people is attacked at its weakest point and defended. God gives his enemies water and then fights for them — and the arms that had to be held up on the hill were a temporary version of hands that would one day be stretched out and held in place by nails, with nobody needing to prop them, for a people still quarrelling at the foot of the hill.

17.theology:
Christ the struck Rock. The rock struck for water (1 Cor. 10:4) is Christ, struck by God's judgment that living water might flow to thirsting sinners.

The ministry of intercession. Moses' uplifted hands win the battle below, prefiguring Christ's ever-living intercession and the church's call to prevailing prayer.

The LORD our Banner. The battle and the victory are God's. We fight under his standard and credit the triumph to him alone.
17.examples:
Then: God brought water from a struck rock to a thirsting, doubting people, and gave victory over Amalek through the uplifted hands of Moses, held steady by Aaron and Hur until sundown.

Now: Christ our Rock was struck that the living water of the Spirit might flow to us; he ever lives, with hands once outstretched on the cross, to intercede for us. And the church wins its battles under the LORD's banner, holding up one another in prayer.

18.title: Wise Counsel and Shared Burdens
