18.text: <sup>1</sup>Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home,<sup>3</sup>along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"),<sup>4</sup>and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh").<sup>5</sup>Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God.<sup>6</sup>And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"<sup>7</sup>Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent.<sup>8</sup>Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them.<sup>9</sup>And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>10</sup>Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>11</sup>Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people."<sup>12</sup>And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.<sup>13</sup>The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening.<sup>14</sup>When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?"<sup>15</sup>And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God;<sup>16</sup>when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws."<sup>17</sup>Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good.<sup>18</sup>You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.<sup>19</sup>Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God,<sup>20</sup>and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do.<sup>21</sup>Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>22</sup>And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you.<sup>23</sup>If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."<sup>24</sup>So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.<sup>25</sup>Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>26</sup>And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves.<sup>27</sup>Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
18.overview:
After the great deliverance comes a quieter but vital chapter on leadership and community. Jethro, Moses' Midianite father-in-law, hears all that God has done, comes to Moses, and rejoices, confessing, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods." Here is an early fruit of the exodus among the nations — a Gentile priest worshiping the God of Israel. The mighty acts of God draw the watching world to praise.

Then Jethro observes Moses single-handedly judging the people from morning to evening and gives wise counsel: this will wear you out; the burden is too heavy to bear alone. Appoint capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate a bribe, and share the load. The principle is profound for every leader and every church: ministry is not a solo performance but a shared calling. As MacArthur notes, the wise leader multiplies himself through others, raising up and entrusting godly people with real responsibility.

This is the seed of biblical delegation and the discipleship principle — the same wisdom that shapes the appointment of elders and deacons in the New Testament church. The qualifications Jethro names — fearing God, trustworthy, hating bribes — are deeply spiritual, not merely managerial. God's work must be done by God's kind of people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: Jethro brings Zipporah and Moses' two sons. Moses tells him everything — the deliverance and all the hardship — and Jethro responds with a confession, Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, a burnt offering, and a meal with the elders before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Confession in Exodus Comes From an Outsider

Jethro is a Midianite priest. He was not in Egypt and did not walk through the sea, and he is the first person in the book to state plainly that the LORD is supreme. The Egyptians were told repeatedly that they would know, and did not. A foreign priest hears it secondhand over dinner and believes.

That pattern never stops — the Roman centurion at the cross saying truly this man was the Son of God while the authorities jeer; the Samaritan leper who came back; the God-fearing Egyptians who marked a door. The people best placed to believe frequently do not, and the outsider hearing it for the first time frequently does.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The boys' names are a short autobiography — Gershom, I have been a sojourner in a foreign land; Eliezer, The God of my father was my help. Moses named his sons after his exile and his rescue.

Now: Moses tells the story unedited: the deliverance and all the hardship — the thirst, the bitter water, the grumbling, Amalek. He does not tidy the testimony to make God look better, and the hearer believes anyway. A rescue narrative with the hard parts left in is more convincing, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home, along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"), and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh"). Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God. And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jethro arrives, bringing Zipporah and the two sons Moses had sent home at some point during the confrontation with Egypt. The names of the boys are given, and they are a short autobiography: Gershom, I have been a sojourner in a foreign land, and Eliezer, The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh. Moses named his sons after his exile and his rescue.

Then Moses does something the chapter turns on: Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. Not the edited version. The deliverance and all the hardship — the thirst, the bitter water, the grumbling, Amalek.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent. Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians. Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians. Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people." And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jethro's response is the most striking thing here: Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel... "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you... Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods." Then he offers a burnt offering, and Aaron and all the elders of Israel eat bread with him before God.

Jethro is a Midianite priest. He is not an Israelite, he was not in Egypt, and he did not walk through the sea — and he is the first person in the book of Exodus to make a clear confession of faith in the LORD as supreme. The Egyptians were told repeatedly that they would know, and did not. A foreign priest hears the story secondhand from his son-in-law and believes it.

That pattern never stops. It is the Roman centurion at the cross saying truly this man was the Son of God while the religious authorities jeer, and the Samaritan leper who came back, and the God-fearing Egyptians who marked a door. The people best placed to believe frequently do not, and the outsider hearing it for the first time frequently does.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-23: Jethro watches Moses judge alone from morning till evening and tells him what you are doing is not good... You are not able to do it alone. The remedy is delegation to able men, such as fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, in tiers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seed of Shared Leadership

Moses keeps what only he can do — representing the people before God, and teaching them the way in which they must walk — and gives away the rest. The qualifications are mostly moral rather than technical. This is the pattern behind the seventy elders of Numbers 11 and the apostles in Acts 6: it is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables, and seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom appointed to do it. The work is real, the man is finite, and the answer is not heroism but structure.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses' defence is entirely spiritual and entirely sincere. He is not empire-building; he is doing exactly what the people need, personally, all day, every day. And it is still wrong.

Now: Two things in the rebuke deserve attention. Jethro names both casualties — Moses will wear out, and so will the people with you, because a nation queueing all day is being badly served by the arrangement that looks most devoted. And the diagnosis is arithmetic, not sin: the thing is too heavy for you. There is no suggestion that Moses should pray harder about his stamina.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening. When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?" And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God; when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws." Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day Jethro watches Moses work, and what he sees alarms him. Moses sits alone as judge from morning till evening, with the entire nation queueing.

Moses' defence is entirely spiritual and entirely sincere: the people come to me to inquire of God... and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws. This is real ministry. He is not empire-building; he is doing exactly what the people need, personally, all day, every day.

And Jethro tells him it is wrong. What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.

Two things in that rebuke deserve attention. First, Jethro names both casualties: Moses will burn out, and the people with you will too, because a nation waiting all day in a queue is being badly served by the very arrangement that looks most devoted. Second, the diagnosis is not laziness or pride but arithmetic. The thing is too heavy. There is no rebuke for lack of faith and no suggestion Moses should pray harder about his stamina.

verseByVerse.quote: Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God, and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do. Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you. If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remedy is structure: Moses keeps what only he can do — representing the people before God, and teaching them the way in which they must walk and what they must do — and delegates the rest to capable men in tiers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. The qualifications are worth noting because they are mostly moral rather than technical: able men, such as fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe.

This is the seed of everything the Bible later says about shared leadership — the seventy elders of Numbers 11, and the apostles in Acts 6 saying it is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables, and appointing seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom to do it. The pattern is identical: the work is real, the man is finite, and the answer is not heroism but structure.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 24-27: So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said — and then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
verseByVerse.theology:
Who Is Being Corrected

Moses has spoken with God from a burning bush, faced down Pharaoh, called down ten plagues, divided a sea and brought bread out of the sky. The advice comes from his wife's father, who arrived last week and knows the God of Israel only through a story told over dinner. Moses does not defend himself, appeal to his call, or point out that Jethro was not there — he reorganises the judicial system of the nation on the strength of it. The meekest man on earth (Num. 12:3) is the one who can take a management correction from a relative without feeling his commission has been questioned.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jethro goes home. He does not stay for Sinai, one chapter away, and never enters the land.

Now: He came, he heard, he believed, he blessed, he fixed something that needed fixing, and he left. Not everyone who helps the people of God is called to stay with them, and a contribution is not diminished by being brief.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said. Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves. Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.

Consider who is being corrected. Moses has spoken with God from a burning bush, faced down Pharaoh, called down ten plagues, divided a sea, and brought bread out of the sky. The advice comes from his wife's father, a Midianite priest, who arrived last week and has never met the God of Israel except through a story he was told over dinner.

And Moses does not defend himself, does not appeal to his call, and does not point out that Jethro was not there for any of it. He listens, and he reorganises the entire judicial system of the nation on the strength of it.

It is a small verse and it says a great deal about the man. The meekest man on earth (Num. 12:3) is the one who can take a management correction from a relative without feeling that his commission has been questioned.

Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country. Jethro goes home. He does not stay for Sinai, which is one chapter away, and he does not enter the land. He came, he heard, he believed, he blessed, he fixed something that needed fixing, and he left.

18.theology:
The nations drawn to worship. Jethro the Gentile confesses the LORD's supremacy — a first fruit of God's purpose to be known among all peoples.

Shared leadership and delegation. Ministry is a shared calling. Wise leaders multiply themselves through godly, qualified people rather than carrying every burden alone.

Character before competence. The qualifications for leadership are chiefly spiritual — fearing God, integrity, hating bribes — anticipating New Testament eldership.
18.examples:
Then: A Gentile priest worshiped the God of the exodus, then gave Moses wise counsel to share the crushing burden of leadership with capable, God-fearing men — and the humble leader listened.

Now: Our salvation testifies to the watching world and draws others to worship. And the work of ministry is shared, not centralized: God raises up qualified, godly leaders to carry the load together, and wise leaders humbly receive counsel and delegate the work.

19.title: The Mountain That Burned with Fire
19.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>2</sup>They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain,<sup>3</sup>while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel:<sup>4</sup>'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.<sup>5</sup>Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine;<sup>6</sup>and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."<sup>7</sup>So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him.<sup>8</sup>All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,<sup>10</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments<sup>11</sup>and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.<sup>12</sup>And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain."<sup>14</sup>So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments.<sup>15</sup>And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."<sup>16</sup>On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled.<sup>17</sup>Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain.<sup>18</sup>Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly.<sup>19</sup>And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder.<sup>20</sup>The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish.<sup>22</sup>Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them."<sup>23</sup>And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them."<sup>25</sup>So Moses went down to the people and told them.
19.overview:
Three months out of Egypt, Israel arrives at Sinai, and the covenant is formally established. God's opening words are pure grace: "I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself." Notice the order — redemption first, then covenant; deliverance first, then law. God did not give the law so Israel could earn salvation; he saved them first and then called them to covenant obedience as the redeemed. This is the gospel logic that permeates all of Scripture: we obey because we are saved, not in order to be saved.

God's purpose is breathtaking: "you shall be my treasured possession... a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Peter applies these very words to the church (1 Pet. 2:9). The redeemed are God's prized treasure, set apart to mediate his presence to the world. But to be near this God, the people must be consecrated, for he is holy. The mountain quakes, wrapped in fire and smoke; thunder and trumpet sound; the people tremble. Bounds are set so none may touch the mountain and die.

Here Sproul's great theme thunders forth: the holiness of God. To draw near to God is no light thing. The trembling at Sinai prepares us to marvel that in Christ we now "come to Mount Zion" with boldness (Heb. 12). The fire that terrified Israel is the same holiness that, in Christ, becomes our welcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-6: Three months out, at the mountain of the bush. God reminds them first — I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself — then offers the covenant: you shall be my treasured possession... a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Brought to Myself

Not brought you out of Egypt and not brought you to Canaan. The exodus was never primarily a change of address; it was God collecting a people for himself, and the land is where they will live with him rather than the point of the exercise.

Grace Before Law, and the Order Governs Everything

The rescue came first. Israel was not delivered for keeping the law — the law is given to a people already redeemed, already carried, already brought. Ten chapters of grace precede one syllable of commandment, and the next two chapters cannot be read rightly without that order in view.

Chosen For the Nations, Not Instead of Them

Segullah is a king's personal treasure, kept apart from the state holdings. And a kingdom of priests means the whole nation is to do for the world what a priest does for a congregation: stand in between. The clause all the earth is mine is there so nobody mistakes election for favouritism. Peter hands every word of it to the church — a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession (1 Pet. 2:9) — same titles, same purpose, same order: called out first, then commissioned.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God's first words at Sinai are not a demand but a reminder of what he has already done.

Now: Any reading of the commandments that starts at chapter 20 has already gone wrong. The law arrives addressed to people who were slaves three months ago and are standing at that mountain only because someone carried them there.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain, while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel: 'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months out of Egypt they arrive at the mountain where the bush burned, and God's first words are not a demand but a reminder: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.

Notice the destination in that sentence. Not brought you out of Egypt, and not brought you to Canaan — brought you to myself. The exodus was never primarily a change of address. It was God collecting a people for himself, and the land is where they will live with him, not the point of the exercise.

And the order matters enormously, because everything about how to read the next two chapters depends on it. The rescue came first. Israel was not delivered because they kept the law; the law is being given to a people already redeemed, already carried, already brought. Ten chapters of grace precede one syllable of commandment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the offer: if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

The phrase treasured possession is segullah — a king's personal treasure, the private hoard kept apart from the state holdings. And a kingdom of priests means the whole nation is to do for the world what a priest does for a congregation: stand in between, and represent God to people who do not know him. Israel is not chosen instead of the nations. It is chosen for them, and the clause all the earth is mine is there so nobody mistakes election for favouritism.

Peter picks up every word of this and hands it to the church: you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light (1 Pet. 2:9). Same titles, same purpose, and the same order — called out first, then commissioned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-15 — Consecration for the Holy God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 7-12: The people answer All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and God orders three days of consecration and washed garments, with a boundary round the mountain under penalty of death.

Verses 13-15: Not even the executioner may touch an offender; the people are to be ready for the third day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sincerity Is Not Capacity

They will say all that the LORD has spoken we will do again twice (24:3, 24:7) — and build a golden calf within forty days of the last time. There is no reason to doubt they meant it, and that is the point. Sincerity at the moment of promising is not the same as ability to perform, and everything that follows is an exposition of the difference.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The boundary is absolute — no hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot. Not even the one carrying out the sentence may make contact with someone who has touched the holy mountain.

Now: It is deliberately overwhelming, and it teaches one thing before a word of law is spoken: this God cannot be approached casually. The people who watched him drown an army are now told to stay behind a line.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people answer with total confidence: All that the LORD has spoken we will do.

They will say it again in 24:3 and 24:7. And they will have built a golden calf within forty days of saying it the last time. There is no reason to doubt that they meant it, and that is the point — sincerity at the moment of promising is not the same as capacity to perform, and the entire history that follows is an exposition of the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain." So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments. And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the preparation: three days of consecration, washed garments, and a boundary set round the mountain with a death penalty attached. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death... no hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot. Not even the executioner may make contact with someone who has touched the holy mountain.

It is deliberately overwhelming, and its purpose is to teach one thing before a word of law is spoken: this God cannot be approached casually. The people who watched him drown an army are now being told to stay behind a line.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-25: Thunder, lightning, thick cloud, a mountain smoking like the smoke of a kiln and shaking, and a trumpet growing louder and louder. Moses is sent down to warn the people again lest he break out against them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Hebrews deliberately describes this scene — a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them, with even Moses saying I tremble with fear — and then says: But you have not come to that. You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God... and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb. 12:18-24).

The difference between the two mountains is the whole gospel. At Sinai the barrier was put up to keep people alive; the holiness that would have killed them was real and the fear was appropriate. At Zion that holiness is undiminished and the barrier is gone — not because God became less holy but because a mediator went up the mountain and came back with his own blood, and the boundary was moved to the far side of him. Israel stood at the foot of a burning mountain and begged for the voice to stop. The church is invited to a festal gathering at the top of one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The strangest detail is the trumpet. A blast in a desert with no trumpeter, and it does not fade the way a horn does when a man runs out of breath. It grows.

Now: Moses protests that he has already set the boundary and the people know, and God insists anyway. The concern is not that they will be too frightened to come near. It is that they will not be frightened enough.

verseByVerse.quote: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled. Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain. Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly. And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder. The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third morning arrives and the description is meant to frighten: thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled. The mountain wrapped in smoke like the smoke of a kiln, the whole mass of it shaking, and a trumpet growing louder and louder.

The last detail is the strangest. A trumpet blast, in a desert, with no trumpeter — and it does not fade as a horn does when a man runs out of breath. It grows.

Then Moses is sent down again to warn them again, and he protests that he has already set the boundary and they know. God insists. Go down and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them. The concern is not that the people will be too frightened to come near. It is that they will not be frightened enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish. Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them." And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'" And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them." So Moses went down to the people and told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold this chapter beside the one place in the New Testament that deliberately describes it. The writer to the Hebrews lists it all — a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them — and records that even Moses said I tremble with fear. And then he says: But you have not come to that.

You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering... and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb. 12:18-24).

Two mountains, and the difference between them is the whole gospel. At Sinai the barrier was put up to keep people alive, and the holiness that would have killed them was real, and the fear was appropriate. At Zion the same holiness is undiminished and the barrier is gone — not because God became less holy but because a mediator went up the mountain and came back down with his own blood, and the boundary line was moved to the far side of him. Israel stood at the foot of a burning mountain and begged for the voice to stop. The church is invited to a festal gathering at the top of one.

19.theology:
Grace before law. God redeems first, then gives the covenant. Obedience flows from salvation, never earns it. The whole gospel logic stands here.

A treasured, priestly people. God claims the redeemed as his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests — fulfilled in the church (1 Pet. 2:9).

The holiness of God. The fire, smoke, and trembling at Sinai reveal a holy God whom sinners cannot approach casually — driving us to the Mediator.
19.examples:
Then: Having borne his people on eagles' wings out of Egypt, God established his covenant at a mountain that burned with fire and trembled, calling redeemed slaves to be his treasured, priestly, holy people.

Now: We are saved by grace and then called to holy obedience as God's treasured possession and royal priesthood. The terror of Sinai reminds us how holy God is — and how amazing it is that in Christ we now draw near to that same God with boldness and joy.

20.title: The Ten Words: Law as Gift
20.text: <sup>1</sup>And God spoke all these words, saying,<sup>2</sup>"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>3</sup>"You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>4</sup>"You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>5</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>6</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>7</sup>"You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>8</sup>"Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.<sup>9</sup>Six days you shall labor, and do all your work,<sup>10</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates.<sup>11</sup>For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.<sup>12</sup>"Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not murder.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not commit adultery.<sup>15</sup>"You shall not steal.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."<sup>18</sup>Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off<sup>19</sup>and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die."<sup>20</sup>Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin."<sup>21</sup>The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven.<sup>23</sup>You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.<sup>24</sup>An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.<sup>25</sup>If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
20.overview:
The Ten Commandments — the moral heart of God's law — do not begin with a command but with the gospel: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery." The law is framed by grace. God speaks first as Redeemer, then as Lawgiver. The commandments are not a ladder by which slaves climb to freedom; they are the shape of life for a people already redeemed. As Keller often said, the law is not how we get saved but how saved people live in grateful love.

The commandments fall into two tables: the first four govern our love for God — no other gods, no idols, reverence for his name, the Sabbath; the last six govern our love for neighbor — honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie, or covet. Jesus summarized them all in love for God and neighbor. They are a gift, revealing both the character of the God who gave them and the path of true human flourishing.

Yet the law also has a deeper purpose. As Paul teaches, "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Rom. 3:20). The perfect standard of the commandments exposes our utter inability to keep them and drives us to Christ, who kept the law perfectly in our place and bore its curse on the cross. The law is a schoolmaster leading us to Christ (Gal. 3:24). The thunder at Sinai is meant to make us run to the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — The First Table: Love for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: Before a single command, a sentence of history: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

Verses 3-6: No other gods, and no carved image — for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting iniquity to three or four generations but showing steadfast love to thousands.

Verses 7-8: The name not to be taken in vain; and Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.

Verses 9-11: Six days of labour and a seventh of rest — for sons, daughters, servants, livestock and the sojourner — grounded in creation itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 2 Governs Everything After It

The commandments do not begin obey me and I will be your God. They begin with a God who has already acted, addressing people who are already his. Israel is not being told how to earn deliverance but how a delivered people lives. Get that order wrong and the Decalogue becomes a ladder; keep it, and it is the shape of gratitude — which is how the New Testament handles it: If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15), love first, keeping second.

Why the Second Commandment Is Separate From the First

The first forbids worshipping the wrong God; the second, worshipping the right God in the wrong way. Israel's calf will not be a foreign deity — Aaron announces a feast to the LORD (32:5). They break the second while sincerely intending to keep the first, which is exactly why it needed saying twice.

Jealousy, and the Lopsided Arithmetic

Jealousy is contemptible where a man has no claim and precisely right where he does. God's is not insecurity but the response of a husband to unfaithfulness. And note the asymmetry in verses 5-6: three or four generations against thousands. The clause of those who hate me is load-bearing — Ezekiel states the principle flatly, the soul who sins shall die (Ezek. 18:20) — and what is described is how idolatry propagates through a family that keeps choosing it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Remember the Sabbath, not "institute" it. They had kept it since the manna (16:23), weeks before this mountain. The commandment codifies a gift already given.

Now: Read the list in verse 10. It is not a list of people who may rest but of people the head of a household is forbidden to make work — sons, daughters, servants, foreign workers, animals. A man could not keep this privately while running his farm on somebody else's labour. It is the first labour law in history, protecting those with no power to protect themselves, handed to a nation that was itself slave labour ninety days earlier (Deut. 5:15).

And taking the name in vain is wider than bad language — narrowing it to that is how it gets quietly obeyed and entirely missed. To bear God's name emptily is to carry it without weight, and the heaviest form is the one nobody notices: someone called by the name of Christ whose life empties it of content in front of the people who know them.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke all these words, saying, "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single command, a sentence of history: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

Everything depends on that being verse 2 rather than verse 20. The commandments do not begin obey me and I will be your God. They begin with a God who has already acted, addressing people who are already his, and the whole Decalogue hangs off a rescue that is finished before it is mentioned. Israel is not being told how to earn deliverance. They are being told how a delivered people lives.

Get that order wrong and the Ten Commandments become a ladder. Keep it, and they are the shape of gratitude — which is exactly how the New Testament handles them. If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15) puts the love first and the keeping second, in the same order Sinai does.

And note the pronoun: the LORD your God. This is covenant language, not the decree of a distant legislator. He is not issuing regulations to strangers.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall have no other gods before me. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall have no other gods before me. The Hebrew is literally before my face — not merely "ahead of me in rank" but "in my presence," which is everywhere. There is no location where a rival may be quietly kept.

Then the second: You shall not make for yourself a carved image. The two are distinct and it matters. The first forbids worshipping the wrong God; the second forbids worshipping the right God in the wrong way. Israel's calf in chapter 32 will not be a foreign deity — Aaron announces a feast to the LORD (32:5). They break the second commandment while sincerely intending to keep the first, which is why it needed saying separately.

The reason given is jealousy: for I the LORD your God am a jealous God. That word troubles people, and it should be explained rather than defended. Jealousy is contemptible when a man has no claim on the woman he is jealous over. It is precisely right when he does. God's jealousy is not insecurity; it is the appropriate response of a husband to a wife's unfaithfulness, and Scripture uses exactly that image for it repeatedly.

Then the sentence that troubles readers most: visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.

Two things belong here. The clause of those who hate me is doing real work — it is not innocent descendants punished for an ancestor's sin, and Ezekiel later states the principle flatly: the soul who sins shall die, and a son shall not bear the guilt of his father (Ezek. 18:20). What is being described is the observable way idolatry propagates through a family that keeps choosing it. And then the asymmetry, which is the real point: three or four generations against thousands. The arithmetic is deliberately lopsided. Judgement is measured in handfuls of generations; steadfast love is measured in thousands.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain.

The word translated in vain means empty, worthless, to no purpose. Casual swearing is included, but the commandment is much wider than bad language, and narrowing it to that is how it gets quietly obeyed and entirely missed. To bear God's name emptily is to carry it without weight — to invoke it in an oath you do not intend to keep, to claim his authority for your own preference, to be called by his name and live in a way that makes it meaningless to those watching.

The heaviest form is the one nobody notices: a person who bears the name of Christ and whose life empties it of content in front of the people who know them. That is the commandment's own logic — the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.

Then verse 8, and the fourth commandment begins: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Remember — not "institute". They had already been keeping it since the manna (16:23), weeks before this mountain. The commandment codifies a gift they had already been given.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates.

Read the list. It is not a list of people who may rest; it is a list of people the head of the household is forbidden to make work. Sons and daughters. Servants. Foreign workers. Animals. A man could not keep this commandment privately while running his farm on somebody else's labour. The Sabbath is the first labour law in human history, and it protects precisely those with no power to protect themselves — which is a startling thing to hand to a nation that was itself a slave labour force ninety days ago. Deuteronomy makes that link explicit when it repeats the commandment: you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15). People who have been worked without rest are not to do it to anyone else, down to the ox.

And the reason given here is different and larger: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth... and rested the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy. The rhythm is not an arrangement for human productivity. It is built into the world, and keeping it is an act of imitation.

Underneath it is a claim about trust, which is why the manna taught it first. To stop for a day is to act out the belief that the world is held up by someone else, and that six days of your labour plus God is more than seven days of your labour alone. Refusing to rest is not usually a scheduling problem. It is a quiet statement about who is keeping things going.

And the New Testament does something remarkable with this commandment, so it should be said carefully. Jesus called himself lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28) and repeatedly healed on it, insisting it was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone pass judgement on them regarding a Sabbath, since these things are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col. 2:16-17). And Hebrews says there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, entered by faith rather than by a calendar (Heb. 4:9-10). Godly readers differ over how much of the day's observance carries into the new covenant, and the question is a genuine one. What is not in dispute is where the rest finally comes from: not from a day, but from a person who said come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — The Second Table: Love for Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 12: Honor your father and your mother — the hinge between the commandments about God and those about neighbour.

Verses 13-14: You shall not murder; You shall not commit adultery.

Verses 15-17: Theft, false witness, and the tenth — You shall not covet — which no court could ever try.
verseByVerse.theology:
Honour Outlasts Obedience

Honor is weightier than obey. Obedience has an expiry date; honour does not. A forty-year-old is no longer obliged to obey his father and is still obliged to honour him — which in practice meant caring for parents who could no longer work, the ancient world's only pension. Jesus attacked the Pharisees at exactly this point for a device that let a man dedicate his assets to the temple and avoid supporting his parents: you void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:9-13). Paul notes it is the first commandment with a promise (Eph. 6:2-3), and the promise is corporate: a society whose generations hold together lasts.

The Commandments Read at Their Own Depth

Jesus did not add stricter rules; he exposed what the rules were always about. Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:22); everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5:28). Read that way they leave nobody standing, which Paul says is their function: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20). The law was never a ladder to climb. It is, among other things, a mirror.

The Tenth Proves What the List Always Was

Every other commandment can be broken visibly. This one cannot be seen by anybody, tried by any court, or established by any witness — a man could keep the other nine flawlessly in public while breaking this one continuously in private. Paul, blameless under the law by his own account, said this was the one that finished him: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet" (Rom. 7:7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ratsach is unlawful killing, not all taking of life — the same law prescribes capital punishment and permits warfare. What is forbidden is innocent blood, and the reason lies back in Genesis: an assault on a person is an assault on the God he images (Gen. 9:6). And false witness is narrower and sharper than "do not lie" — it is set in a courtroom, where in a society with no police and no forensics a false witness was a weapon capable of killing (Deut. 19:19).

Now: A word is owed to those for whom the fifth commandment is hard, because some readers had fathers who were cruel and mothers who were absent. Honour is not the same as pretending. It does not require calling evil good, and it does not require handing an abuser continued access. It has real content — respect for the office, care where care is possible, refusal to hold contempt — and it is not a command to lie about what happened.

verseByVerse.quote: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.

The fifth commandment is the hinge. The first four govern how Israel treats God; the last five, how they treat each other — and this one sits between, because the family is where a child first meets authority, and a nation that will not honour its parents will not honour anything.

Honor is a weightier word than obey. Obedience has an expiry date; honour does not. A forty-year-old man is no longer obliged to obey his father and is still obliged to honour him, which in practice meant caring for parents who could no longer work — the ancient world's only pension. Jesus attacked the Pharisees precisely at this point, for a legal device that let a man dedicate his assets to the temple and thereby avoid supporting his parents: you void the word of God by your tradition (Mark 7:9-13).

And Paul notes something about this commandment in particular: it is the first commandment with a promise (Eph. 6:2-3). The promise is corporate as much as personal — that your days may be long in the land. A society in which the generations hold together lasts. One in which they do not, does not.

A word is owed to those for whom this commandment is hard, because some readers had fathers who were cruel and mothers who were absent. Honour is not the same as pretending, and it does not require calling evil good or handing an abuser continued access. It is a real command with real content — respect for the office, care where care is possible, refusal to hold contempt — and it is not a command to lie about what happened.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not murder. "You shall not commit adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not murder. The Hebrew ratsach means unlawful killing, not all taking of life — the same law that says this prescribes capital punishment and permits warfare, so the translation matters. What is forbidden is the taking of innocent human life, and the reason lies back in Genesis: man is made in the image of God, so an assault on a person is an assault on the one he images (Gen. 9:6).

Then Jesus does something with this commandment that no one saw coming. You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder"... But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:21-22). He is not adding a stricter rule. He is exposing what the rule was always about — the commandment governs the heart the act comes out of, and a man who has never killed anyone may have broken it many times before breakfast.

The seventh runs the same way. You shall not commit adultery protects the covenant that the whole Bible uses as its picture of God's relationship to his people, which is why unfaithfulness in a marriage is treated so gravely. And Jesus again takes it inward: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5:27-28).

This is the point at which the commandments stop being a list anyone can be smug about. Read at the level Jesus reads them, they leave nobody standing — which Paul says is precisely their function: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20). The law was never given as a ladder to climb. It was given, among other things, as a mirror.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not steal. "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall not steal establishes property as real. A person may own something, and taking it is wrong — which sounds obvious until you notice how much of Egypt's economy consisted of taking people's labour without paying for it. The commandment also protects the poor, since it is they who have least margin when what little they have is taken.

You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. This is narrower than "do not lie" and sharper. It is set in a courtroom: it forbids testimony that destroys a person. In a society with no police force and no forensic evidence, a false witness was a weapon capable of killing, and the law elsewhere requires that a proven false witness receive the sentence he sought for his victim (Deut. 19:19). Words about people are treated in Scripture as actions done to them.

And then the tenth, which is unlike all the others: You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's.

Every previous commandment could be broken visibly. This one cannot be seen by anybody. No court could try it, no witness could establish it, and a man could keep the other nine flawlessly in public while breaking this one continuously in private. Its presence in the list proves that the Decalogue was never merely a legal code for regulating behaviour. It was always about the heart.

Paul, who described himself as blameless under the law, said it was this commandment that finished him: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet" (Rom. 7:7). The one commandment no one could prosecute is the one that convicted the most scrupulous Pharisee of his generation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-21 — The Trembling People and the Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-21: The people see the thunder and the smoking mountain, stood far off, and beg for a mediator: You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die. Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mediator Was Their Own Request

They had promised in 19:8 to do everything God said; ten commandments later they are backing away. And they ask for a mediator not because anyone explained the doctrine but because they stood in the presence of God's holiness for the length of ten sentences and concluded they could not survive direct contact. The instinct is correct, and everything that follows — priesthood, tabernacle, sacrifice — is God's answer to a request his people made themselves, from genuine terror, at the foot of a hill.

Do Not Fear, So That You May Fear

Moses' reply looks contradictory and is not. Two different things share one word: the terror that makes a person run from God is to go, and the reverence that keeps them from sin is to remain. The second is not a milder version of the first but its opposite — one drives away, the other holds close.

Far Off, and Brought Near

Verse 21 is the whole chapter in one image: The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. One man goes up; everyone else watches him disappear into the dark. That is the old covenant, and its limit is written into it — Israel's access was only ever as good as their mediator, and this one would die on the wrong side of the Jordan. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13). Sinai's people stood at a distance and sent one man in. At Calvary one man went in and brought the distant people with him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: They had promised in 19:8 to do everything God said, and ten commandments later they are backing away from the mountain.

Now: What they ask for is a mediator, and they ask for it out of accurate instinct rather than instruction. Everything Scripture goes on to build in answer to that request ends at a torn curtain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die." Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin." The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people watch the mountain and they cannot bear it. Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off.

They had promised in 19:8 to do everything God said. Ten commandments later they are backing away from the mountain, and their request to Moses is one of the most revealing sentences in the Old Testament: You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die.

They want a mediator. Not because someone has explained the doctrine to them, but because they have stood in the presence of God's holiness for the length of ten sentences and concluded that they cannot survive direct contact. That instinct is correct, and everything the Bible goes on to build — priesthood, tabernacle, sacrifice — is God's answer to a request his people made themselves, from genuine terror, at the foot of a burning hill.

Moses' reply looks contradictory and is not: Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin. Do not be afraid — so that you may fear. Two different things share one word. The terror that makes a person run from God is to go; the reverence that keeps them from sin is to remain. And the second is not a lesser version of the first but its opposite: one drives away, and the other holds close.

Then verse 21, which is the whole chapter in a single image: The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.

One man goes up. Everybody else stays back at a safe distance and watches him disappear into the dark. That is the shape of the old covenant, and its limitation is written into it — Israel's access to God was only ever as good as their mediator, and this one would eventually die on the wrong side of the Jordan.

Which is why the moment the curtain of the temple tore from top to bottom mattered so much. The same holiness, the same thick darkness, the same impossibility of casual approach — and a mediator who did not merely walk into the dark on behalf of the people but bore it, so that the people who stood far off could be brought near. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13). Sinai's people stood at a distance and sent one man in. At Calvary one man went in and brought the distant people with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-26: The altar is to be of earth, or of stones no tool has touched — if you wield your tool on it you profane it — and approached without steps.
verseByVerse.theology:
Nothing of the Worshipper on the Altar

The reason for unshaped stone is not that craftsmanship is wrong; God is about to Spirit-fill named craftsmen for the tabernacle (31:1-5). The point is what an altar is for. It is the place where a substitute dies in the worshipper's place, and nothing the worshipper contributes may appear on it — a tooled stone would let a man look at the place of atonement and see his own workmanship in it. Even the ban on steps is to the same end: nothing of the worshipper on display, not even on the way up.

The Law and the Altar in One Breath

Ten commandments have just been given that nobody in the camp will keep, and the immediate provision is an altar. The God who issues a law his people cannot keep opens, in the same breath, the way to be forgiven for not keeping it. At the end of that road there is a cross which nobody decorated, where the offering was made entirely by God, and to which no one has ever added so much as a chisel mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The first altar Israel is authorised to build must be made of dirt, or of stones nobody has shaped. Every surrounding nation carved its holy places elaborately; Israel is forbidden to improve on the raw material at all.

Now: These verses look like an anticlimax after the thunder and are nothing of the kind. They are the chapter's answer to its own problem — and the instinct they forbid, to add something of our own to the place where atonement happens, has never gone away.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold. An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you. If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it. And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with instructions about altars, and they look like an anticlimax after the thunder. They are not.

An altar of earth you shall make for me... If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it.

The first altar Israel is authorised to build must be made of dirt, or of stones nobody has shaped. The moment a chisel touches it, it is profaned. Every surrounding nation carved its holy places elaborately; Israel is forbidden to improve on the raw material at all.

The reason is not that craftsmanship is wrong — God is about to fill the tabernacle with the most skilled work in the camp, and to name and Spirit-fill the craftsmen who do it (31:1-5). The point is what an altar is for. It is the place where a substitute dies in the worshipper's place, and nothing the worshipper contributes may appear on it. A tooled stone would let a man look at the place of atonement and see his own workmanship in it.

And the last verse forbids steps, so that nakedness is not exposed on the way up. Even the manner of approach is regulated so that nothing of the worshipper is on display.

Put the two together and the chapter closes exactly where it began. Ten commandments have just been given that no one in the camp will keep. The immediate provision is an altar — unshaped, uncarved, with nothing of human contribution in it, approached without display — because the God who has just issued a law his people cannot keep opens, in the same breath, the way for them to be forgiven for not keeping it. And at the end of that long road there is a cross, which nobody decorated, on which the offering was made entirely by God, and to which no one has ever been able to add so much as a chisel mark.

20.theology:
Law framed by grace. The commandments begin with redemption ("I brought you out"). Obedience flows from salvation; the law is a gift to the redeemed, not a ladder to earn rescue.

The two tables of love. Love for God (commands 1-4) and love for neighbor (commands 5-10), summarized by Jesus as the whole of the law.

The law as schoolmaster. The perfect standard exposes our sin (Rom. 3:20) and drives us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who kept it for us and bore its curse.
20.examples:
Then: From a mountain of fire God spoke ten words to his redeemed people, framed by the gospel of their deliverance — the shape of life with God — while the terrified people begged for a mediator.

Now: The law shows us both how to love God and neighbor and how far we fall short. Its perfect standard drives us to Christ, who kept it perfectly and bore its curse. We obey not to be saved but because we are saved — in grateful love to our Redeemer.

21.title: The Dignity of Persons Under God's Law
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now these are the rules that you shall set before them.<sup>2</sup>When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.<sup>3</sup>If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him.<sup>4</sup>If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone.<sup>5</sup>But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,'<sup>6</sup>then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.<sup>7</sup>"When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do.<sup>8</sup>If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.<sup>9</sup>If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter.<sup>10</sup>If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.<sup>11</sup>And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.<sup>12</sup>"Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.<sup>14</sup>But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die.<sup>15</sup>"Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>"Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>"Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>"When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed,<sup>19</sup>then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed.<sup>20</sup>"When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged.<sup>21</sup>But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money.<sup>22</sup>"When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine.<sup>23</sup>But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life,<sup>24</sup>eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,<sup>25</sup>burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.<sup>26</sup>"When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye.<sup>27</sup>If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.<sup>28</sup>"When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable.<sup>29</sup>But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.<sup>30</sup>If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him.<sup>31</sup>If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule.<sup>32</sup>If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.<sup>33</sup>"When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,<sup>34</sup>the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his.<sup>35</sup>"When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share.<sup>36</sup>Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
21.overview:
After the Ten Commandments comes the Book of the Covenant (chs. 21-23), the case law that applies the moral law to the realities of life in a fallen, ancient world. To modern ears these laws can seem strange, but read rightly they reveal a God deeply concerned with justice, mercy, and the dignity of every person — especially the weak and the vulnerable. As Carson notes, these laws are stunningly humane compared to the brutal codes of Israel's neighbors.

The chapter opens with laws about servants, and immediately we see God's heart: even bondservice is limited, regulated, and oriented toward eventual freedom. The seventh-year release for the Hebrew servant echoes the exodus itself — God's redeemed people must extend the freedom they received. The law protects servants from abuse, secures the rights of the vulnerable, and treats every human life as bearing the image of God.

The famous "eye for eye" principle (lex talionis) is not a license for vengeance but a restraint upon it — a principle of proportionate justice that limited retaliation in a violent age. The whole chapter teaches that human life and dignity are precious to God, anchored in creation in his image and pointing forward to the Redeemer who would give his own life to ransom ours.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Servants
sections.commentary:
The covenant code begins with the most vulnerable: servants. A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh — a built-in limit echoing the exodus and anticipating the year of Jubilee. Even within an ancient economy of debt-bondage, God orients everything toward freedom. The servant who, out of love, chooses to remain with a good master is honored with a permanent place in the household.
