Calvin saw in these provisions God's tender care that no person be ground down without recourse. The dignity of every image-bearer is woven into the law.

Provisions for female servants protect them from exploitation, securing their rights to food, clothing, and marital protection. In a world that treated such persons as disposable, God's law surrounds them with safeguards. The God who heard the groaning of slaves in Egypt will not permit his people to become careless oppressors.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Violence
sections.commentary:
These laws distinguish between premeditated murder and accidental killing, establishing the principle that human life — made in God's image — is sacred. Intentional murder warrants death; unintentional killing is treated with mercy and provision (the seed of the cities of refuge). Striking or cursing one's parents is gravely serious, upholding the fifth commandment. The protection of persons, including unborn life harmed in a struggle, reflects God's concern for the most defenseless.

The lex talionis — "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" — is widely misunderstood. As Carson explains, it is not a charter for revenge but a strict limit upon it: the punishment may not exceed the crime. In its context it was a profound restraint upon escalating violence and a guarantee of proportionate justice for rich and poor alike. Jesus later addresses its misuse as a personal excuse for retaliation (Matt. 5:38-39), calling his people to a higher righteousness of mercy.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Property and Responsibility
sections.commentary:
Even an ox that gores reveals God's justice: an owner who knew his animal was dangerous and failed to restrain it bears responsibility for the harm it causes. These laws teach personal accountability and the protection of the community from negligence. They presume a society where each person answers for the consequences of his actions and the welfare of his neighbor.

Underlying every statute is the conviction that we are responsible before God for our neighbor's safety and flourishing. The law refuses the modern fiction that what I do affects only myself. In God's economy, love for neighbor is not optional sentiment but enforceable duty — a foreshadowing of the love that fulfills the whole law (Rom. 13:10).

sections.title: The Heart of the Law: Mercy and Justice Together
sections.commentary:
Read as a whole, the Book of the Covenant reveals a God in whom justice and mercy are perfectly wed. The penalties are exacting because sin is serious and persons are precious; yet provision, limit, and mercy temper every statute. As Carson observes, these laws are strikingly humane against the backdrop of the brutal codes of the ancient Near East, where the powerful crushed the weak with impunity.

Behind every case law stands the character of the God who gave it — the God who heard the groaning of slaves and will not have his redeemed people become careless oppressors. The law is a mirror of God's heart, and ultimately a tutor that leads us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who fulfilled its every demand and bore its every curse, that mercy and justice might embrace at the cross.

21.theology:
The dignity of the image of God. Every person — servant, child, victim — is precious because made in God's image. The law surrounds the vulnerable with protection.

Justice and its limits. The lex talionis restrains vengeance and guarantees proportion. God's justice is exacting but never cruel; it protects rather than oppresses.

Personal responsibility before God. We answer to God for our neighbor's welfare and safety. Love for neighbor is a real, enforceable obligation, not mere sentiment.
21.examples:
Then: God's covenant law applied his holy character to daily life, protecting servants, restraining violence, and upholding the dignity of every person in a brutal ancient world far harsher than its neighbors' codes.

Now: God still cares for the vulnerable and the oppressed, and still holds us responsible for our neighbor's welfare. His law reveals a God of justice and mercy — and points us to the Redeemer who gave his life to ransom ours, the ultimate proof of how precious human life is to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-11: Hebrew debt-servitude limited to six years — in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing — with the pierced ear for the servant who chooses to stay, and protections for a daughter sold into service, including release without payment of money if her food, clothing or marital rights are reduced.
verseByVerse.theology:
Regulating What Already Existed

That the first case law concerns slavery is startling in a book about God freeing slaves, and needs saying carefully. Scripture is not endorsing the institution but regulating one that existed everywhere, and the regulation is radical for the ancient world: a fixed term, an automatic release, and no purchase price to get out. A man sold himself to clear a debt, and the debt could not own him for life.

It is fair to feel the distance between this and the abolition we would want, and honest to say Scripture moves toward it rather than arriving at once. But note where it ends: Paul writes to a slave-owner about a runaway and asks him to receive the man no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother (Philem. 16). Once that sentence exists in the church, the institution has no ground left to stand on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The pierced ear is not a brand of ownership but a mark of chosen belonging — I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free. Israel's law makes room for a man to stay because he loves the household rather than because it owns him.

Now: The provisions for the daughter all run one way: she may not be sold on, must be treated as a daughter if given to a son, and if her keep is reduced she leaves free and owing nothing. The vulnerable party is the one given the exit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these are the rules that you shall set before them. When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing. If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him. If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone. But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,' then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after the thunder of Sinai comes case law, and the shift of register is jarring until you see what it is for. The Ten Commandments state principles; these chapters show what those principles look like when two men's oxen collide. A law that never touches Tuesday is not a law anyone lives under.

And the very first case is slavery — which is startling in a book about God freeing slaves, and needs saying carefully. Scripture here is not endorsing the institution; it is regulating one that already existed everywhere, and the regulation is radical by the standards of the ancient world. Hebrew debt-servitude runs six years and ends: in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing. A man sold himself to clear a debt, and the debt could not own him for life.

Then the provision for the servant who does not want to leave — I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free — whose ear is pierced against the doorpost as a permanent mark of chosen belonging. Israel's law makes room for a man to stay because he loves the household rather than because he is owned by it.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do. If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her. If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter. If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights. And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rules for a daughter sold into service are protective rather than permissive: she may not be sold on to foreigners, she must be treated as a daughter if given to a son, and if a man takes another wife he may not reduce her food, clothing or marital rights. And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money. The vulnerable party is given an exit with no financial penalty.

It is fair to feel the distance between this and the abolition we would want, and honest to say that Scripture moves toward it rather than arriving at once. But note where it ends. Paul writes to a slave-owner about a runaway and asks him to receive the man back no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother (Philem. 16) — and once that sentence exists in the church, the institution has no ground left to stand on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — Capital Crimes Against Life and Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-17: Capital cases — murder distinguished from accidental death by intent, with a place of refuge; striking or cursing a parent; and kidnapping.
verseByVerse.theology:
Kidnapping Is Capital

Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death. Set that beside verse 2. Voluntary debt-servitude with a fixed term is regulated; stealing a person is a hanging offence — as was, by this chapter's standard, every stage of the trade that later crossed the Atlantic.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Intent changes everything. If he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, there is refuge. Israelite law will not treat an accident as a crime.

Now: Striking or cursing a parent is capital, which shows how load-bearing the fifth commandment was in Israel's ordering of society.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee. But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die. "Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death. "Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death. "Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The capital cases come first, and the distinctions they draw are the interesting part. Murder is death — but if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, there is a place of refuge. Intent changes everything, and Israelite law will not treat an accident as a crime.

Striking or cursing a parent is capital, which tells you how load-bearing the fifth commandment was. And so is kidnapping: Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death. Set that beside verse 2. Voluntary debt-servitude with a fixed term is regulated; stealing a person is a capital crime. The slave trade that later crossed the Atlantic was, by the standards of this chapter, a hanging offence at every stage.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-27 — Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-27: Injury and compensation — eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot — and two laws protecting servants from their own masters.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eye for Eye Is a Ceiling, Not a Floor

It sounds savage and is the opposite. In a world of blood feuds where an insult could escalate into a massacre, the rule caps the penalty at the injury. It is the origin of proportionality in law, and its whole force is to stop revenge growing. Jesus quotes it and moves the question — But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38-39) — not calling the law unjust, but shifting from what a court may impose to what a disciple may personally demand, and refusing his followers the right to insist on even the just amount.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two laws here were unheard-of elsewhere: a master who kills his slave is punished, and a master who knocks out a slave's tooth must set him free.

Now: A tooth costs a man his entire workforce, and damage to a servant's body forfeits the right to hold him — which prices a slave's mouth above a master's labour supply. No surrounding legal code did anything of the kind.

verseByVerse.quote: "When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed, then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed. "When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged. But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money. "When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine. But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe. "When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye. If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the famous formula: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot. It sounds savage and is the opposite. In a world of blood feuds where an insult could escalate into a massacre, this is a ceiling, not a floor — the penalty may not exceed the injury. It is the origin of proportionality in law, and its whole force is to stop revenge from growing.

Jesus quotes it and does something unexpected: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye"... But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38-39). He is not calling the law unjust. He is moving the question from what a court may impose to what a disciple may personally demand — and refusing his followers the right to insist on even the just amount.

The section closes with two laws about servants that were unheard-of elsewhere: a master who kills his slave is punished, and a master who knocks out a slave's tooth must set him free. A tooth costs a man his entire workforce. Damage to a servant's body is treated as forfeiting the right to hold him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-36 — The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-36: The goring ox — no liability for the unforeseeable, full liability where its owner has been warned but has not kept it in — followed by the uncovered pit and the ox that kills another ox.
verseByVerse.theology:
Holiness That Reaches the Ox

God has just appeared on a mountain in fire, and within a chapter he is legislating about livestock and open pits. That is not a descent from the sublime; it is the point of the covenant. The God of the thunder intends to govern the field and the well and the argument between neighbours, and a holiness that does not reach the ox is not the holiness he is offering.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Known risk, ignored, becomes the owner's. That is negligence law four thousand years early, turning on exactly the question a modern court would ask: what did he know, and what did he do about it?

Now: Read end to end, what is striking about these cases is how ordinary they are. The covenant is not a religion bolted onto life. It is a claim on the whole of it, including the boring parts.

verseByVerse.quote: "When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable. But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death. If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him. If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule. If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with oxen, and the ox is the point at which this law reveals its temperament.

An ox that gores someone to death is destroyed and the owner is not liable — an animal did something unforeseeable. But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, the owner is liable for a death. Known risk, ignored, becomes his. That is negligence law, four thousand years early, and it turns on exactly the question a modern court would ask: what did he know, and what did he do about it?

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his. "When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share. Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a run of cases about a pit left uncovered and an ox that kills another man's ox, all resolved by working out who could reasonably have prevented the loss and making him bear it.

What is striking, reading these end to end, is how ordinary they are. God has just appeared on a mountain in fire, and within a chapter he is legislating about livestock and open pits. That is not a descent from the sublime. It is the point of the whole covenant: the God of the thunder intends to govern the field and the well and the argument between neighbours, and a holiness that does not reach the ox is not the holiness he is offering.

22.title: Care for the Vulnerable
22.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.<sup>2</sup>If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him,<sup>3</sup>but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.<sup>4</sup>If the stolen beast is found alive in his possession, whether it is an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double.<sup>5</sup>"If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed over, or lets his beast loose and it feeds in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best in his own field and in his own vineyard.<sup>6</sup>"If fire breaks out and catches in thorns so that the stacked grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, he who started the fire shall make full restitution.<sup>7</sup>"If a man gives to his neighbor money or goods to keep safe, and it is stolen from the man's house, then, if the thief is found, he shall pay double.<sup>8</sup>If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come near to God to show whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property.<sup>9</sup>For every breach of trust, whether it is for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a cloak, or for any kind of lost thing, of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of both parties shall come before God. The one whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor.<sup>10</sup>"If a man gives to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any beast to keep safe, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, without anyone seeing it,<sup>11</sup>an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution.<sup>12</sup>But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner.<sup>13</sup>If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for what has been torn.<sup>14</sup>"If a man borrows anything of his neighbor, and it is injured or dies, the owner not being with it, he shall make full restitution.<sup>15</sup>If the owner was with it, he shall not make restitution; if it was hired, it came for its hiring fee.<sup>16</sup>"If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall give the bride-price for her and make her his wife.<sup>17</sup>If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins.<sup>18</sup>"You shall not permit a sorceress to live.<sup>19</sup>"Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.<sup>20</sup>"Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child.<sup>23</sup>If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry,<sup>24</sup>and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless.<sup>25</sup>"If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him.<sup>26</sup>If ever you take your neighbor's cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down,<sup>27</sup>for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.<sup>28</sup>"You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.<sup>29</sup>"You shall not delay to offer from the fullness of your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.<sup>30</sup>You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.<sup>31</sup>"You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
22.overview:
The covenant law continues with regulations on property, restitution, and social responsibility — but its deepest pulse is the protection of the vulnerable. Laws on theft and damage require not mere punishment but restitution: the wrongdoer must make the victim whole and more. God's justice aims at restoration, not just retribution.

Then the chapter rises to its heart with laws protecting the sojourner, the widow, and the fatherless — the three groups most defenseless in ancient society. And the motive God gives is the exodus itself: "You shall not wrong a sojourner... for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." The redeemed must remember their redemption and treat the vulnerable as God treated them. Grace received becomes grace extended. This is the ethic of the gospel: "freely you have received; freely give."

Most tender of all is God's warning about the poor man's cloak taken in pledge: return it by sunset, "for that is his only covering... And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate." The God of the burning bush who heard Israel's cry still bends his ear to the cry of the poor. As Keller has powerfully shown, concern for the marginalized is not a peripheral add-on to biblical faith but flows from the very heart of the God who redeems.

sections.title: Laws of Restitution
sections.commentary:
When property is stolen or destroyed, the law requires restitution — often multiplied. A thief must restore far more than he took. This is restorative justice: the goal is not merely to punish the offender but to make the victim whole and to teach the offender the weight of his wrong. Where the thief cannot pay, he himself is sold, that restitution may be made. Property is treated seriously because it represents a person's labor and livelihood, yet always in service of relationships rather than mere materialism.

These laws presume a community bound together in mutual responsibility, where wrongs are righted and trust restored. Behind every statute stands the eighth commandment — "you shall not steal" — applied with wisdom to the tangled realities of life. Justice that restores rather than merely retaliates reflects the heart of the God who restores sinners.

sections.title: Protecting the Vulnerable
sections.commentary:
Here the law's heart beats most clearly. The sojourner, the widow, the fatherless — those without a protector in the ancient world — are placed under God's own protection. "You shall not wrong a sojourner... for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." The memory of their own bondage is to make Israel tender toward the vulnerable. Grace received must become grace extended. Keller has shown that this concern for the marginalized springs from the very nature of the God who redeems the helpless.

The warning is solemn: "If they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn." God personally takes up the cause of the defenseless. The poor man's pledged cloak must be returned by nightfall — "for that is his only covering... if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate." The God who heard Israel's groaning in Egypt still hears the cry of the poor. To oppress the weak is to provoke the wrath of their Defender.

sections.title: Devotion to God
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes by binding social ethics to worship: do not revile God or curse a ruler; give God the firstfruits and the firstborn; be holy people set apart to him. Care for neighbor and devotion to God are not two separate spheres but one seamless life of covenant faithfulness. The vertical and the horizontal are inseparable — love for God and love for neighbor flow from the same redeemed heart.

To be God's "holy" people (v. 31, "consecrated men") means a whole life shaped by belonging to him. The redeemed are claimed entirely — their property, their worship, their treatment of the poor, their reverence for authority — all under the lordship of the God who brought them out of Egypt.

sections.title: Love for God and Love for Neighbor United
sections.commentary:
Chapter 22 refuses to separate the vertical from the horizontal. Laws protecting the poor, the widow, and the sojourner stand side by side with commands to give God the firstfruits and to be a holy people. Care for neighbor and devotion to God are one seamless life of covenant faithfulness. Jesus would later bind the whole law into these two: love God, love neighbor (Matt. 22:37-40).

The recurring motive — "you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" — anchors all ethics in redemption. A people who have received mercy must show mercy. As Keller has shown, biblical justice toward the vulnerable is not a political add-on but flows from the very heart of the redeeming God, fulfilled in Christ who, though rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor. 8:9).

22.theology:
Restorative justice. Restitution aims to make the victim whole, reflecting a God whose justice restores rather than merely punishes.

God the defender of the vulnerable. The sojourner, widow, and orphan are under God's own protection. "If they cry out, I will hear, for I am compassionate."

Grace received, grace extended. "You were sojourners in Egypt." Remembered redemption fuels mercy toward the weak — the very ethic of the gospel.
22.examples:
Then: God's law required restitution for wrongs and placed the most defenseless — the immigrant, the widow, the orphan, the poor — under his personal protection, motivated by Israel's own rescue from bondage.

Now: The God who redeemed us calls us to care for the vulnerable as he cared for us. Mercy to the marginalized is not optional charity but flows from the heart of our Redeemer. He still hears the cry of the poor — and warns those who oppress them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-8: Theft and restitution — fivefold for an ox, fourfold for a sheep, double if found alive — and the distinction between a burglar killed at night and one killed in daylight.

Verses 9-15: Property held on trust: animals that die, are stolen or are torn, and borrowed animals injured. Where evidence fails, the matter goes to an oath before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Restitution Rather Than Punishment

The thief does not merely suffer; he restores, and restores more than he took, so the victim ends up better off than before the crime. That is a different instinct from the one most legal systems run on. Our reflex is to ask what the offender deserves; Israel's law asks first what the injured party lost, and makes the offender carry it.

The principle surfaces in the New Testament in an unexpected mouth. Coming down from the tree, Zacchaeus said if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke 19:8) — quoting this chapter, applying it to himself voluntarily, at the rate for a stolen sheep, across a tax career's worth of extortion. Grace had reached him minutes earlier, and the first thing it produced was restitution.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The night-and-day distinction is about visibility. In the dark you cannot know whether an intruder is armed or how many there are; in daylight you can, and lethal force stops being self-defence. The law measures what the householder could reasonably have known.

Now: Where evidence fails, everything rests on an oath before God and the owner accepting it. That is the quiet assumption under the whole chapter, and it should be named: these laws only work among people who fear God. A society can legislate about oxen indefinitely, but the moment the oath means nothing the apparatus collapses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep. If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him, but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft. If the stolen beast is found alive in his possession, whether it is an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double. "If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed over, or lets his beast loose and it feeds in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best in his own field and in his own vineyard. "If fire breaks out and catches in thorns so that the stacked grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, he who started the fire shall make full restitution. "If a man gives to his neighbor money or goods to keep safe, and it is stolen from the man's house, then, if the thief is found, he shall pay double. If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come near to God to show whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law on theft turns on restitution rather than punishment. A man who steals an ox repays five, a sheep four; if the animal is found alive in his possession, double. The thief does not merely suffer — he restores, and restores more than he took, so that the victim ends up better off than before the crime.

That is a different instinct from the one most legal systems run on. Our reflex is to ask what the offender deserves. Israel's law asks first what the injured party has lost, and makes the offender carry it.

And the principle turns up in the New Testament in the mouth of a man nobody expected. When Zacchaeus climbed down out of the tree he said, if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke 19:8). He was quoting this chapter and applying it to himself voluntarily, at the going rate for a stolen sheep, on a tax career's worth of extortion. Grace had reached him about four minutes earlier, and the first thing it produced was restitution.

One case deserves a note because it looks harsh: a burglar killed breaking in at night carries no bloodguilt, but the same killing after sunrise does. The distinction is visibility. In the dark you cannot know whether the intruder is armed or how many there are; in daylight you can, and lethal force stops being self-defence. The law is measuring what the householder could reasonably have known.

verseByVerse.quote: For every breach of trust, whether it is for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a cloak, or for any kind of lost thing, of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of both parties shall come before God. The one whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor. "If a man gives to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any beast to keep safe, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, without anyone seeing it, an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution. But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner. If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for what has been torn. "If a man borrows anything of his neighbor, and it is injured or dies, the owner not being with it, he shall make full restitution. If the owner was with it, he shall not make restitution; if it was hired, it came for its hiring fee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a run of cases about property held on trust — an animal left with a neighbour that dies, is stolen, or is torn by a wild beast; a borrowed animal injured while its owner was not present.

What holds them together is the question of where the risk sits. If a man was paid to keep the animal, he bears more; if the owner was present, he bears it himself; if there is no evidence either way, the matter goes to an oath before God and the owner shall accept the oath. In a world without contracts, insurance or CCTV, the system rests finally on people telling the truth in God's presence and being believed.

That is the quiet assumption underneath the whole chapter, and it should be named: these laws only work among people who fear God. A society can legislate about oxen indefinitely, but the moment the oath means nothing the whole apparatus collapses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-20: The seducer must pay the bride-price whether or not he is permitted to marry; and sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods each carry death.
verseByVerse.theology:
Boundary Markers

These penalties are severe precisely because Canaan practised all three as religion. They mark out a nation that is to be unlike every society around it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A woman in that culture who lost her marriage prospects lost her economic future with them.

Now: The protection runs one way only. The man carries the full cost and has no option to walk away, whatever the father decides.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall give the bride-price for her and make her his wife. If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins. "You shall not permit a sorceress to live. "Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. "Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A short section of capital and sexual law. A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride-price and marry her — or, if her father refuses, pay it anyway. The protection is entirely one-directional: a woman in that culture had lost her marriage prospects and therefore her economic future, and the law makes the man carry the full cost with no option to walk away.

Then sorcery, bestiality, and sacrificing to any god but the LORD, each carrying death. These are the boundary markers of a nation that is to be different from every society around it, and they are severe precisely because Canaan practised all three as religion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 21-27: The sojourner, the widow and the fatherless are not to be mistreated — if they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry. No interest is to be charged to a poor neighbour, and a cloak taken in pledge must be returned by sunset.
verseByVerse.theology:
Memory as the Engine of Ethics

You shall not wrong a sojourner... for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. Israel is not told that foreigners have rights in the abstract but to remember what it felt like — a far harder thing to argue your way out of.

God Undertakes to Answer It Personally

The threat in verses 23-24 is shaped exactly like the crime: mistreat widows and orphans, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless. He does not merely disapprove of the exploitation of the defenceless.

A Character Reference, Not a Penalty Clause

In the middle of a code about oxen and pits, God stops to consider whether one poor man will be cold tonight — that is his only covering... in what else shall he sleep? — and legislates on the strength of it. And what guarantees the law is not a sanction but who he is: I will hear, for I am compassionate. The God of the thunder on the mountain is listening for one cold man's complaint about a coat. James keeps the whole tone of it: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ban on interest is not a ban on commerce — interest on a business loan to a foreigner was permitted.

Now: It is a ban on making money out of a neighbour's disaster. The distinction is not the transaction but who is on the other side of it and why they came.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless. "If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him. If ever you take your neighbor's cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the heart of the chapter, and it is where Israel's law is least like its neighbours'.

You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. The reason is memory. Israel is not told that foreigners have rights in the abstract; it is told to remember what it felt like, which is a far harder thing to argue your way out of.

Then the widow and the fatherless, and a warning with startling heat in it: if you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry... and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless. The punishment is shaped exactly like the crime. God does not merely disapprove of the exploitation of the defenceless; he undertakes to answer it personally.

Then lending. If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him. Not a ban on commerce — interest on a business loan to a foreigner was permitted — but a ban on making money out of a neighbour's disaster.

And then the verse that shows what kind of God is behind this legislation. A poor man's cloak may be taken as security for a loan, but it must be returned before sunset, for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.

Sit with that. In the middle of a legal code about oxen and pits, God stops to consider whether a particular poor man will be cold tonight, and legislates on the strength of it. And the guarantee attached is not a penalty clause but a character reference: I will hear, for I am compassionate. The God of the thunder on the mountain is listening for one cold man's complaint about a coat.

James picks up the whole tone of this section in a sentence: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-31 — Reverence Toward God and Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-31: Do not revile God or curse a ruler; firstfruits and firstborn given without delay; a newborn animal left seven days with its mother — and the reason for all of it, You shall be consecrated to me.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything Downstream of One Sentence

Not you shall be moral and not you shall be law-abiding, but set apart, belonging to someone. Every regulation in these three chapters follows from that — which is why Peter could take the same logic to churches full of Gentiles: as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct (1 Pet. 1:15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul quoted verse 28 at his own trial, having unknowingly insulted the high priest (Acts 23:5).

Now: The seven days a newborn animal spends with its mother before it may be offered is a small mercy tucked inside a sacrificial regulation — the sort of detail that shows what kind of legislator is at work here.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people. "You shall not delay to offer from the fullness of your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me. You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me. "You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with a handful of commands that seem unrelated and share one root: everything belongs to God first.

You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people — a verse Paul quoted at his own trial when he had unknowingly insulted the high priest (Acts 23:5). The firstfruits and the firstborn are given without delay. And the newborn animal stays seven days with its mother before it may be offered, which is a small mercy tucked inside a sacrificial regulation.

The last line supplies the reason for all of it: You shall be consecrated to me. Not you shall be moral, and not you shall be law-abiding. Set apart, belonging to someone. Every regulation in these three chapters is downstream of that sentence — which is why Peter could take the same logic to churches full of Gentiles and write as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct (1 Pet. 1:15).

23.title: Sacred Time and the Guiding Angel
23.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness.<sup>2</sup>You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice,<sup>3</sup>nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit.<sup>4</sup>"If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him.<sup>5</sup>If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him.<sup>6</sup>"You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit.<sup>7</sup>Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked.<sup>8</sup>And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right.<sup>9</sup>"You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>"For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield,<sup>11</sup>but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard.<sup>12</sup>"Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed.<sup>13</sup>"Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.<sup>14</sup>"Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me.<sup>15</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed.<sup>16</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor.<sup>17</sup>Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.<sup>18</sup>"You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning.<sup>19</sup>"The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared.<sup>21</sup>Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him.<sup>22</sup>"But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.<sup>23</sup>"When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out,<sup>24</sup>you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces.<sup>25</sup>You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.<sup>26</sup>None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days.<sup>27</sup>I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.<sup>28</sup>And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you.<sup>29</sup>I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you.<sup>30</sup>Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.<sup>31</sup>And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you.<sup>32</sup>You shall make no covenant with them and their gods.<sup>33</sup>They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
23.overview:
The covenant code concludes with laws on justice, the appointment of sacred time, and a glorious promise of God's guiding presence. First come commands for impartial justice — do not follow a crowd in doing wrong, do not pervert justice for the poor or the rich, help even your enemy's straying ox. Justice in God's kingdom is blind to bribes and faction; it loves truth and the neighbor, even the enemy. Jesus' command to love our enemies is rooted here.

Then God appoints sacred time: the Sabbath year for the land and the poor, the weekly Sabbath for rest, and the three annual feasts — Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering. God structures time itself around worship and rest and remembrance. Sacred rhythms are a gift, teaching his people that life is not an endless grind but a pilgrimage punctuated by celebration of God's goodness.

The chapter crescendos with a breathtaking promise: "I send an angel before you... my name is in him." Many have seen here the Angel of the LORD, a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son, in whom God's own name dwells. This guiding, guarding presence will lead Israel into the land. As Sproul observed, God never sends his people anywhere he does not go with them. The same Lord who bears the divine name leads his people still.

sections.title: Justice and Integrity
sections.commentary:
God demands scrupulous justice: no false reports, no following the crowd into wrong, no partiality — neither favoring the poor out of sentiment nor the rich out of greed. Truth and righteousness must govern every verdict. Remarkably, the law commands kindness even to an enemy: if you find your enemy's ox wandering, bring it back; if his donkey lies under its burden, help it up. Here, embedded in the law, is the seed of Jesus' command to love our enemies (Matt. 5:44).

The repeated concern for the sojourner — "you know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt" — keeps tying ethics back to redemption. The people of God are to embody the very justice and compassion they received from him. A redeemed people cannot be a partial, cruel, or dishonest people.

sections.title: The Sabbaths and Feasts
sections.commentary:
God appoints sacred time. The seventh-year rest for the land provides for the poor and the wild creatures and teaches trust in God's provision. The weekly Sabbath gives rest to servant, animal, and sojourner alike — rest is a gift extending even to the lowliest. Three annual feasts — Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering — gather the people before God in remembrance and thanksgiving. Time itself is sanctified, structured around worship rather than mere productivity.

These rhythms declare that human life is not an endless treadmill of labor but a pilgrimage marked by rest and celebration of God's goodness. The feasts rehearse the story of redemption and provision year after year. They anticipate the great festival of the redeemed in the presence of God, the rest that remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:9).

sections.title: The Angel of the LORD
sections.commentary:
The covenant code ends with a magnificent promise: "Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared." This is no ordinary messenger — "my name is in him." Many interpreters, from the church fathers onward, have seen here the Angel of the LORD, a pre-incarnate manifestation of the divine Son, in whom God's own name and authority dwell. To obey him is to obey God; to rebel against him is to rebel against God.

The God who redeemed his people will also lead them, guard them, and bring them to the place he has prepared — language Jesus echoes when he says, "I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). Sproul stressed that God never commissions his people without accompanying them. The promise of the guiding presence, fulfilled in Christ who is Immanuel, God with us, is the great comfort of the pilgrim people of God.

sections.title: The Pattern of Pilgrimage: Worship, Rest, and Guidance
sections.commentary:
The chapter weaves together justice, sacred time, and the promise of God's guiding presence into a single vision of the pilgrim life. God's people are to walk in truth and mercy, to rhythm their lives by Sabbath and feast, and to journey under the leading of the Angel in whom God's name dwells. Life with God is neither aimless drudgery nor self-directed wandering, but a guided pilgrimage toward the place God has prepared.

Jesus echoes this whole pattern: he calls us to a righteousness exceeding the scribes', offers rest to the weary, and promises, "I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2). The Angel of the LORD who led Israel is fulfilled in Immanuel, God with us, who leads his people home. The God who redeems is the God who guides and goes before.

23.theology:
Impartial justice and enemy-love. God's law forbids partiality and commands kindness even to enemies — the root of Jesus' command to love our enemies.

Sacred time. Sabbaths and feasts sanctify time around rest, worship, and remembrance, anticipating the eternal rest of God's people.

The guiding presence of God. The Angel in whom God's name dwells leads and guards his people to the prepared place — fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel.
23.examples:
Then: God concluded his covenant law by commanding impartial justice and even enemy-love, sanctifying time through Sabbaths and feasts, and promising to send his Angel — bearing God's own name — to lead Israel to the prepared land.

Now: God still calls his people to truth, justice, and love of enemies, and still gives sacred rhythms of rest and worship. And he never sends us anywhere alone: in Christ, Immanuel, God with us, the guiding presence leads us home to the place he has prepared.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: Laws for the courtroom — no false report, no malicious witness, and you shall not fall in with the many to do evil. Partiality is forbidden in both directions. And in the middle, the command to lift an enemy's fallen donkey with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Crowd Pressure, Legislated Against

Not bribery and not malice, but the ordinary human instinct to go where the room is going. Israel is told the number of people holding a view is not evidence for it, and that a witness who trims his testimony to the majority has perverted justice as surely as one who lied for money.

Partiality Runs Both Ways

Nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit sits a few verses from you shall not pervert the justice due to your poor. The law is fiercely protective of the poor everywhere except in the witness box, where sympathy corrupts as surely as contempt. Justice is not the same thing as taking the weaker side.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Not merely refraining from harming an enemy — going and heaving his animal upright alongside him, in the road, where you will both be sweating and neither will know what to say.

Now: It is very hard to keep hating a man you have just done that with, which is presumably the idea. Centuries later someone stated it as a principle: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt. 5:44). The seed of it is a donkey in a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice, nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit. "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him. "You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit. Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked. And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right. "You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The laws on justice go after the ways courts actually fail, and they are uncomfortably current.

You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness. Then the sentence that names the commonest failure of all: You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice.

That is crowd pressure, legislated against. Not bribery, not malice — the ordinary human instinct to go where the room is going. Israel is told that the number of people holding a view is not evidence for it, and that a witness who trims his testimony to the majority has perverted justice as surely as one who lied for money.

Then a startling balance. Nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit sits a few verses from you shall not pervert the justice due to your poor. Both directions are forbidden. The law is fiercely protective of the poor everywhere except in the witness box, where sympathy is as corrupting as contempt. Justice is not the same thing as taking the weaker side.

And in the middle of it, a small law with a long reach: If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him.

Not merely refrain from harming your enemy — go and heave his animal upright alongside him, in the road, where you will both be sweating and neither of you will know what to say. It is very hard to keep hating a man you have just done that with, which is presumably the idea. Centuries later someone would put it as a principle: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt. 5:44). The seed of it is a donkey in a ditch.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-13 — The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-13: The sabbath year, in which the land lies fallow that the poor of your people may eat; and the weekly sabbath, that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Year Transferred to Those With No Land

Leaving fields fallow is good agriculture, but that is not the reason given. The named beneficiary is the poor, who may glean freely from whatever the untended ground produces, with the wild animals taking the remainder. God builds into Israel's economy a year in which the whole harvest goes to people who own none of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Once again the list is of those who do not own the land they work.

Now: The rhythm that began as a gift of manna has become the mechanism by which Israel is prevented from grinding down its own workforce — including the animals and the foreign labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: "For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard. "Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed. "Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sabbath principle now extends from the week to the calendar. Every seventh year the land lies fallow — let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat.

Note who the year is for. It is good agriculture, but that is not the reason given: the beneficiary named is the poor, who may glean freely from whatever the untended fields produce. And then the wild animals get the remainder. God builds a year into Israel's economy that transfers the whole harvest to those with no land.

Then the weekly sabbath restated with the same emphasis: that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed. Once again the list is of those who do not own the land they work. The rhythm that began as a gift of manna has become the mechanism by which Israel is prevented from grinding down its own workforce.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-19: Three annual feasts — Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering — at which three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Frame the Gospel Hangs On

Christ was crucified at Passover and Unleavened Bread; raised as the firstfruits (Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Cor. 15:20); and the Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Weeks — Pentecost. Two of the three were fulfilled on their own festival days, in the same city, within fifty days of each other. The third, Ingathering, is the harvest at the end of the year, and it has not happened yet.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The whole nation stops work three times a year and travels.

Now: For a farming people that is a substantial act of trust. The fields are left, and God undertakes to look after what is left behind.

verseByVerse.quote: "Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me. You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed. You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD. "You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning. "The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three annual festivals are commanded, and each is tied to a harvest: Unleavened Bread in the spring, Harvest at the first fruits, and Ingathering at the end of the year. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.

The whole nation stops work three times a year and travels, which for a farming people is a substantial act of trust — the fields are left, and God undertakes to look after what is left behind.

These three are also the frame on which the gospel later hangs. Christ was crucified at Passover and Unleavened Bread, raised as the firstfruits (Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Cor. 15:20), and the Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Weeks — Pentecost. Two of the three feasts were fulfilled on their own festival days, in the same city, within fifty days of each other. The third, Ingathering, is the harvest at the end of the year, and it has not happened yet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-33 — The Angel and the Promise of Conquest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 20-33: Behold, I send an angel before you... for my name is in him; the promise that God will drive out the nations little by little; and the warning to make no covenant with them or their gods.
verseByVerse.theology:
My Name Is in Him

Israel is told to obey this messenger as they would obey God, and warned that he has authority to withhold pardon — which no created servant possesses. This is the figure who spoke from the bush as God in the first person, and readers have long recognised in him a self-manifestation of God, ahead of the day when the Word would take flesh and the name would dwell among us unmistakably.

God Explains His Own Slowness

I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate... Little by little I will drive them out. He could clear Canaan in a season, and a nation that size in an empty country would be overrun by wilderness before it could fill the space. The progress is deliberately gradual, matched to what Israel can occupy and hold.

The same pattern governs the Christian life. Sanctification is almost never a single clearance; it is territory taken slowly, at a rate matched to what can be held, and the slowness is not God's reluctance but his knowledge of the ground. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6) — the completion certain, the timetable his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The final warning is about compromise: if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.

Now: Israel ignored it exactly, and the entire book of Judges is the footnote.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him. "But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries. "When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out, you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces. You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you. None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days. I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you. And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you. I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land. And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you. You shall make no covenant with them and their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a promise that is stranger than it looks. Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him.

Take those last five words seriously. My name is in him. Israel is told to obey this messenger as they would obey God, and warned that he has authority to withhold pardon — which is not something any created servant possesses. This is the same figure who spoke from the bush as God in the first person, and readers have long recognised in him a self-manifestation of God, ahead of the day when the Word would take flesh and the name would dwell among us in a way nobody could mistake.

Then the conquest promises, and one that answers a question people ask about their own lives: I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.

God explains his own slowness. He could clear Canaan in a season, and a nation of that size in an empty country would be overrun by wilderness before it could fill the space. So the progress is deliberately gradual, matched to what Israel can actually occupy and hold.

Carry that into the Christian life, because the same pattern governs it. Sanctification is almost never a single clearance; it is territory taken slowly, at a rate matched to what can be held, and the slowness is not God's reluctance but his knowledge of the ground. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6) — the completion is certain and the timetable is his.

The chapter's final warning is about compromise: make no covenant with them or their gods, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you. Israel will ignore this exactly, and the entire book of Judges is the footnote.

24.title: The Blood of the Covenant
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar.<sup>2</sup>Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him."<sup>3</sup>Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do."<sup>4</sup>And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.<sup>5</sup>And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar.<sup>7</sup>Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient."<sup>8</sup>And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up,<sup>10</sup>and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness.<sup>11</sup>And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction."<sup>13</sup>So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God.<sup>14</sup>And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them."<sup>15</sup>Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.<sup>16</sup>The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.<sup>17</sup>Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
24.overview:
The covenant is solemnly ratified, and the means is blood. Moses builds an altar, sacrifices are offered, and the blood is divided: half thrown against the altar (representing God), half thrown on the people, with the words "Behold the blood of the covenant." A covenant relationship between a holy God and a sinful people can be sealed only in blood. As Hebrews says, "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb. 9:22).

Jesus deliberately echoes this very moment at the Last Supper: "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:28). The blood of bulls at Sinai could only point forward; the blood of Christ actually cleanses. Sinai's covenant is sealed in animal blood; the new covenant is sealed in the blood of the Lamb of God. Every drop at the altar of Sinai was a signpost to Calvary.

Then comes one of the most astonishing scenes in all Scripture: the elders go up the mountain and "they saw the God of Israel," and they "ate and drank" in his presence. A covenant meal in the presence of God — fellowship restored, sinners feasting before the holy One and not consumed. This covenant meal anticipates the Lord's Supper and ultimately the marriage supper of the Lamb, when the redeemed will see God face to face and eat and drink in his everlasting presence.

sections.title: The Covenant Confirmed
sections.commentary:
Moses relays all the LORD's words and rules, and the people respond with one voice: "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do." Moses writes down the words of the LORD, building an altar and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes. The covenant is not a vague spiritual sentiment but a concrete, recorded, binding agreement between God and his people, with clear terms and a wholehearted response. The written word grounds the covenant in objective, enduring revelation.

The people's confident pledge — "all that the LORD has spoken we will do" — is sincere, yet the rest of Exodus (the golden calf!) will show how quickly human resolve fails. This is precisely why the covenant must be sealed in blood: forgiveness and atonement, not human performance, will be its foundation.

sections.title: The Blood of the Covenant
sections.commentary:
Burnt offerings and peace offerings are sacrificed, and Moses takes the blood, throwing half against the altar and reading the Book of the Covenant. When the people again pledge obedience, Moses throws the other half of the blood on them: "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you." The covenant binds God and people together in blood. Sin has made a barrier that only sacrificial blood can bridge; the relationship is sealed by death.

Jesus' words at the Last Supper deliberately echo this scene: "This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt. 26:28). Hebrews makes the connection explicit (Heb. 9:18-22): the blood of bulls and goats could never take away sin, but pointed forward to the blood of Christ. Sinai's altar is a signpost to Calvary. Every covenant with God is sealed in blood — and the only blood that finally cleanses is the blood of the Lamb.

sections.title: The Covenant Meal
sections.commentary:
Then the astonishing happens: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up the mountain and "they saw the God of Israel," with what looked like a pavement of sapphire under his feet, clear as the sky. And the text marvels: "he did not lay his hand on the chief men... they beheld God, and ate and drank." Sinners feast in the presence of the holy God and are not consumed. The covenant sealed in blood opens the way to fellowship and communion.

This covenant meal in God's presence anticipates the Lord's Supper, where we commune with the risen Christ, and ultimately the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9), when the redeemed will see God face to face and eat and drink in his everlasting joy. Ferguson notes that the goal of redemption is always communion — to see God and live, to feast in his presence forever. What was glimpsed on Sinai is our eternal destiny in Christ.

sections.title: Moses Enters the Glory
sections.commentary:
God calls Moses up to receive the tablets of stone, and the glory of the LORD settles on Sinai like a devouring fire. Moses enters the cloud and remains forty days and forty nights. The mediator goes up into the very presence of God on behalf of the people, who wait below. This pattern — a mediator ascending into God's glory for the people — points forward to Christ, who has gone up into the true sanctuary, into the presence of God, on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).

The glory like a devouring fire reminds us that this is the same holy God of the burning bush and the trembling mountain. Yet now, through covenant blood, a mediator may dwell forty days in that fire and live. The barrier of sin is being addressed; the way into God's presence is opening — a way fully opened only when Christ entered heaven itself for us.

24.theology:
The covenant sealed in blood. "Behold the blood of the covenant." A holy God and sinful people can be bound only through sacrificial blood — fulfilled in Christ's blood of the new covenant (Matt. 26:28).

Communion with God as the goal. The elders see God and eat and drink in his presence — a covenant meal anticipating the Lord's Supper and the marriage supper of the Lamb.

The mediator who ascends. Moses enters God's glory for the people, prefiguring Christ who entered heaven itself on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).
24.examples:
Then: The covenant was ratified in blood thrown on altar and people, and the elders ascended to see God and eat and drink in his presence — sinners feasting before the holy One and not consumed.

Now: The blood of bulls pointed to the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins. By that blood we are brought into communion with God, feasting at the Lord's table now and at the marriage supper of the Lamb forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Blood of the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-8: An altar with twelve pillars; half the blood thrown against the altar, the Book of the Covenant read aloud, the people's third promise — All that the LORD has spoken we will do — and the other half thrown over them: Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Basin, Two Parties

Blood on the altar, which is God's side; blood on the people, which is theirs. The same death now stands over both. That is what a covenant is — not a contract between equals but a bond sealed in death, with both sides inside it. Hebrews takes this exact scene as its proof that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins (Heb. 9:18-22).

The Sentence Jesus Took

On the night he was betrayed, at Passover, a man took a cup and said This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24). Every Jew at that table knew where the words came from; they belonged to Moses and a basin and a mountain. He took them, changed one word, and made it my blood — announcing that the ceremony at the foot of Sinai had found its original.

Which matters because of what the people had just promised. They meant all that the LORD has spoken we will do, and they were standing under blood while they said it, and within forty days they were dancing round a calf. The blood of Exodus 24 sealed a covenant Israel broke almost at once. The blood of the new covenant seals one where the obedience required has already been supplied by the one whose blood it is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Twelve pillars, one for each tribe, so that no one could later claim the covenant had been made over their heads.
