Now: This is the third time Israel has said it (19:8, 24:3, 24:7), and the third time it is sincere. Sincerity was never the missing ingredient.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar. Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him." Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD. And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar. Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient." And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses builds an altar at the foot of the mountain with twelve pillars round it, one for each tribe, and young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the ceremony that makes this chapter one of the most important in the Old Testament.

Moses takes half the blood and throws it against the altar. Then he reads the Book of the Covenant aloud, and the people answer for the third time — All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient. Then he takes the other half of the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."

Blood on the altar, which is God's side. Blood on the people, which is theirs. One basin divided between the two parties, so that the same death now stands over both. That is what a covenant is — not a contract between equals but a bond sealed in death, and both sides are inside it.

The writer to the Hebrews takes this scene as his proof that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins, quoting Moses' words almost exactly: This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you (Heb. 9:18-22).

But the sentence has a more famous afterlife than that. On the night he was betrayed, in an upper room in Jerusalem, at Passover, a man took a cup and said: This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24). Every Jew at that table knew where the words came from. They had heard them read since childhood; they belonged to Moses and a basin and a mountain. And he took them, and changed one word, and made it my blood.

He was not inventing a metaphor. He was announcing that the ceremony at the foot of Sinai had found its original — that the blood which had been thrown against an altar and over a crowd was always a rehearsal for blood that would be poured out for many, and that the covenant it sealed was about to be replaced by one that could actually be kept.

Which matters, because of what the people had just promised. All that the LORD has spoken we will do. They meant it, and they were standing under blood while they said it, and within forty days they would be dancing round a calf. The blood of Exodus 24 sealed a covenant Israel broke almost immediately. The blood of the new covenant seals one where the obedience required has already been supplied by the one whose blood it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-11 — They Beheld God and Ate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-11: Seventy-four men go up and saw the God of Israel, with a pavement of sapphire under his feet. He did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.theology:
Blood First, Then a Meal

On the mountain that had been fenced with a death penalty four chapters earlier, where touching the base of it was fatal, seventy-four men sat down in God's presence and had lunch — immediately after blood had been thrown over them. It is the first time since Eden that human beings eat in God's company without dying.

That order is the whole logic of Scripture. It is why the church's central act is not a lecture but a table, why the same sequence runs through the upper room — the cup of the covenant, then bread and wine shared with the one whose blood it was — and where all of it is going: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The text says they saw God twice, plainly, and then goes out of its way to record that nobody died. That tells you exactly what everyone in the story expected to happen.

Now: The description is careful about its limits. They saw what was under his feet — a pavement of sapphire, like the sky for clearness. The narrator will describe the floor and will not describe the person standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then three verses so unexpected that readers often pass over them without registering what happened.

Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.

Seventy-four men climbed a mountain and saw God. The text says it twice, plainly, and then goes out of its way to record that nobody died — he did not lay his hand on them — which tells you exactly what everyone in the story expected to happen.

And the description is careful about its limits. They saw what was under his feet: a pavement of sapphire, like the sky for clearness. The narrator will describe the floor and will not describe the person standing on it.

Then the last four words, and they are the point: they beheld God, and ate and drank.

They had a meal. On the mountain that had been fenced with a death penalty four chapters ago, where touching the base of it was fatal, seventy-four men sat down in the presence of God and had lunch. It is the first time in Scripture since Eden that human beings eat in God's company without dying, and it happens immediately after blood has been thrown over them.

That order is the whole logic of the Bible. Blood first, then a meal. It is why the church's central act is not a lecture but a table, and why the same sequence runs through the upper room — the cup of the covenant, and then bread and wine shared with the one whose blood it was. And it is where all of it is going: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — Into the Cloud of Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-18: Moses is called up for the tablets, leaving Aaron and Hur in charge. The cloud covers the mountain six days; the glory looks to those below like a devouring fire; and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Devouring Fire

The same phrase Hebrews uses at the end of its own argument about the two mountains — our God is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29). The people at the bottom are watching a blaze on a summit and know their leader has walked into it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Forty days is a very long time to watch a fire on a mountain with no word from the man inside it.

Now: The narrator drops the detail without comment, and a reader who knows what is coming can already hear the conversation starting at the bottom of the hill — as for this Moses, we do not know what has become of him (32:1). The golden calf is not built by people who have forgotten God. It is built by people who got tired of waiting for him, five and a half weeks after promising to do everything he said, with the fire still burning in plain sight.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction." So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God. And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them." Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud. Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel. Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is called higher, to receive the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction. He leaves Aaron and Hur in charge, which will turn out badly, and takes Joshua part of the way.

Then the cloud covers the mountain for six days, and on the seventh God calls him out of it. Below, the elders can see what is happening: the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel.

A devouring fire — the same phrase Hebrews uses of God at the end of its own argument about the two mountains (our God is a consuming fire, Heb. 12:29). The people at the bottom are watching a blaze on a summit and know their leader has walked into it.

And then the last line: Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

Forty days is a very long time to watch a fire on a mountain with no word from the man inside it. The narrator drops the detail without comment, and the reader who knows what is coming can already hear the conversation starting at the bottom of the hill — as for this Moses, we do not know what has become of him (32:1). The golden calf is not built by people who have forgotten God. It is built by people who got tired of waiting for him, five and a half weeks after promising to do everything he said, with the fire still burning on the mountain in plain sight.

25.title: That I May Dwell in Their Midst
25.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me.<sup>3</sup>And this is the contribution that you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>4</sup>blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, goats' hair,<sup>5</sup>tanned rams' skins, goatskins, acacia wood,<sup>6</sup>oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense,<sup>7</sup>onyx stones, and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece.<sup>8</sup>And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.<sup>9</sup>Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it.<sup>10</sup>"They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>11</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside shall you overlay it, and you shall make on it a molding of gold around it.<sup>12</sup>You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it.<sup>13</sup>You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.<sup>14</sup>And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark by them.<sup>15</sup>The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it.<sup>16</sup>And you shall put into the ark the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>17</sup>"You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth.<sup>18</sup>And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat.<sup>19</sup>Make one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat shall you make the cherubim on its two ends.<sup>20</sup>The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubim be.<sup>21</sup>And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>22</sup>There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel.<sup>23</sup>"You shall make a table of acacia wood. Two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>24</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it.<sup>25</sup>And you shall make a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and a molding of gold around the rim.<sup>26</sup>And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and fasten the rings to the four corners at its four legs.<sup>27</sup>Close to the frame the rings shall lie, as holders for the poles to carry the table.<sup>28</sup>You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, and the table shall be carried with these.<sup>29</sup>And you shall make its plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings; you shall make them of pure gold.<sup>30</sup>And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.<sup>31</sup>"You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it.<sup>32</sup>And there shall be six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it;<sup>33</sup>three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand.<sup>34</sup>And on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers,<sup>35</sup>and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out from the lampstand.<sup>36</sup>Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it, the whole of it a single piece of hammered work of pure gold.<sup>37</sup>You shall make seven lamps for it. And the lamps shall be set up so as to give light on the space in front of it.<sup>38</sup>Its tongs and their trays shall be of pure gold.<sup>39</sup>It shall be made, with all these utensils, out of a talent of pure gold.<sup>40</sup>And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain.
25.overview:
We arrive at the great theme that crowns the book of Exodus: God's desire to dwell with his people. "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." The God who came down to deliver now wants to come down to stay. The whole apparatus of the tabernacle exists for one stunning purpose — that the infinite, holy God might dwell among his redeemed people. This is the heartbeat of the gospel: God with us.

The instructions begin with a freewill offering — God's house is built by willing hearts — and then with the most sacred objects. First the Ark of the Covenant, overlaid with gold, with the mercy seat above it and two cherubim, where God promises, "There I will meet with you." The mercy seat (the kapporet) is where the blood of atonement is sprinkled — and Paul says Christ is our "mercy seat" (Rom. 3:25, hilasterion), the place where God's justice and mercy meet. Then the table of the bread of the Presence and the golden lampstand, each rich with meaning.

Crucially, everything must be made "exactly as I show you concerning the pattern." The tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5). It points beyond itself — first to the incarnation, where the Word "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14), and finally to the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Rev. 21:3). All of it whispers: God wants to be with you.

sections.title: The Freewill Offering
sections.commentary:
God begins not by conscripting materials but by inviting them: "from every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution." God's dwelling is built by willing, generous hearts — a principle Paul takes up in 2 Corinthians 9:7, "God loves a cheerful giver." The materials are listed in lavish detail: gold, silver, bronze, fine linen, precious stones. The redeemed give back to God from the very wealth he provided when they plundered Egypt. Grace received overflows in generous giving.

The purpose is breathtaking: "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." Here is the goal of the whole exodus. God did not redeem his people merely to free them from Egypt but to dwell among them forever. And it must be built "exactly as I show you concerning the pattern" — the earthly tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5), pointing beyond itself to greater things.

sections.title: The Ark of the Covenant
sections.commentary:
The most sacred object comes first: the Ark, an acacia chest overlaid inside and out with pure gold, containing the testimony (the tablets of the law). Upon it rests the mercy seat (kapporet), with two cherubim of gold facing one another, their wings overshadowing it. Here, above the mercy seat, between the cherubim, God promises to meet with his people: "There I will meet with you... I will speak with you." The throne of God on earth is a throne of mercy resting upon the law.

The mercy seat is where, on the Day of Atonement, the blood of sacrifice was sprinkled, covering the broken law beneath. Paul declares that Christ is our hilasterion — our mercy seat (Rom. 3:25) — the place where the blood is applied and God's wrath is propitiated. Sproul taught that here, supremely, the justice of God (the law) and the mercy of God (the blood-covered seat) meet. The Ark is a gospel sermon in gold and acacia: God meets sinners only at the place of atonement, fulfilled in Christ.

sections.title: The Table of the Bread of the Presence
sections.commentary:
The golden table holds the bread of the Presence — twelve loaves representing the twelve tribes, continually before the LORD. It signifies that God's people live always in his presence and that he provides for them, feeding them and welcoming them to his table. The bread set before God's face speaks of fellowship and communion: a perpetual meal in the presence of God.

The bread points forward to Christ, the bread of the Presence and the bread of life (John 6:35), and to the table of the Lord where we commune with him. God's people are always before his face, always provided for, always invited to feast in his presence. The table foreshadows the eternal communion of the redeemed.

sections.title: The Golden Lampstand
sections.commentary:
The lampstand (menorah) of pure hammered gold, with its branches like an almond tree in bloom, gives light continually in the holy place. It signifies God as the light of his people and the light of his presence that never goes out. The intricate beauty — buds, blossoms, almond flowers — reflects the glory and life of God's presence. Light in the sanctuary means life, guidance, and the radiance of God himself.

The lampstand anticipates Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12), and the church, called to be lampstands bearing his light (Rev. 1:20). In the New Jerusalem there will be no need of sun or lamp, "for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb" (Rev. 21:23). The light that burned in the holy place will blaze forever in the presence of God. And again the refrain: make it "after the pattern" shown on the mountain — earthly worship copying heavenly reality.

25.theology:
God's desire to dwell with his people. "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst." The goal of redemption is God's presence — fulfilled in the incarnation and the New Jerusalem.

The mercy seat and atonement. God meets sinners only at the blood-covered mercy seat, where justice and mercy meet — fulfilled in Christ our hilasterion (Rom. 3:25).

Worship after the heavenly pattern. The tabernacle is a copy of a heavenly reality (Heb. 8:5), pointing beyond itself to Christ and to the eternal dwelling of God with man.
25.examples:
Then: God commanded a sanctuary, built by willing hearts after a heavenly pattern, so that he might dwell among his redeemed people — with the Ark and its blood-covered mercy seat as the throne where he would meet them.

Now: God's great desire is still to dwell with his people. The tabernacle pointed to Christ, in whom the fullness of God tabernacled among us, and to the day when the dwelling of God will be with man forever. We meet God only at the mercy seat — at the cross of Christ, where mercy and justice embrace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Freewill Offering and the Pattern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: A contribution taken only from every man whose heart moves him; the list of materials; the purpose — let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst — and the pattern shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence the Rest of Exodus Serves

That I may dwell in their midst. This is what God has been after since 3:8 — not merely a rescued people or a people in a land, but a people he lives among. The book began with I have come down; it ends with him moving in.

A Scale Model of Something Real

Nothing here is Moses' design. Hebrews makes much of the repeated according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain: the earthly sanctuary is a copy and shadow of the heavenly things (Heb. 8:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Where does a nation of escaped slaves get gold, silver, fine linen and onyx? From Egypt. This is the silver and gold of 12:35-36 — the back wages promised to Abraham (Gen. 15:14) — now being turned into a sanctuary. The plunder of the oppressor becomes the furniture of worship.

Now: No levy, no assessment, no quota — only what people want to give. And by chapter 36 Moses has to order them to stop, because too much has come in. It is the only recorded case in Scripture of a building fund being closed early.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me. And this is the contribution that you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze, blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, goats' hair, tanned rams' skins, goatskins, acacia wood, oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense, onyx stones, and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece. And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst. Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first word about the tabernacle is not about architecture. It is about giving: From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me.

No levy, no assessment, no quota. The materials for God's dwelling are to come only from people who want to give them — and by chapter 36 Moses will have to issue an order telling everyone to stop, because they have brought too much. That is the only recorded instance in Scripture of a building fund being closed early.

The list of materials is worth a glance: gold, silver, bronze, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, fine linen, goats' hair, ram skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, onyx. Where does a nation of escaped slaves get any of that? From Egypt. This is the silver and gold of 12:35-36, the back wages God promised Abraham (Gen. 15:14), and it is now being turned into a sanctuary. The plunder of the oppressor becomes the furniture of worship.

Then the purpose, and it is the sentence the whole second half of Exodus exists to serve: And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.

That is what God has been after since 3:8. Not merely a rescued people or a people in a land, but a people he lives among. The book began with God saying I have come down; it will end with him moving in.

And one instruction governs everything that follows: Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle... so you shall make it. Nothing here is Moses' design. Hebrews makes much of this — the earthly sanctuary is a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, which is why Moses was told to make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain (Heb. 8:5). The tent is a scale model of something real.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-22 — The Ark and the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-22: The ark, gold within and without, its poles never removed, holding the testimony — and the mercy seat above it with two cherubim, where God says I will meet with you... I will speak with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Arrangement Means

Inside the box is the law Israel has broken. Above it is where God's presence rests and his voice comes from. Between the two — between a holy God and a broken commandment — is a lid of solid gold, and once a year blood is sprinkled on it.

The Hebrew kapporet comes from the root meaning to cover or atone; the Greek translators rendered it hilastērion. And Paul, reaching for a word for what God did at the cross, uses exactly that one: God put forward Christ Jesus as a propitiation by his blood — as the mercy seat (Rom. 3:25). The place where blood covers a broken law and God speaks to his people without destroying them turns out to be a person.

The Cherubim Have Changed Job

They last appeared at the gate of Eden with a flaming sword, keeping people out. Here they are again in gold, over the place of atonement — bowed, facing inward, looking at blood. The guards at the door have become witnesses at the mercy seat.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The poles stay in the rings permanently.

Now: Which means the ark is always ready to move. Israel's God does not settle into a fixed address; he travels with a walking people, and the furniture is built for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside shall you overlay it, and you shall make on it a molding of gold around it. You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it. You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark by them. The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it. And you shall put into the ark the testimony that I shall give you. "You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat. Make one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat shall you make the cherubim on its two ends. The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubim be. And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you. There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ark comes first, because it is the centre. A wooden chest overlaid with gold inside and out, with poles that are never to be removed, containing the tablets of the covenant.

The poles matter. They stay in the rings permanently, which means the ark is always ready to move. Israel's God does not settle into a fixed address; he travels with a walking people, and the furniture is built for it.

Then the lid, and everything turns on it. You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold... and you shall put the mercy seat on top of the ark. Two cherubim of hammered gold face each other with wings overshadowing it, and God says: There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you.

Consider the arrangement. Inside the box is the law Israel has broken. Above the box is the place where God's presence rests and his voice comes from. Between the two — between a holy God and a broken commandment — there is a lid of solid gold, and once a year blood is sprinkled on it.

The Hebrew word is kapporet, from the root meaning to cover or atone. The Greek translators rendered it hilastērion. And Paul, reaching for a word to describe what God did at the cross, uses exactly that one: God put forward Christ Jesus as a propitiation by his blood — as the mercy seat (Rom. 3:25). The place where blood covers a broken law and God speaks to his people without destroying them is a person.

Cherubim last appeared in Scripture at the gate of Eden with a flaming sword, keeping people out. Here they are again, in gold, over the place of atonement — bowed, facing inward, looking at blood. The guards at the door have become witnesses at the mercy seat.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-30 — The Table of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 23-30: The table of the bread of the Presence, with twelve loaves set before me regularly.
verseByVerse.theology:
Bread of the Face

The Hebrew is literally bread set before God's face — a standing meal in his house, twelve loaves for twelve tribes, replaced every Sabbath. Every tribe is represented on that table whether or not the tribe is behaving, and the loaves went out fresh each week regardless of what Israel had done that week.

The man who fed five thousand on a hillside and said I am the bread of life had already appealed to these loaves, reminding the Pharisees that David and his men ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat (Luke 6:3-4) — using it to prove that mercy outranks ritual. The bread that sat before God's face is now offered to anyone hungry.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The priests ate the loaves when they were replaced; nothing was wasted.

Now: A permanent place-setting for every tribe, kept up through every week of Israel's history, is a quiet statement that God's welcome does not fluctuate with performance.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a table of acacia wood. Two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. You shall overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it. And you shall make a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and a molding of gold around the rim. And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and fasten the rings to the four corners at its four legs. Close to the frame the rings shall lie, as holders for the poles to carry the table. You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, and the table shall be carried with these. And you shall make its plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings; you shall make them of pure gold. And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The table of the bread of the Presence, overlaid with gold, with its plates and dishes and the loaves that are to be before me regularly.

Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out fresh every Sabbath and eaten by the priests. It is a standing meal in the house of God, and the name in Hebrew is literally bread of the face — bread set before God's face, in his presence, permanently.

Every tribe is represented on that table whether or not the tribe is behaving. The loaves were replaced weekly regardless of what Israel had done that week.

And the man who fed five thousand people on a hillside and then said I am the bread of life had, at least once, appealed directly to these loaves — reminding the Pharisees how David and his men ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat (Luke 6:3-4), and using it to prove that mercy outranks ritual. The bread that sat before God's face is now offered to anybody who is hungry.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 31-40: The lampstand — one talent of pure gold, hammered from a single piece, with six branches and cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Tree in the Dark

It is not assembled from parts but beaten from one lump, so stem and branches are a single object. And it is a tree: inside a tent of skins and linen, in a desert, God's light comes from a golden tree in permanent blossom whose lamps must never go out.

There was a garden once with a tree in the middle and light and God walking about in it, and the way back was shut. Everything about this tent is a curtained, guarded attempt to recover some of that, and the almond blossom is not decoration — it is a memory of Eden burning in the dark.

In the Revelation John turns toward the voice and finds seven golden lampstands, and is told they are the churches, with one like a son of man walking among them (Rev. 1:12-20). The light in the holy place was a single stand tended daily so it would not fail. The light in the world now is the church, and the reason it does not go out is that he is walking among them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The lampstand gets more loving detail than almost anything else in the chapter.

Now: In a tent with no windows, this was the only light there was. Everything the priests saw of God's house, they saw by it.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it. And there shall be six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it; three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand. And on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers, and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out from the lampstand. Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it, the whole of it a single piece of hammered work of pure gold. You shall make seven lamps for it. And the lamps shall be set up so as to give light on the space in front of it. Its tongs and their trays shall be of pure gold. It shall be made, with all these utensils, out of a talent of pure gold. And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lampstand is described in more loving detail than almost anything else in the chapter: a single piece of hammered pure gold, one talent of it, with a central shaft and six branches, each decorated with cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower.

Two things are striking. First, it is not assembled from parts — it is beaten from one lump, so that stem and branches are a single object. Second, it is a tree. Inside a tent of animal skins and linen, in a desert, God's light comes from a golden tree in permanent blossom, and its lamps must never go out.

There was a garden once with a tree in the middle and light and God walking about in it, and the way back was shut. Everything about this tent is a controlled, curtained, guarded attempt to get some of that back, and the almond blossom on the lampstand is not decoration — it is a memory of Eden burning in the dark.

In the Revelation John turns to see the voice speaking to him and finds seven golden lampstands, and is told they are the churches, with one like a son of man walking among them (Rev. 1:12-20). The light in the holy place was a single stand with seven lamps fed by oil, tended daily so it would not fail. The light in the world now is the church, and the reason it does not go out is that he is walking among them.

26.title: The Way into the Presence
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked into them.<sup>2</sup>The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall be the same size.<sup>3</sup>Five curtains shall be coupled to one another, and the other five curtains shall be coupled to one another.<sup>4</sup>And you shall make loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set. Likewise you shall make loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the second set.<sup>5</sup>Fifty loops you shall make on the one curtain, and fifty loops you shall make on the edge of the curtain that is in the second set; the loops shall be opposite one another.<sup>6</sup>And you shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains one to the other with the clasps, so that the tabernacle may be a single whole.<sup>7</sup>"You shall also make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle; eleven curtains shall you make.<sup>8</sup>The length of each curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains shall be the same size.<sup>9</sup>You shall couple five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves, and the sixth curtain you shall double over at the front of the tent.<sup>10</sup>You shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in the second set.<sup>11</sup>"You shall make fifty clasps of bronze, and put the clasps into the loops, and couple the tent together that it may be a single whole.<sup>12</sup>And the part that remains of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remains, shall hang over the back of the tabernacle.<sup>13</sup>And the extra that remains in the length of the curtains, the cubit on the one side, and the cubit on the other side, shall hang over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and that side, to cover it.<sup>14</sup>And you shall make for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins on top.<sup>15</sup>"You shall make upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood.<sup>16</sup>Ten cubits shall be the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame.<sup>17</sup>There shall be two tenons in each frame, for fitting together. So shall you do for all the frames of the tabernacle.<sup>18</sup>You shall make the frames for the tabernacle: twenty frames for the south side;<sup>19</sup>and forty bases of silver you shall make under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons;<sup>20</sup>and for the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side twenty frames,<sup>21</sup>and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame, and two bases under the next frame.<sup>22</sup>And for the rear of the tabernacle westward you shall make six frames.<sup>23</sup>And you shall make two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear;<sup>24</sup>they shall be separate beneath, but joined at the top, at the first ring. Thus shall it be with both of them; they shall form the two corners.<sup>25</sup>And there shall be eight frames, with their bases of silver, sixteen bases; two bases under one frame, and two bases under another frame.<sup>26</sup>"You shall make bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle,<sup>27</sup>and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the side of the tabernacle at the rear westward.<sup>28</sup>The middle bar, halfway up the frames, shall run from end to end.<sup>29</sup>You shall overlay the frames with gold and shall make their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold.<sup>30</sup>Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.<sup>31</sup>"And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it.<sup>32</sup>And you shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, on four bases of silver.<sup>33</sup>And you shall hang the veil from the clasps, and bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil. And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy.<sup>34</sup>You shall put the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place.<sup>35</sup>And you shall set the table outside the veil, and the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle opposite the table, and you shall put the table on the north side.<sup>36</sup>"You shall make a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework.<sup>37</sup>And you shall make for the screen five pillars of acacia, and overlay them with gold. Their hooks shall be of gold, and you shall cast five bases of bronze for them.
26.overview:
The instructions turn to the structure of the tabernacle itself — its curtains, frames, and coverings, and above all its veil. To modern readers the architectural detail can seem tedious, but every measurement and material preaches a sermon about how a holy God may be approached by sinful people. The tabernacle is a graded structure of increasing holiness: the outer court, the Holy Place, and the Most Holy Place where God's presence dwells above the Ark.

The most theologically charged feature is the veil — "the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy." This thick curtain, embroidered with cherubim, barred the way into God's immediate presence. Only the high priest could pass through it, and only once a year, and only with blood. The veil declared, in fabric, the great problem of the universe: sinners cannot come to a holy God. There is a barrier, guarded by cherubim, just as cherubim guarded the way back to Eden (Gen. 3:24).

And here the gospel breaks in with glory. When Christ died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt. 27:51). The veil that barred the way was rent — by God, from the top — when Christ's flesh was torn. Hebrews says we now enter the Most Holy Place "by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh" (Heb. 10:20). The whole structure of the tabernacle cries out: there is a way into the presence of God, and it is Christ.

sections.title: The Inner Curtains
sections.commentary:
The tabernacle's beauty is hidden, seen only from within. The innermost curtains are of fine twined linen in blue, purple, and scarlet, with cherubim skillfully woven in — a glimpse of heavenly glory for those who draw near. Over these are layers of goats' hair, ram skins dyed red, and durable leather, protecting the glory within from the harsh wilderness. The most glorious things are reserved for those who enter; the outside is plain and weather-worn.

So it is with the things of God: the world sees a humble exterior, but those who draw near behold glory. The cherubim woven into the curtains remind the worshiper that he is entering the realm of heaven, the dwelling of the God whom angels serve. Every fiber of the tabernacle is saturated with meaning, declaring that this is holy space, set apart for the presence of God.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.commentary:
The frames of acacia wood overlaid with gold, set in silver bases, give the structure its standing strength. Each board fits precisely into its neighbor, bound together with bars, forming one stable dwelling. The careful joinery preaches the unity and order of God's house — many parts fitted into one structure to house the divine presence. Paul will later describe the church as a building "joined together" and "growing into a holy temple in the Lord" (Eph. 2:21).

And again the standard is exactness: "set up the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain." Nothing is left to human invention. Worship is to be ordered by God's revelation, not human imagination — a principle that runs through all of Scripture. God determines how he is to be approached.

sections.title: The Veil and the Most Holy Place
sections.commentary:
The climax of the chapter is the veil: "the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy." This thick curtain, embroidered with cherubim, hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place where the Ark and the presence of God dwelt. Only the high priest could pass through it, only once a year, only with blood. The cherubim woven into it recall the cherubim guarding Eden (Gen. 3:24): the way back to God's immediate presence is barred to sinners.

The veil proclaimed the great problem of the cosmos in cloth: sinful humanity cannot come to the holy God. But when Christ died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt. 27:51) — torn by God himself, from heaven down, as the flesh of Christ was torn. Hebrews 10:19-20 declares that we now have confidence to enter the holy places "by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh." The barrier is gone. In Christ, the way into the presence of God is open forever.

sections.title: One House, One People, One Way
sections.commentary:
The tabernacle's many parts — curtains, frames, bars, veil — are fitted into a single dwelling for the one God, foreshadowing the church, "joined together" and "growing into a holy temple in the Lord" (Eph. 2:21). The hidden glory within, seen only by those who enter, pictures the truth that the world sees a humble exterior while those who draw near behold the glory of God.

Above all, the veil declares both the barrier of sin and, in light of the cross, the open way. What Sinai's fire and the tabernacle's veil kept closed, the torn flesh of Christ has opened forever (Heb. 10:19-20). The whole structure preaches the gospel: there is one God, one people, and one way into his presence — and that way is Christ.

26.theology:
The holiness of God and the barrier of sin. The graded structure and the veil declare that sinners cannot casually approach the holy God; there is a barrier, guarded by cherubim as at Eden.

Christ the torn veil. At the cross the veil was torn from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51). We enter God's presence through the new and living way of Christ's flesh (Heb. 10:20).

Worship after the pattern. The tabernacle is built exactly as God commanded — worship is governed by God's revelation, not human invention.
26.examples:
Then: God commanded a tabernacle of hidden glory, ordered exactly to his pattern, whose veil — embroidered with cherubim like those guarding Eden — barred the way into his immediate presence.

Now: The veil declared that sinners cannot approach a holy God. But at the cross that veil was torn from top to bottom. Through the torn flesh of Christ, the way into God's presence is open forever. We who once stood outside now draw near with confidence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-14: Four layers — goatskins and red ram skins outside, goats' hair curtains beneath, and inside the ten curtains of fine twined linen with cherubim worked into them, joined by fifty clasps so that the tabernacle may be a single whole.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Glory Is on the Inside

A traveller passing the camp would see a large, drab, weatherproof tent and have no idea the interior was embroidered with angels. Isaiah wrote of someone with no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa. 53:2). What God chooses to dwell in has never been impressive from the outside.

A Single Whole

Many separate pieces fastened until they are one thing — which is exactly how the New Testament describes the church it calls a temple: joined together and being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Eph. 2:21-22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Goats' hair was the standard material of every bedouin tent in that desert. From outside, God's house looked like everybody else's.

Now: Only the priests ever saw the linen and the cherubim. Much of what is most beautiful about the house of God is still not visible from the road.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked into them. The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall be the same size. Five curtains shall be coupled to one another, and the other five curtains shall be coupled to one another. And you shall make loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set. Likewise you shall make loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the second set. Fifty loops you shall make on the one curtain, and fifty loops you shall make on the edge of the curtain that is in the second set; the loops shall be opposite one another. And you shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains one to the other with the clasps, so that the tabernacle may be a single whole. "You shall also make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle; eleven curtains shall you make. The length of each curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains shall be the same size. You shall couple five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves, and the sixth curtain you shall double over at the front of the tent. You shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in the second set. "You shall make fifty clasps of bronze, and put the clasps into the loops, and couple the tent together that it may be a single whole. And the part that remains of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remains, shall hang over the back of the tabernacle. And the extra that remains in the length of the curtains, the cubit on the one side, and the cubit on the other side, shall hang over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and that side, to cover it. And you shall make for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins on top.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tent is built in four layers, and the order they are listed in is the order you would meet them walking inward.

From outside, all anyone sees is the top covering: a covering of goatskins over ram skins dyed red. Weatherproof, plain, unremarkable. Beneath that are curtains of goats' hair, the standard material of every bedouin tent in the desert. And only inside, visible to the priests alone, are the ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns with cherubim worked into them.

So the glory is on the inside. A traveller passing the camp would see a large, drab, functional tent and have no idea that the interior was embroidered with angels. Isaiah wrote of someone with no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa. 53:2) — and the pattern is the same. What God chooses to dwell in is not impressive from the outside, and never has been.

The curtains are joined by fifty loops and fifty golden clasps so that the tabernacle may be a single whole. The phrase recurs. Many separate pieces, fastened until they are one thing — which is precisely how the New Testament describes the church it calls a temple: joined together and being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Eph. 2:21-22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 15-30: Forty-eight acacia boards overlaid with gold, each standing in two silver bases, held by bars through gold rings — erected according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Whole House Stands on Ransom Money

Chapter 30 explains where the silver came from: the census half-shekel, a ransom for his life paid by every man counted in Israel. So the entire structure rests on foundations made of redemption money. Every board in God's house stands on the price paid for a life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Acacia is a desert tree — gnarled, thorny, hard, and the only serious timber available out there.

Now: Each plank was cut from something that grew in a wilderness, planed, overlaid with gold, and stood upright in silver to hold up the house of God. Readers have never found that picture hard to apply.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood. Ten cubits shall be the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame. There shall be two tenons in each frame, for fitting together. So shall you do for all the frames of the tabernacle. You shall make the frames for the tabernacle: twenty frames for the south side; and forty bases of silver you shall make under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons; and for the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side twenty frames, and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame, and two bases under the next frame. And for the rear of the tabernacle westward you shall make six frames. And you shall make two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear; they shall be separate beneath, but joined at the top, at the first ring. Thus shall it be with both of them; they shall form the two corners. And there shall be eight frames, with their bases of silver, sixteen bases; two bases under one frame, and two bases under another frame. "You shall make bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the side of the tabernacle at the rear westward. The middle bar, halfway up the frames, shall run from end to end. You shall overlay the frames with gold and shall make their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold. Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The frame is acacia wood overlaid with gold: forty-eight upright boards, each standing in two silver bases, held together by bars running through gold rings.

The detail worth pausing on is the silver. Where did it come from? Chapter 30 will explain — it is the census money, the half-shekel ransom for his life paid by every man counted in Israel. So the entire structure rests on foundations made of redemption money. Every board in God's house stands on the price paid for a life.

And the boards themselves are worth a thought. Acacia is a desert tree — gnarled, thorny, hard, the only serious timber available out there. Each plank is cut from something that grew in a wilderness, planed, overlaid with gold, and stood upright in silver to hold up the house of God. It is not difficult to see why readers have always found the picture hard to resist.

Then, again: Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain. Third time. Nothing is left to preference.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-37 — The Veil and the Screen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 31-37: Two hangings — a screen at the entrance, and inside a veil... made with cherubim skillfully worked into it, which shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Limitation of the Old Covenant, Hanging in Fabric

God has come down to dwell among his people, which is glorious — and there is still a curtain, almost nobody may go past it, and the cherubim woven into it are the same figures who guarded Eden. The tabernacle says two things at once: God is here, and you may not come in.

Torn From the Top

At the moment Jesus cried out and died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51). From the top — nobody reached up and cut it. The barrier that stood between God and everyone but one man on one day was destroyed from the God-side, at the exact moment the true sacrifice was finished.

Hebrews does not understate what that means: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19-20). The veil was his body, and it was torn so that the room nobody could enter is now the room believers are told to walk into with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The outer screen is embroidered; the inner veil has angels on it. Only one of the two was a barrier.

Now: Behind it went the ark and the mercy seat; in front of it the table and the lampstand. One curtain divided the place where priests worked daily from the place one man entered once a year, carrying blood.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it. And you shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, on four bases of silver. And you shall hang the veil from the clasps, and bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil. And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy. You shall put the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place. And you shall set the table outside the veil, and the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle opposite the table, and you shall put the table on the north side. "You shall make a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. And you shall make for the screen five pillars of acacia, and overlay them with gold. Their hooks shall be of gold, and you shall cast five bases of bronze for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two hangings divide the tent, and the difference between them is the point of the chapter.

The outer one is a screen for the entrance of blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen — embroidered, but only embroidered. The inner one is different: a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it. Angels on it, like the ones at Eden's gate.

And its function is stated plainly: the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy. Behind it goes the ark with the mercy seat. In front of it, the table and the lampstand. One curtain, dividing the place where priests work daily from the place one man may enter once a year with blood.

That veil is the whole limitation of the old covenant hanging in fabric. God has come down to dwell among his people, which is glorious — and there is still a curtain, and almost nobody may go past it, and the cherubim woven into it are the same figures who guarded Eden. The message of the tabernacle is simultaneously God is here and you may not come in.

Which is why the single most important thing that ever happened to a piece of cloth is recorded in three Gospels in almost identical words. At the moment Jesus cried out and died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51). From the top — no one reached up and cut it. The barrier that had stood between God and everyone but one man on one day was destroyed from the God-side, at the exact moment the true sacrifice was completed.

Hebrews spells out what that means and does not understate it: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19-20). The veil was his body. It was torn so that the room nobody could enter is now the room believers are told to walk into with confidence.

27.title: The Altar Where Blood Is Shed
27.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits.<sup>2</sup>And you shall make horns for it on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay it with bronze.<sup>3</sup>You shall make pots for it to receive its ashes, and shovels and basins and forks and fire pans. You shall make all its utensils of bronze.<sup>4</sup>You shall also make for it a grating, a network of bronze, and on the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners.<sup>5</sup>And you shall set it under the ledge of the altar so that the net extends halfway down the altar.<sup>6</sup>And you shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze.<sup>7</sup>And the poles shall be put through the rings, so that the poles are on the two sides of the altar when it is carried.<sup>8</sup>You shall make it hollow, with boards. As it has been shown you on the mountain, so shall it be made.<sup>9</sup>"You shall make the court of the tabernacle. On the south side the court shall have hangings of fine twined linen a hundred cubits long for one side.<sup>10</sup>Its twenty pillars and their twenty bases shall be of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.<sup>11</sup>And likewise for its length on the north side there shall be hangings a hundred cubits long, its pillars twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.<sup>12</sup>And for the breadth of the court on the west side there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, with ten pillars and ten bases.<sup>13</sup>The breadth of the court on the front to the east shall be fifty cubits.<sup>14</sup>The hangings for the one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases.<sup>15</sup>On the other side the hangings shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases.<sup>16</sup>For the gate of the court there shall be a screen twenty cubits long, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. It shall have four pillars and with them four bases.<sup>17</sup>All the pillars around the court shall be filleted with silver. Their hooks shall be of silver, and their bases of bronze.<sup>18</sup>The length of the court shall be a hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, and the height five cubits, with hangings of fine twined linen and bases of bronze.<sup>19</sup>All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, and all its pegs and all the pegs of the court, shall be of bronze.<sup>20</sup>"You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn.<sup>21</sup>In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD. It shall be a statute forever to be observed throughout their generations by the people of Israel.
27.overview:
The first thing a worshiper encountered upon entering the courtyard of the tabernacle was the great bronze altar — and this placement is no accident. Before anyone could draw near to God, before any approach to the Holy Place, there had to be sacrifice. The altar of burnt offering stood at the entrance, declaring that the way to God begins at the place where blood is shed. There is no fellowship with the holy God except through atonement.

The altar was made of acacia wood overlaid with bronze — bronze, the metal that can endure fire, for here the fire of God's judgment fell upon the substitute. Day after day, sacrifice after sacrifice, the blood flowed. Hebrews reminds us that these endless sacrifices could never finally take away sin (Heb. 10:11); they pointed forward to the one sacrifice that would. The bronze altar at the gate is a signpost to the cross at the entrance of our salvation.

The chapter also describes the courtyard with its linen hangings and the oil for the lamp that must burn continually. The court sets apart sacred space; the perpetual light signifies God's unceasing presence and the worship that never stops. As MacArthur observes, every detail of the tabernacle preaches the same gospel: a holy God, sinful people, and the blood that opens the way between them — all fulfilled in Christ, who is at once the altar, the sacrifice, and the light.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar
sections.commentary:
The altar of burnt offering, five cubits square and overlaid with bronze, stood at the very entrance of the tabernacle court. Its placement preaches a sermon: before anyone could approach the presence of God, they had to pass the altar of sacrifice. The way to God begins at the place where blood is shed. There is no entry into fellowship with the holy God except through atonement — a truth woven into the very geography of worship.

Bronze is the metal that endures fire, and here the fire of divine judgment fell — not on the worshiper, but on the substitute laid upon the altar. The horns of the altar, the basins for blood, the grate for the fire: every feature served the shedding and offering of blood. Hebrews teaches that these endless sacrifices could never finally take away sin (Heb. 10:11), but pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, who bore the fire of judgment in our place. The bronze altar is the cross in shadow.

sections.title: The Court of the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
The courtyard, enclosed with fine linen hangings on bronze-based posts, sets apart sacred space from the common world. Within this enclosure stood the altar and the laver, and beyond, the tent of meeting. The single gate on the east side — one way in — reminds us that there is one appointed way to approach God, not many. Jesus declares, "I am the door" (John 10:9) and "I am the way" (John 14:6). There is one entrance to the presence of God.

The white linen surrounding the court speaks of the purity required to approach God, a purity no sinner possesses in himself but which is provided through the sacrifice within. The boundary declares that God's presence is holy ground; one cannot wander in carelessly. Access is real, but it is on God's terms — through the one gate, past the one altar.

sections.title: The Oil for the Lamp
sections.commentary:
The people are to bring pure beaten olive oil so that the lamp may burn continually, from evening to morning, before the LORD. The perpetual light signifies the unceasing presence of God among his people and the worship that never ceases. Even in the darkness of night, the light burns in the holy place — God's presence does not sleep, and the worship of his people is to be constant.

The continual light anticipates Christ, the light that shines in the darkness and is never overcome (John 1:5), and the church, called to keep the lamp of witness burning. It points to the eternal day of the New Jerusalem, where the Lamb is the lamp and there is no night at all (Rev. 21:23-25). The light that burned in the tent foreshadows the unending light of God's presence among his redeemed.

sections.title: From Altar to Presence: The Gospel Geography of Worship
sections.commentary:
The court of the tabernacle lays out the gospel in space. One enters through a single gate, comes first to the bronze altar of sacrifice, then to the laver of cleansing, and only then approaches the holy place lit by the continual lamp. Sacrifice, cleansing, and light — the order is the order of salvation: atonement, purification, and the illumination of God's presence.

Every step points to Christ, who is the one door (John 10:9), the sacrifice on the altar, the cleansing water, and the light of the world (John 8:12). MacArthur notes that nothing in the tabernacle is arbitrary; the very layout preaches that the way to God runs through the blood, leads through cleansing, and ends in the light of his presence — fulfilled wholly in Christ.

27.theology:
No approach to God without sacrifice. The bronze altar at the gate declares that the way to God begins at the place of shed blood — fulfilled in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

One appointed way. The single gate and altar prefigure Christ, the one door and the one way to the Father (John 10:9; 14:6).

The unceasing presence and light of God. The continual lamp signifies God's constant presence and unending worship, fulfilled in Christ the light and the eternal day of the New Jerusalem.
27.examples:
Then: At the entrance to God's dwelling stood the bronze altar, where the fire of judgment fell on the substitute — declaring that no one approaches the holy God except through shed blood, past the one appointed gate.

Now: The cross stands at the entrance of our salvation: there is no fellowship with God except through the sacrifice of Christ, the true altar and Lamb. He is the one door, the one way, and the light that burns forever. We approach God only through him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-8: The bronze altar of burnt offering — the largest object in the complex, standing in the open just inside the gate, and made hollow, with boards so it can be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order of the Furniture Is a Sermon

Nobody reaches the lampstand, the bread or the mercy seat except past the altar. There is no route into the presence of God that does not begin at the place where something dies in your place.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: It is the only major item overlaid with bronze rather than gold. Gold is for the inner rooms; bronze is for the place where fire burns all day and blood runs down — a metal chosen for heat and for scouring.

Now: Even the altar is built light enough to travel. Whatever else moved when Israel moved, the place of sacrifice went with them.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits. And you shall make horns for it on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay it with bronze. You shall make pots for it to receive its ashes, and shovels and basins and forks and fire pans. You shall make all its utensils of bronze. You shall also make for it a grating, a network of bronze, and on the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners. And you shall set it under the ledge of the altar so that the net extends halfway down the altar. And you shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze. And the poles shall be put through the rings, so that the poles are on the two sides of the altar when it is carried. You shall make it hollow, with boards. As it has been shown you on the mountain, so shall it be made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar of burnt offering is the first thing anyone meets. It stands in the open courtyard, directly inside the gate, and nobody reaches the tent without passing it.

It is also the largest object in the complex — roughly seven and a half feet square — and the only major item overlaid with bronze rather than gold. Gold is for the inner rooms; bronze is for the place where fire burns all day and blood runs down. The metal is chosen for heat and for scouring.

The order of the furniture is a sermon in itself. You cannot get to the lampstand, the bread or the mercy seat except past the altar. There is no route into the presence of God that does not begin at the place where something dies in your place.

And it is hollow — make it hollow, with boards — light enough to be carried. Even the altar travels.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-19 — The Court of the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-19: The courtyard enclosed by linen hangings on bronze-based pillars, roughly a hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five, with a single thirty-foot gate on the east.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gate, and Both Halves of What It Says

The entire perimeter is closed except for one screen. An Israelite could walk the whole circuit and find no other way in — which is the architecture of a claim made explicitly later: I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9).

It is exclusive: one way in, and the linen wall otherwise unbroken. And it is generous: thirty feet wide, the widest opening in the whole structure, facing the direction most of the camp lived in, with nobody standing in it to turn anyone away.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything in the courtyard is bronze; everything inside the tent is gold.

Now: The gradient runs from common to holy as you move inward, and every worshipper could see at a glance where he was standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the court of the tabernacle. On the south side the court shall have hangings of fine twined linen a hundred cubits long for one side. Its twenty pillars and their twenty bases shall be of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver. And likewise for its length on the north side there shall be hangings a hundred cubits long, its pillars twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver. And for the breadth of the court on the west side there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, with ten pillars and ten bases. The breadth of the court on the front to the east shall be fifty cubits. The hangings for the one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases. On the other side the hangings shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases. For the gate of the court there shall be a screen twenty cubits long, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. It shall have four pillars and with them four bases. All the pillars around the court shall be filleted with silver. Their hooks shall be of silver, and their bases of bronze. The length of the court shall be a hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, and the height five cubits, with hangings of fine twined linen and bases of bronze. All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, and all its pegs and all the pegs of the court, shall be of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The courtyard is enclosed by linen hangings on bronze-based pillars, about a hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five, with one gate.

One. The entire perimeter is closed except for a single screen on the east side, thirty feet wide, of blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen. An Israelite could walk the whole circuit of the enclosure and find no other way in.

That is deliberate, and it is the architecture of a claim the New Testament makes explicitly. I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). Note both halves of what the single gate says. It is exclusive — there is one way in and the linen wall is otherwise unbroken. And it is generous — the gate is thirty feet wide, the widest opening in the whole structure, facing the direction the camp mostly lived in, with nobody standing in it to turn anyone away.

Everything inside the courtyard is bronze; everything inside the tent is gold. The gradient runs from the common to the holy as you move inward, and every worshipper could see where he stood on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 20-21: Pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn — tended by Aaron and his sons from evening to morning before the LORD, as a statute forever.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Presence Is Maintained

Israel sleeps; the priests do not. All night, in the only lit room in the camp, someone is trimming wicks and topping up oil so that when the nation wakes there is still light burning in the house of God. It is a small duty and it is permanent — and it says something true about how God's presence is kept among his people: not by a single dramatic act but by somebody getting up in the dark to do an unwatched job that would only be noticed if it stopped.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Beaten, not pressed — the first oil from the olive, crushed by hand, the purest and costliest grade, required for the light and nothing else.

Now: The best of what Israel produced went into a lamp that most of the nation never saw burning.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn. In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD. It shall be a statute forever to be observed throughout their generations by the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with two verses about oil, and they are quietly one of the most pastoral things in the tabernacle instructions.

You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn. Beaten, not pressed — the first oil from the olive, crushed by hand, the purest and most costly grade, and it is required for the light and nothing else.

Then: Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD.

The lamp is tended through the night. Israel sleeps; the priests do not. All night, in the only lit room in the camp, someone is trimming wicks and topping up oil so that when the nation wakes there is still light burning in the house of God.

It is a small duty and it is a statute forever. And it says something true about how God's presence is maintained among his people: not by a single dramatic act but by somebody getting up in the dark, regularly, to do an unwatched job that everyone would notice only if it stopped.

28.title: Israel on the High Priest's Heart
