28.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel, to serve me as priests—Aaron and Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.<sup>2</sup>And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty.<sup>3</sup>You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill, that they make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood.<sup>4</sup>These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a coat of checker work, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons to serve me as priests.<sup>5</sup>They shall receive gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>6</sup>"And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and of fine twined linen, skillfully worked.<sup>7</sup>It shall have two shoulder pieces attached to its two edges, so that it may be joined together.<sup>8</sup>And the skillfully woven band on it shall be made like it and be of one piece with it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>9</sup>You shall take two onyx stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel,<sup>10</sup>six of their names on the one stone, and the names of the remaining six on the other stone, in the order of their birth.<sup>11</sup>As a jeweler engraves signets, so shall you engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel. You shall enclose them in settings of gold filigree.<sup>12</sup>And you shall set the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance.<sup>13</sup>You shall make settings of gold filigree,<sup>14</sup>and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords; and you shall attach the corded chains to the settings.<sup>15</sup>"You shall make a breastpiece of judgment, in skilled work. In the style of the ephod you shall make it—of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen shall you make it.<sup>16</sup>It shall be square and doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth.<sup>17</sup>You shall set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle shall be the first row;<sup>18</sup>and the second row an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond;<sup>19</sup>and the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;<sup>20</sup>and the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They shall be set in gold filigree.<sup>21</sup>There shall be twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They shall be like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes.<sup>22</sup>You shall make for the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold.<sup>23</sup>And you shall make for the breastpiece two rings of gold, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece.<sup>24</sup>And you shall put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece.<sup>25</sup>The two ends of the two cords you shall attach to the two settings of filigree, and so attach it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod.<sup>26</sup>You shall make two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the ephod.<sup>27</sup>And you shall make two rings of gold, and attach them in front to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at its seam above the skillfully woven band of the ephod.<sup>28</sup>And they shall bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, so that it may lie on the skillfully woven band of the ephod, so that the breastpiece shall not come loose from the ephod.<sup>29</sup>So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And in the breastpiece of judgment you shall put the Urim and the Thummim, and they shall be on Aaron's heart, when he goes in before the LORD. Thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the people of Israel on his heart before the LORD regularly.<sup>31</sup>"You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue.<sup>32</sup>It shall have an opening for the head in the middle of it, with a woven binding around the opening, like the opening in a garment, so that it may not tear.<sup>33</sup>On its hem you shall make pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, around its hem, with bells of gold between them,<sup>34</sup>a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, around the hem of the robe.<sup>35</sup>And it shall be on Aaron when he ministers, and its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before the LORD, and when he comes out, so that he does not die.<sup>36</sup>"You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a signet, 'Holy to the LORD.'<sup>37</sup>And you shall fasten it on the turban by a cord of blue. It shall be on the front of the turban.<sup>38</sup>It shall be on Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts. It shall regularly be on his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"You shall weave the coat in checker work of fine linen, and you shall make a turban of fine linen, and you shall make a sash embroidered with needlework.<sup>40</sup>"For Aaron's sons you shall make coats and sashes and caps. You shall make them for glory and beauty.<sup>41</sup>And you shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them and ordain them and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests.<sup>42</sup>You shall make for them linen undergarments to cover their naked flesh. They shall reach from the hips to the thighs;<sup>43</sup>and they shall be on Aaron and on his sons when they go into the tent of meeting or when they come near the altar to minister in the Holy Place, lest they bear guilt and die. This shall be a statute forever for him and for his offspring after him.
28.overview:
God now turns to the priesthood, designing garments for Aaron the high priest "for glory and for beauty." Every thread is rich with meaning, but the most moving detail is this: the names of the twelve tribes of Israel are engraved on precious stones and worn by the high priest — on his shoulders and over his heart — whenever he enters the presence of God. The high priest carries the people into God's presence, bearing them on the place of strength (the shoulders) and the place of love (the heart).

What a tender picture of mediation. Aaron does not enter for himself alone; he enters representing the people, bearing their names before the LORD "for remembrance." When God looks upon the high priest, he sees his people named and carried into his presence. This is the very essence of the gospel: we come to God not on our own standing but borne upon the heart of our Great High Priest.

For Jesus is the fulfillment. He is the High Priest who has "passed through the heavens" (Heb. 4:14), bearing our names — bearing us — into the very presence of God. He carries his people on his shoulders like the shepherd seeking the lost sheep, and on his heart like the bridegroom cherishing his bride. As Ferguson says, the believer's deepest comfort is that Christ ever lives, with our names engraved on his heart, to appear in the presence of God for us (Heb. 9:24). The breastpiece also bore the Urim and Thummim for discerning God's will, and a gold plate on the turban read "Holy to the LORD" — for the priest must represent a holy people to a holy God.

sections.title: Garments for Glory and Beauty
sections.commentary:
God sets apart Aaron and his sons to serve as priests and commands holy garments "for glory and for beauty," made by craftsmen filled with the Spirit of skill. The priesthood is God's gracious provision: sinful people cannot approach him directly, so he appoints mediators to stand between. The beauty and glory of the garments reflect the dignity of the office and the holiness of the God they serve. Nothing shabby or careless will do in the presence of the Holy One.

The very existence of the priesthood declares a profound truth: we need a mediator. Left to ourselves, we cannot come to God. The whole institution points forward to the one who would be both priest and sacrifice — Christ, our Great High Priest, who needs no successor because he lives forever (Heb. 7:24-25).

sections.title: The Ephod and the Breastpiece
sections.commentary:
The most moving feature of the priestly garments is the bearing of Israel's names. Two onyx stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod are engraved with the names of the twelve tribes, "stones of remembrance," so that "Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance." And the breastpiece of judgment, set with twelve precious stones, also bears the tribal names, so that "Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart" whenever he enters the Holy Place.

Here is mediation at its most tender. The high priest carries the people into God's presence — on his shoulders, the place of strength, and on his heart, the place of love. When God looks upon the priest, he sees his people named, carried, remembered. Jesus fulfills this perfectly: our Great High Priest bears us on his shoulders like the shepherd who finds his lost sheep, and on his heart like the bridegroom who cherishes his bride. Our names are engraved on his heart as he appears in the presence of God for us (Heb. 9:24). The breastpiece also held the Urim and Thummim, by which God's will was discerned — the priest mediated not only the people to God but God's guidance to the people.

sections.title: The Robe, the Turban, and the Holy Crown
sections.commentary:
The robe is fringed with golden bells and pomegranates, so that the sound is heard when the priest enters and leaves the Holy Place — a sign that he goes in and comes out alive, accepted on behalf of the people. Most striking is the gold plate on the turban, engraved "Holy to the LORD," worn on Aaron's forehead so that he may "bear any guilt" connected with the holy things and the people be accepted before the LORD.

The plate declares the necessity of holiness in approaching God, and the priest's role in bearing the guilt of the people so they may be accepted. This points unmistakably to Christ, who bore our guilt (Isa. 53:6) and is himself "Holy to the LORD," the spotless High Priest who makes us acceptable to God. Every garment, from the engraved stones to the holy crown, declares that we are brought to God only through a mediator who bears us, bears our guilt, and is himself holy. That mediator is Christ.

sections.title: The High Priest as a Portrait of Christ
sections.commentary:
Taken together, the priestly garments form a complete portrait of mediation fulfilled in Christ. The names borne on shoulder and heart show the priest carrying his people into God's presence by strength and love; the Urim and Thummim show him mediating God's guidance to the people; the plate "Holy to the LORD" shows him bearing their guilt that they might be accepted. Every element points beyond Aaron to a greater High Priest.

Hebrews gathers it all into Christ, who has passed through the heavens (4:14), bears us into the presence of God (9:24), is himself holy and undefiled (7:26), and ever lives to intercede for us (7:25). The believer's deepest comfort, as Ferguson says, is that our names are engraved on the heart of our great High Priest, who appears in the presence of God on our behalf — and is himself "Holy to the LORD."

28.theology:
The necessity of a mediator. The priesthood exists because sinners cannot approach God directly. We need one to stand between — fulfilled in Christ, our Great High Priest.

Borne on the heart of the priest. The high priest carries Israel's names on his shoulders and heart into God's presence — a picture of Christ who bears us, by strength and love, before the Father (Heb. 9:24).

Holiness and the bearing of guilt. "Holy to the LORD" and the bearing of the people's guilt point to Christ, who is holy and who bore our guilt that we might be accepted.
28.examples:
Then: God clothed the high priest in garments of glory, engraving Israel's names on stones worn over his shoulders and heart, so that he carried the people into God's presence and bore their guilt that they might be accepted.

Now: Jesus is our Great High Priest, who bears us into the very presence of God — on his shoulders like the shepherd, on his heart like the bridegroom. Our names are engraved on his heart. He bore our guilt and is himself "Holy to the LORD," so that we are accepted in him forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-5 — Garments for Glory and for Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-5: Aaron and his sons brought near to serve as priests, with garments made for glory and for beauty.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Man Brought Near

The verb in verse 1 is the word for approach. The priest is the one brought near so that others can be, and everything that follows dresses a representative.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Aaron is the man who will make the golden calf four chapters from now. Nadab and Abihu are named here too, and will die offering unauthorised fire (Lev. 10).

Now: God appoints this family before the sin, knowing about the sin, and does not revoke it afterwards. The first priestly household in Israel is not a promising one, and it is the one he chose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel, to serve me as priests—Aaron and Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty. You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill, that they make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood. These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a coat of checker work, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons to serve me as priests. They shall receive gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The garments are to be made for glory and for beauty. That phrase is used twice in the chapter and is the only justification given for a great deal of gold thread and precious stone.

But the real business of the chapter is in verse 1: Bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him. The verb is the word for approach — the priest is the man brought near so that others can be. Everything that follows dresses a representative.

And consider who is being consecrated. Aaron is the man who will make the golden calf four chapters from now. God appoints him to the priesthood before the sin, knowing about the sin, and does not revoke it afterwards. Nadab and Abihu are named here too, and they will die offering unauthorised fire (Lev. 10). The first priestly family in Israel is not a promising one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6-14 — The Ephod: Israel on the Shoulders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 6-14: The ephod, with two onyx stones on the shoulder pieces engraved with the twelve tribal names — Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried In

The shoulder is where weight is borne. When the high priest walked into the sanctuary he came in carrying the whole nation — not symbolically in his intentions but physically, on his body, in stone, with every tribe named.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Six names on each stone, all twelve accounted for.

Now: Nobody was left outside for being unimportant, or for being in disgrace that year. All twelve, every time he went in.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and of fine twined linen, skillfully worked. It shall have two shoulder pieces attached to its two edges, so that it may be joined together. And the skillfully woven band on it shall be made like it and be of one piece with it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen. You shall take two onyx stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel, six of their names on the one stone, and the names of the remaining six on the other stone, in the order of their birth. As a jeweler engraves signets, so shall you engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel. You shall enclose them in settings of gold filigree. And you shall set the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance. You shall make settings of gold filigree, and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords; and you shall attach the corded chains to the settings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ephod is a sleeveless garment of gold, blue, purple and scarlet, with two onyx stones on the shoulder pieces. On the stones are engraved the names of the twelve tribes, six on each.

And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance.

The shoulder is where weight is carried. When the high priest walked into the sanctuary, he came in bearing the whole nation — not symbolically in his intentions but physically, on his body, in stone, with every tribe named. Nobody was left outside because they were unimportant or in disgrace that year. All twelve, every time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-30 — The Breastpiece: Israel over the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 15-30: The breastpiece of judgment — twelve engraved stones in four rows, chained to the shoulder pieces so it cannot swing loose — worn on his heart, holding the Urim and the Thummim.
verseByVerse.theology:
On the Shoulders and on the Heart

Carried by strength and carried by love, both at once, every time he went in. It is hard to read that and not think of the one who always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25) — a high priest who needs no engraved stones to remember his people's names, and who bears them not on his clothing but in his body, with the marks of the nails still in it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scripture never explains what the Urim and Thummim were or how they worked, and the honest thing is to say so.

Now: What matters is where they sat. The means of knowing God's will was kept in the same pouch as the names of his people, over the priest's heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a breastpiece of judgment, in skilled work. In the style of the ephod you shall make it—of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen shall you make it. It shall be square and doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth. You shall set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle shall be the first row; and the second row an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond; and the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; and the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They shall be set in gold filigree. There shall be twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They shall be like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes. You shall make for the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold. And you shall make for the breastpiece two rings of gold, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece. And you shall put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece. The two ends of the two cords you shall attach to the two settings of filigree, and so attach it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod. You shall make two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the ephod. And you shall make two rings of gold, and attach them in front to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at its seam above the skillfully woven band of the ephod. And they shall bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, so that it may lie on the skillfully woven band of the ephod, so that the breastpiece shall not come loose from the ephod. So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD. And in the breastpiece of judgment you shall put the Urim and the Thummim, and they shall be on Aaron's heart, when he goes in before the LORD. Thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the people of Israel on his heart before the LORD regularly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the breastpiece, and it is the heart of the chapter. Twelve stones in four rows, each engraved with a tribal name — and it is worn on the chest, fastened with gold chains to the shoulder pieces so it cannot swing loose.

So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD.

On the shoulders and on the heart. Carried by strength and carried by love, and both at once, every time he went in. It is difficult to read that and not think of the one who always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25) — a high priest who does not need engraved stones to remember his people's names, and who bears them not on his clothing but in his body, with the marks of the nails still in it.

Into the breastpiece go the Urim and the Thummim, and Scripture never explains what they were. They were used to seek God's decision on hard questions, and the honest thing is to admit that we do not know their mechanism. What matters is where they sat: the means of knowing God's will was kept in the same pouch as the names of his people, over the priest's heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-43 — The Robe, the Golden Plate, and the Holy Vestments
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 31-43: The blue robe with bells and pomegranates so that he does not die; the gold plate on the turban engraved Holy to the LORD, to bear any guilt from the holy things; and linen undergarments.
verseByVerse.theology:
Even the Gifts Carry Guilt

The offerings themselves, brought in devotion, are contaminated enough to need covering — and the priest wears a plate saying Holy to the LORD precisely so that God can accept worship that is not clean. Nothing anybody brings is good enough on its own, including their best.

A Man Who Is Nothing in Himself

He carries names that are not his, wears a plate that makes acceptable gifts that are not his, and is heard by people he cannot see. Zechariah saw a high priest standing in filthy garments while Satan accused him, and the angel said Remove the filthy garments from him... Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments (Zech. 3:3-4). That is what the gospel does with everyone it saves, and it is why the great multitude at the end is described, of everything that might have been said of them, as people wearing white robes they did not make.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The bells are for the people outside. They cannot see into the sanctuary; they can only listen. As long as the bells are moving, the priest is alive and the sacrifice has been accepted.

Now: Silence would mean the worst had happened. A whole nation standing in a courtyard, straining to hear a sound from behind a curtain — that is the old covenant in one image.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue. It shall have an opening for the head in the middle of it, with a woven binding around the opening, like the opening in a garment, so that it may not tear. On its hem you shall make pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, around its hem, with bells of gold between them, a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, around the hem of the robe. And it shall be on Aaron when he ministers, and its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before the LORD, and when he comes out, so that he does not die. "You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a signet, 'Holy to the LORD.' And you shall fasten it on the turban by a cord of blue. It shall be on the front of the turban. It shall be on Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts. It shall regularly be on his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD. "You shall weave the coat in checker work of fine linen, and you shall make a turban of fine linen, and you shall make a sash embroidered with needlework. "For Aaron's sons you shall make coats and sashes and caps. You shall make them for glory and beauty. And you shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them and ordain them and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. You shall make for them linen undergarments to cover their naked flesh. They shall reach from the hips to the thighs; and they shall be on Aaron and on his sons when they go into the tent of meeting or when they come near the altar to minister in the Holy Place, lest they bear guilt and die. This shall be a statute forever for him and for his offspring after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The robe of the ephod is blue, with pomegranates and golden bells alternating round the hem — and its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before the LORD, and when he comes out, so that he does not die.

The bells are for the people outside. They cannot see into the sanctuary; they can only listen. And as long as the bells are moving, the priest is alive and the sacrifice has been accepted. Silence would mean the worst had happened.

Then the turban, and on it a plate of pure gold engraved with two words: Holy to the LORD. It is worn on the forehead that Aaron may bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts.

Read that carefully, because it is startling. Even Israel's gifts carry guilt. The offerings themselves, brought in devotion, are contaminated enough to need covering — and the priest wears a gold plate saying Holy to the LORD precisely so that God can accept worship that is not clean. Nothing anybody brings is good enough on its own, including their best.

The chapter ends with linen undergarments, which sounds anticlimactic and is the same lesson as the altar without steps (20:26): nothing of the priest's own flesh is to be exposed in the holy place. He comes in wearing what he was given, entirely covered, representing others.

Put the whole outfit together and it describes a man who is nothing in himself: he carries names that are not his, wears a plate that makes acceptable gifts that are not his, and is heard by people he cannot see. Zechariah saw a vision of a high priest standing in filthy garments while Satan accused him, and the angel said Remove the filthy garments from him... Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments (Zech. 3:3-4). That is what the gospel does with everyone it saves, and it is why the great multitude at the end is described, of all the things that could have been said about them, as people wearing white robes they did not make.

29.title: Consecrated by Blood and Sacrifice
29.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now this is what you shall do to them to consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. Take one bull of the herd and two rams without blemish,<sup>2</sup>and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil. You shall make them of fine wheat flour.<sup>3</sup>You shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, and bring the bull and the two rams.<sup>4</sup>You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water.<sup>5</sup>Then you shall take the garments, and put on Aaron the coat and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastpiece, and gird him with the skillfully woven band of the ephod.<sup>6</sup>And you shall set the turban on his head and put the holy crown on the turban.<sup>7</sup>You shall take the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him.<sup>8</sup>Then you shall bring his sons and put coats on them,<sup>9</sup>and you shall gird Aaron and his sons with sashes and bind caps on them. And the priesthood shall be theirs by a statute forever. Thus you shall ordain Aaron and his sons.<sup>10</sup>"Then you shall bring the bull before the tent of meeting. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the bull.<sup>11</sup>Then you shall kill the bull before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting,<sup>12</sup>and shall take part of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and the rest of the blood you shall pour out at the base of the altar.<sup>13</sup>And you shall take all the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and burn them on the altar.<sup>14</sup>But the flesh of the bull and its skin and its dung you shall burn with fire outside the camp; it is a sin offering.<sup>15</sup>"Then you shall take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram,<sup>16</sup>and you shall kill the ram and shall take its blood and throw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>17</sup>Then you shall cut the ram into pieces, and wash its entrails and its legs, and put them with its pieces and its head,<sup>18</sup>and burn the whole ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to the LORD. It is a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"You shall take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram,<sup>20</sup>and you shall kill the ram and take part of its blood and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron and on the tips of the right ears of his sons, and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the great toes of their right feet, and throw the rest of the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>21</sup>Then you shall take part of the blood that is on the altar, and of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and his sons' garments with him. He and his garments shall be holy, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.<sup>22</sup>"You shall also take the fat from the ram and the fat tail and the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right thigh (for it is a ram of ordination),<sup>23</sup>and one loaf of bread and one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer out of the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>You shall put all these on the palms of Aaron and on the palms of his sons, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>25</sup>Then you shall take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering, as a pleasing aroma before the LORD. It is a food offering to the LORD.<sup>26</sup>"You shall take the breast of the ram of Aaron's ordination and wave it for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be your portion.<sup>27</sup>And you shall consecrate the breast of the wave offering that is waved and the thigh of the priests' portion that is contributed from the ram of ordination, from what was Aaron's and his sons'.<sup>28</sup>It shall be for Aaron and his sons as a perpetual due from the people of Israel, for it is a contribution. It shall be a contribution from the people of Israel from their peace offerings, their contribution to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>"The holy garments of Aaron shall be for his sons after him; they shall be anointed in them and ordained in them.<sup>30</sup>The son who succeeds him as priest, who comes into the tent of meeting to minister in the Holy Place, shall wear them seven days.<sup>31</sup>"You shall take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place.<sup>32</sup>And Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram and the bread that is in the basket in the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>33</sup>They shall eat those things with which atonement was made at their ordination and consecration, but an outsider shall not eat of them, because they are holy.<sup>34</sup>And if any of the flesh for the ordination or of the bread remain until the morning, then you shall burn the remainder with fire. It shall not be eaten, because it is holy.<sup>35</sup>"Thus you shall do to Aaron and to his sons, according to all that I have commanded you. Through seven days shall you ordain them,<sup>36</sup>and every day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. Also you shall purify the altar, when you make atonement for it, and shall anoint it to consecrate it.<sup>37</sup>Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar shall become holy.<sup>38</sup>"Now this is what you shall offer on the altar: two lambs a year old day by day regularly.<sup>39</sup>One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight.<sup>40</sup>And with the first lamb a tenth measure of fine flour mingled with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine for a drink offering.<sup>41</sup>The other lamb you shall offer at twilight, and shall offer with it a grain offering and its drink offering, as in the morning, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>42</sup>It shall be a regular burnt offering throughout your generations at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, where I will meet with you, to speak to you there.<sup>43</sup>There I will meet with the people of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by my glory.<sup>44</sup>I will consecrate the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron also and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests.<sup>45</sup>I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God.<sup>46</sup>And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.
29.overview:
This chapter describes the elaborate consecration of the priests — and the central theme is blood. Before Aaron and his sons can serve in God's presence, they must be washed, clothed, anointed, and atoned for through sacrifice after sacrifice. Even the mediators need a mediator's cleansing. The blood is applied to the ear, the thumb, and the toe — consecrating what they hear, what they do, and where they walk. The whole person is claimed for God's service through atoning blood.

The repeated sacrifices — the bull for a sin offering, the rams for ordination and burnt offering — underscore how costly it is to draw near to a holy God. Hebrews makes the contrast explicit: the priests "were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office; but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently" (Heb. 7:23-24). The endless sacrifices that could never make perfect (Heb. 10:1) point to the one sacrifice of Christ, who "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb. 10:12).

And then comes the daily burnt offering — a lamb every morning and every evening, perpetually, generation after generation. At the place of this continual sacrifice, God makes his great promise: "There I will meet with you... I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God." The purpose of all the blood is communion: that the holy God might dwell among his people. The whole sacrificial system exists to make possible the words "I will dwell among you" — words fulfilled finally when the Lamb of God was slain once for all, that God might dwell with us forever.

sections.title: The Cleansing and Clothing
sections.commentary:
The consecration begins with washing, then clothing in the holy garments, then anointing with oil. Even the priests — the mediators — must first be cleansed before they can serve. No one approaches God's service in his own natural condition. The washing signifies the need for purity; the anointing signifies the setting apart for sacred service and the empowering of the Spirit. The priests are made fit for ministry not by their own qualifications but by God's cleansing and consecrating provision.

This pattern of washing and anointing points forward to the cleansing we receive in Christ (Titus 3:5) and the anointing of the Spirit that sets apart and empowers God's people. We do not consecrate ourselves; God cleanses, clothes, and anoints those he calls to serve him.

sections.title: Sacrifice and the Application of Blood
sections.commentary:
The heart of the consecration is blood. A bull is offered as a sin offering, a ram as a burnt offering, and a second ram for ordination. The blood of the ordination ram is applied to the priests' right ear, right thumb, and right big toe — consecrating what they hear, what they do, and where they walk. The whole person is claimed for God through atoning blood. Then blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on the priests and their garments, making them holy.

The repetition of sacrifice underscores how costly it is to draw near to a holy God. As Hebrews teaches, these endless offerings could never finally perfect the worshiper (Heb. 10:1-4); they pointed forward to Christ's one perfect sacrifice. Sproul stressed that the lavish bloodshed of the Old Testament was God's way of imprinting on his people the seriousness of sin and the costliness of atonement — preparing them to understand the cross. The blood on ear, hand, and foot anticipates the whole-life consecration of those redeemed by the blood of Christ.

sections.title: The Daily Burnt Offering and God's Dwelling
sections.commentary:
The chapter culminates in the daily burnt offering: a lamb every morning and every evening, continually, throughout the generations. And at the place of this perpetual sacrifice, God makes his magnificent promise: "There I will meet with you, to speak to you there... I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them."

Here is the goal of the entire sacrificial system: communion. All the blood, all the consecration, all the daily lambs exist for this — that the holy God might dwell among his people. The continual lamb morning and evening points unmistakably to the Lamb of God, slain once for all, by whose blood God now dwells among us forever. "I will dwell among them" is the promise the whole tabernacle serves — and it finds its yes and amen in Christ, who tabernacled among us, and in the New Jerusalem, where God dwells with his people eternally (Rev. 21:3).

sections.title: The Whole System Cries Out for Christ
sections.commentary:
The lavish, repeated bloodshed of the consecration — bull and rams, blood on ear and thumb and toe, daily lambs morning and evening — was God's way of imprinting on his people the seriousness of sin and the costliness of atonement. As Sproul taught, all this prepared Israel to understand the cross. The endless sacrifices that could never make perfect (Heb. 10:1) point relentlessly to the one sacrifice that does.

And the goal of it all is communion: "I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God." The blood serves the dwelling; the sacrifice serves the presence. The whole system cries out for the Lamb of God, slain once for all, by whose blood God now dwells among us forever — the promise fulfilled in Christ who tabernacled among us, and consummated when the dwelling of God is with man (Rev. 21:3).

29.theology:
Even mediators need atonement. The priests must be washed and atoned for by blood before they can serve. No one approaches God in his natural condition.

The costliness of atonement. The repeated sacrifices preach the seriousness of sin and point to Christ's one perfect, final sacrifice (Heb. 10:12) that the daily lambs could never accomplish.

The goal of sacrifice is communion. "I will dwell among them" — all the blood serves this end: that the holy God might dwell with his people, fulfilled in Christ.
29.examples:
Then: The priests were consecrated through washing, anointing, and the blood of sacrifice applied to ear, hand, and foot, while a lamb was offered every morning and evening — all so that God might dwell among his people.

Now: The endless sacrifices that could never perfect us pointed to the one Lamb of God, slain once for all. By his blood we are cleansed, consecrated, and brought near, so that God dwells among us forever. The whole bloody system exists to secure the promise: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: The ordination — washing, then clothing, then anointing — and the phrase for it, literally you shall fill the hands of Aaron and his sons.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Priest Did Not Qualify; He Was Processed

Nothing in the sequence is achieved by the men themselves. They are washed by someone else, dressed by someone else, and oil is poured on them by someone else. And the Hebrew for ordination is fill the hand: a man's hands were filled with what he would handle for the rest of his life. He brings nothing to the office; the office puts something into his hands.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Washed, dressed, anointed — and the order never varies anywhere in Scripture.

Now: They may not serve until all three are done, and none of the three is something a man can do to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is what you shall do to them to consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. Take one bull of the herd and two rams without blemish, and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil. You shall make them of fine wheat flour. You shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, and bring the bull and the two rams. You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water. Then you shall take the garments, and put on Aaron the coat and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastpiece, and gird him with the skillfully woven band of the ephod. And you shall set the turban on his head and put the holy crown on the turban. You shall take the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him. Then you shall bring his sons and put coats on them, and you shall gird Aaron and his sons with sashes and bind caps on them. And the priesthood shall be theirs by a statute forever. Thus you shall ordain Aaron and his sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ordination begins with washing, then clothing, then anointing — and the order never varies anywhere in Scripture. Aaron and his sons are washed with water before they are dressed, dressed before they are anointed, and anointed before they may serve.

Nothing in that sequence is achieved by the men themselves. They are washed by someone else, dressed by someone else, and oil is poured on them by someone else. A priest in Israel did not qualify; he was processed.

The phrase for ordination is literally fill the hand — you shall fill the hands of Aaron and his sons. A man's hands were filled with what he would be handling for the rest of his life. He does not bring anything to the office; the office puts something into his hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-18 — Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-18: The bull and the first ram, with Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the bull, blood on the horns of the altar, and the carcass burned outside the camp; it is a sin offering.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Laying On of Hands

It is not a blessing and not a gesture of ownership but transfer — the worshipper identifying himself with a living animal so that what happens next happens to the animal instead of to him. That gesture is the visual centre of the whole sacrificial system.

Outside the Camp

Hebrews picks the detail up with great force: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12). The place of disgrace, where the refuse went, is where he died.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Blood goes on the horns — the projections at the corners, the highest and most visible points of the altar.

Now: A fugitive who reached the tabernacle and took hold of the horns was claiming sanctuary. Blood is applied precisely where people grabbed when they had nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall bring the bull before the tent of meeting. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the bull. Then you shall kill the bull before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and shall take part of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and the rest of the blood you shall pour out at the base of the altar. And you shall take all the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and burn them on the altar. But the flesh of the bull and its skin and its dung you shall burn with fire outside the camp; it is a sin offering. "Then you shall take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram, and you shall kill the ram and shall take its blood and throw it against the sides of the altar. Then you shall cut the ram into pieces, and wash its entrails and its legs, and put them with its pieces and its head, and burn the whole ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to the LORD. It is a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the sacrifices, and the gesture that runs through all of them: Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the bull.

That action is the visual centre of the entire sacrificial system. It is not a blessing and not a gesture of ownership. It is transfer — the worshipper putting his hands on a living animal to identify himself with it, so that what happens next happens to the animal instead of to him. The bull is then killed, and its blood put on the horns of the altar.

Note where the blood goes: on the horns, the projections at the corners, the highest and most visible points. A fugitive who reached the tabernacle and took hold of the horns of the altar was claiming sanctuary. Blood is applied precisely to the place people grabbed when they had nowhere else to go.

The bull's flesh and hide and dung are burned outside the camp; it is a sin offering. That detail is picked up centuries later with great force: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12). The place of disgrace, where the refuse went, is where he died.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 19-28: The ram of ordination, its blood put on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe; blood and oil sprinkled on Aaron and his garments; and portions placed in the priests' hands and waved as a wave offering before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
Ear, Hand, Foot

What he hears, what he does, where he goes. The three points at which a man's life actually happens are marked with blood before he may serve — a physical argument that nothing about a priest is fit for God's presence until it has been covered.

Blood First, Then Oil

The order holds everywhere in Scripture: atonement precedes anointing. The Spirit is given to people who have first been cleansed, never as a substitute for it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Portions of the ram are literally placed into their hands — the filling of the hands that gives ordination its name.

Now: Even what they offer is handed to them first.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram, and you shall kill the ram and take part of its blood and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron and on the tips of the right ears of his sons, and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the great toes of their right feet, and throw the rest of the blood against the sides of the altar. Then you shall take part of the blood that is on the altar, and of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and his sons' garments with him. He and his garments shall be holy, and his sons and his sons' garments with him. "You shall also take the fat from the ram and the fat tail and the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right thigh (for it is a ram of ordination), and one loaf of bread and one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer out of the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD. You shall put all these on the palms of Aaron and on the palms of his sons, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. Then you shall take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering, as a pleasing aroma before the LORD. It is a food offering to the LORD. "You shall take the breast of the ram of Aaron's ordination and wave it for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be your portion. And you shall consecrate the breast of the wave offering that is waved and the thigh of the priests' portion that is contributed from the ram of ordination, from what was Aaron's and his sons'. It shall be for Aaron and his sons as a perpetual due from the people of Israel, for it is a contribution. It shall be a contribution from the people of Israel from their peace offerings, their contribution to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second ram is the ram of ordination, and what is done with its blood is peculiar and precise. It is put on the tip of Aaron's right ear, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.

Ear, hand, foot: what he hears, what he does, where he goes. The three points at which a man's life actually happens are marked with blood before he is allowed to serve. It is a physical argument that nothing about a priest — not his listening, not his work, not his walking — is fit for God's presence until it has been covered.

Then blood and oil together are sprinkled on Aaron and his garments. Blood first, then oil. That order holds everywhere in Scripture: atonement precedes anointing, and the Spirit is given to people who have first been cleansed, never as a substitute for it.

Portions of the ram are then placed in the priests' hands and waved as a wave offering before the LORD — the literal filling of the hands that gives ordination its name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-37 — Seven Days, and an Atoned Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 29-37: The garments pass to Aaron's sons; the ordination runs seven days with a sin offering daily; and seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Even the Altar Needs Cleansing

The place where atonement is made must itself be atoned for, because it was built by sinful hands out of materials from a fallen world. Everything in the system requires cleansing, including the instruments of cleansing — which is the argument Hebrews builds on: these sacrifices can never take away sins, and their endless repetition is itself the proof (Heb. 10:11).

Set against that: by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb. 10:14). Seven days of bulls and rams to make one man fit to stand in a tent, against one afternoon that settled the matter permanently.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seven days of sacrifice to consecrate one family for one job.

Now: And it had to be redone for every generation of priests that followed, because they kept dying.

verseByVerse.quote: "The holy garments of Aaron shall be for his sons after him; they shall be anointed in them and ordained in them. The son who succeeds him as priest, who comes into the tent of meeting to minister in the Holy Place, shall wear them seven days. "You shall take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place. And Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram and the bread that is in the basket in the entrance of the tent of meeting. They shall eat those things with which atonement was made at their ordination and consecration, but an outsider shall not eat of them, because they are holy. And if any of the flesh for the ordination or of the bread remain until the morning, then you shall burn the remainder with fire. It shall not be eaten, because it is holy. "Thus you shall do to Aaron and to his sons, according to all that I have commanded you. Through seven days shall you ordain them, and every day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. Also you shall purify the altar, when you make atonement for it, and shall anoint it to consecrate it. Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar shall become holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The garments pass to Aaron's sons after him, and the ordination lasts seven days, with a sin offering every day. Seven days of sacrifice to consecrate one family for one job.

Then the altar itself must be atoned for: seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and the altar shall be most holy.

The altar needs cleansing. The place where atonement is made must itself be atoned for, because it was built by sinful hands out of materials from a fallen world. Everything in this system requires cleansing, including the instruments of cleansing — which is precisely the argument Hebrews builds on: these sacrifices can never take away sins, and their endless repetition is itself the proof (Heb. 10:11).

Set against that, the sentence Hebrews reaches: by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb. 10:14). Seven days of bulls and rams to make one man fit to stand in a tent, against one afternoon that finished the matter permanently.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38-46 — The Daily Lamb, and God Dwelling Among Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 38-46: The daily offering of two lambs, morning and twilight, for ever — and then the reason for all of it: I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God... who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Reason Given for the Exodus

Not that I might give them a land and not that they might be free, but that I might dwell among them. The plagues, the sea, the manna and the mountain were all so that God could live in the middle of his people. That was the object of the whole exercise from the burning bush onward.

And it is the sentence the rest of Scripture keeps reaching for. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14) uses the word for pitching a tent. Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? (1 Cor. 3:16). And at the end, the loud voice from the throne: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3). Chapters of cubits and rams and hyssop all serve one ambition, held from Egypt to the new creation — that God should live with us, and not at a distance.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two lambs a day, every day, for ever.

Now: Whatever else happened in Israel — harvest, war, plague, coronation, exile — a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk. The nation's day was bracketed by sacrifice at both ends.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is what you shall offer on the altar: two lambs a year old day by day regularly. One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight. And with the first lamb a tenth measure of fine flour mingled with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine for a drink offering. The other lamb you shall offer at twilight, and shall offer with it a grain offering and its drink offering, as in the morning, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. It shall be a regular burnt offering throughout your generations at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, where I will meet with you, to speak to you there. There I will meet with the people of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by my glory. I will consecrate the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron also and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests. I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daily offering: two lambs, one in the morning and one at twilight, every day, for ever. Whatever else happened in Israel — harvest, war, plague, coronation, exile — a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk, and the nation's day was bracketed by sacrifice at both ends.

And then, at the very end of all these instructions, God says why he has been giving them:

There I will meet with you, to speak to you... I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.

Read the reason he gives for the exodus. Not that I might give them a land, and not that they might be free. Who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. The plagues, the sea, the manna, the mountain — all of it was so that God could live in the middle of his people. That was the object of the whole exercise from the burning bush onward.

And it is the sentence the rest of the Bible keeps reaching for. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14) uses the word for pitching a tent. Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? (1 Cor. 3:16). And at the end, the loud voice from the throne: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3). Chapters of cubits and rams and hyssop are all in service of one ambition, held from Egypt to the new creation — that God should live with us, and not at a distance.

30.title: Every Detail of Worship Ordained by God
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall make an altar on which to burn incense; you shall make it of acacia wood.<sup>2</sup>A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its breadth. It shall be square, and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be of one piece with it.<sup>3</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And you shall make a molding of gold around it.<sup>4</sup>And you shall make two golden rings for it. Under its molding on two opposite sides of it you shall make them, and they shall be holders for poles with which to carry it.<sup>5</sup>You shall make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.<sup>6</sup>And you shall put it in front of the veil that is above the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony, where I will meet with you.<sup>7</sup>And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it,<sup>8</sup>and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it, a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations.<sup>9</sup>You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you shall not pour a drink offering on it.<sup>10</sup>Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year. With the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement for it once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD."<sup>11</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>12</sup>"When you take the census of the people of Israel, then each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them when you number them.<sup>13</sup>Each one who is numbered in the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Everyone who is numbered in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the LORD's offering.<sup>15</sup>The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD's offering to make atonement for your lives.<sup>16</sup>You shall take the atonement money from the people of Israel and shall give it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives."<sup>17</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>18</sup>"You shall also make a basin of bronze, with its stand of bronze, for washing. You shall put it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it,<sup>19</sup>with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet.<sup>20</sup>When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn a food offering to the LORD, they shall wash with water, so that they may not die.<sup>21</sup>They shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they may not die. It shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his offspring throughout their generations."<sup>22</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>23</sup>"Take the finest spices: of liquid myrrh 500 shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, that is, 250, and 250 of aromatic cane,<sup>24</sup>and 500 of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil.<sup>25</sup>And you shall make of these a sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil.<sup>26</sup>With it you shall anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony,<sup>27</sup>and the table and all its utensils, and the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense,<sup>28</sup>and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils and the basin and its stand.<sup>29</sup>You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy.<sup>30</sup>You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests.<sup>31</sup>And you shall say to the people of Israel, 'This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations.<sup>32</sup>It shall not be poured on the body of an ordinary person, and you shall make no other like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you.<sup>33</sup>Whoever compounds any like it or whoever puts any of it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.'"<sup>34</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Take sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense (of each shall there be an equal part),<sup>35</sup>and make an incense blended as by the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.<sup>36</sup>You shall beat some of it very small, and put part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting where I shall meet with you. It shall be most holy for you.<sup>37</sup>And the incense that you shall make according to its composition, you shall not make for yourselves. It shall be for you holy to the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
30.overview:
This chapter gathers several final furnishings and ordinances of worship — the altar of incense, the atonement money, the bronze laver, the anointing oil, and the holy incense — and through them all runs one great truth: every detail of worship is ordained by God, not invented by man. We do not get to decide how to approach God; he tells us. As Calvin insisted, the second commandment teaches that God alone determines how he is to be worshiped.

The altar of incense, standing before the veil, signifies the prayers of God's people rising before him — "let my prayer be counted as incense before you" (Ps. 141:2); and in Revelation the incense is "the prayers of the saints" (Rev. 5:8). The atonement money reminds Israel that every life must be ransomed; the bronze laver of washing reminds them that those who serve God must be clean. The anointing oil consecrates everything for holy use, and the fragrant incense is reserved for God alone — worship is to be set apart, never made common.

Each ordinance whispers the gospel. The incense of prayer ascends because Christ our High Priest has opened the way. The ransom money points to the precious blood by which we were ransomed (1 Pet. 1:18-19). The laver points to the washing of regeneration. As MacArthur observes, nothing in the worship of God is arbitrary; every detail is a finger pointing to Christ, in whom all the shadows find their substance.

sections.title: The Altar of Incense
sections.commentary:
The golden altar of incense stands before the veil, before the mercy seat, where God meets his people. On it, fragrant incense burns perpetually, morning and evening, a sweet aroma rising before the LORD. The incense signifies the prayers of God's people ascending to him: "Let my prayer be counted as incense before you" (Ps. 141:2). In Revelation, the golden bowls of incense are explicitly "the prayers of the saints" (Rev. 5:8). The fragrance of acceptable worship rises continually before God's throne.

That the altar stands before the veil, nearest the presence, teaches that prayer is among the most intimate acts of worship. Yet the incense rises only because atonement has been made — the altar's horns are touched with the blood of the sin offering once a year (v. 10). Our prayers ascend acceptably only because Christ our High Priest has opened the way and ever lives to intercede. The sweet incense of our prayers is made fragrant by his mediation.

sections.title: The Atonement Money
sections.commentary:
When the people are numbered, each must give a half-shekel as a ransom for his life — the same amount for rich and poor, "that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives." Every life requires a ransom; no one is exempt, and no one can pay more or less. Before God, all stand on level ground: all are sinners, all need atonement, all are ransomed at the same price.

This points forward to the great ransom: "you were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet. 1:18-19). The half-shekel could only symbolize; the blood of Christ actually ransoms. And the equality of the payment foreshadows the gospel truth that all are saved on the same terms — not by merit, status, or wealth, but by the one ransom paid for all.

sections.title: The Bronze Laver
sections.commentary:
A bronze basin filled with water stands between the altar and the tent, and the priests must wash their hands and feet before they minister, "lest they die." Those who serve the holy God must be clean. The laver teaches that atonement (the altar) must be accompanied by cleansing (the laver) — those brought near must also be made pure. The washing is a daily necessity, a continual reminder that holiness is required of those who draw near.

This points to the cleansing we receive in Christ — "the washing of regeneration" (Titus 3:5) — and the ongoing cleansing of confession and the Word (Eph. 5:26; 1 John 1:9). Jesus' washing of the disciples' feet (John 13) draws on this very theme: those who have been bathed need only to have their feet washed. The redeemed are cleansed once for all yet daily renewed.

sections.title: The Anointing Oil and the Incense
sections.commentary:
God prescribes a holy anointing oil of finest spices and a fragrant incense, both consecrated for sacred use alone. The oil sets apart the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priests as holy; the incense is reserved exclusively for the worship of God. Both are forbidden for common use, on pain of being cut off — for the things of God must not be treated as common. Worship is to be set apart, holy, distinct from the profane.

The anointing oil signifies the Spirit's setting apart for holy service — the very word "Messiah" and "Christ" mean "Anointed One." Jesus is the supremely Anointed, set apart by the Spirit for his saving work (Luke 4:18). The careful regulation of every element of worship teaches that we do not approach God on our own terms but on his. Nothing in the worship of God is arbitrary; every detail points to Christ, the fulfillment and substance of all the shadows.

sections.title: Approaching God on His Terms
sections.commentary:
The varied ordinances of this chapter — incense, ransom, laver, oil — converge on a single principle: we approach God only on his terms, by his appointed means. The regulative pattern of worship, rooted in the second commandment, runs through them all. We do not invent our way to God; he tells us how to come, and every appointed means is a finger pointing to Christ.

The incense of prayer rises through our Intercessor (Rev. 5:8); the ransom is paid not in silver but in his precious blood (1 Pet. 1:18-19); the laver's washing is the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5); the anointing oil signifies the Spirit who sets apart the Anointed One and his people. In Christ, every shadow finds its substance, and we worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:24).

30.theology:
Worship ordained by God. Every furnishing and ordinance is prescribed by God, not invented by man. We approach God on his terms, not our own (the regulative principle, rooted in the second commandment).

Prayer as incense. The altar of incense pictures the prayers of the saints rising before God, made acceptable through Christ's mediation (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 5:8).

Ransom and cleansing. The atonement money and the laver point to the ransom of Christ's blood (1 Pet. 1:18-19) and the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5).
30.examples:
Then: God prescribed every detail of worship — the incense of prayer, the ransom money, the laver of cleansing, the holy oil and incense — teaching Israel that he alone determines how he is to be approached, and that all worship requires atonement and cleansing.

Now: Our prayers rise as incense, made fragrant by Christ our Intercessor. We are ransomed not by silver but by his precious blood, and cleansed by the washing of regeneration. Every shadow of the tabernacle finds its substance in him — and we worship God on his terms, in spirit and truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-10: The altar of incense before the veil, burning morning and evening as a regular incense offering before the LORD, its horns receiving blood once a year.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sacrifice Outside, Prayer Inside

Twice a day, at exactly the hours the lambs were killed in the courtyard, smoke rose against the veil and drifted over it into the Most Holy Place. Scripture is explicit about the meaning — let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Ps. 141:2); and the golden bowls in the Revelation are full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). Luke opens his Gospel at this altar, with the whole multitude of the people praying outside at the hour of incense (Luke 1:8-11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: It stands as close to the ark as anything can without being behind the curtain.

Now: Once a year its horns receive blood from the sin offering. Even the place where prayer ascends has to be atoned for — a plain admission that our prayers are not clean either.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make an altar on which to burn incense; you shall make it of acacia wood. A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its breadth. It shall be square, and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And you shall make a molding of gold around it. And you shall make two golden rings for it. Under its molding on two opposite sides of it you shall make them, and they shall be holders for poles with which to carry it. You shall make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. And you shall put it in front of the veil that is above the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony, where I will meet with you. And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it, and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it, a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations. You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you shall not pour a drink offering on it. Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year. With the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement for it once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar of incense stands in the Holy Place, immediately in front of the veil, and incense is burned on it every morning and every evening — a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations.

It sits as close to the ark as anything can without being behind the curtain. Twice a day, at exactly the hours the lambs were being killed in the courtyard, smoke rose up against the veil and drifted over the top of it into the Most Holy Place. Sacrifice outside, prayer inside, at the same moment.

Scripture is explicit about what the smoke means. Let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Ps. 141:2), and in the Revelation the golden bowls held by the elders are full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). And Luke opens his Gospel at this altar: Zechariah is burning incense while the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense — and an angel appears beside it (Luke 1:8-11).

Once a year the horns of this altar receive blood from the sin offering. Even the place where prayer ascends has to be atoned for, which is a plain admission that our prayers are not clean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11-16: The census tax — a ransom for his life — fixed so that the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Flat Price

Everybody pays the same, and it is a small sum — about two days' wages. The point is not efficient revenue but a statement no Israelite could miss: the value of a human life is not graduated by wealth, and nobody can pay more to be worth more.

Peter shows what it was pointing at: you were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18-19). The half shekel was flat because the real price would be flat — one payment, of infinite value, with nobody in the queue contributing to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: To be counted in Israel, a man had to pay for his own life.

Now: This is the silver that became the bases of the tabernacle (26:19). The whole house of God stood on ransom money.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "When you take the census of the people of Israel, then each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them when you number them. Each one who is numbered in the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD. Everyone who is numbered in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the LORD's offering. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD's offering to make atonement for your lives. You shall take the atonement money from the people of Israel and shall give it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The census tax, and the reason given for it is unexpected: each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them.

To be counted in Israel, a man had to pay for his own life. And the amount is fixed: The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel.

Everybody pays the same, and it is a small sum — about two days' wages. The point is not to raise revenue efficiently but to make a statement no Israelite could miss: the value of a human life is not graduated by wealth, and no one can pay more to be worth more. Rich and poor are ransomed at an identical price.

Peter takes exactly that thought and shows what it was pointing at: you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18-19). The half shekel was flat because the real price would be flat — one payment, of infinite value, and nobody in the queue contributing anything to it.

And this is the silver that became the bases of the tabernacle (26:19). The whole house of God stood on ransom money.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 17-21: The bronze basin between the altar and the tent, where the priests shall wash with water, so that they may not die.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Bath, Many Washings

The priests were washed once at their ordination, and that washing was never repeated — a man was consecrated once. But hands and feet are washed every time they approach, because hands get dirty doing the work and feet get dirty crossing the courtyard.

It is the distinction Jesus drew when Peter, told his feet were to be washed, demanded a full bath: The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean (John 13:10). A believer is not re-converted every time he sins. He is washed once, and then keeps coming back for his feet.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The basin stands between the place of sacrifice and the door of the tent.

Now: Nobody walked from the altar into God's house without stopping at it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "You shall also make a basin of bronze, with its stand of bronze, for washing. You shall put it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn a food offering to the LORD, they shall wash with water, so that they may not die. They shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they may not die. It shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his offspring throughout their generations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bronze basin stands between the altar and the tent, and the rule attached to it is absolute: they shall wash with water, so that they may not die.
