The priests have already been washed once, at their ordination. That washing was never repeated — a man was consecrated once. But the daily washing of hands and feet happens every time they approach, because hands get dirty doing the work and feet get dirty walking about the courtyard.

One bath, many washings. It is the distinction Jesus made in an upper room when Peter, told his feet were to be washed, demanded a complete bath instead: The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean (John 13:10). A believer is not re-converted every time he sins. He is washed once and then keeps coming back for his feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-33: The anointing oil of myrrh, cinnamon, aromatic cane and cassia, used on everything in the tent and on the priests — and forbidden for any other use on pain of being cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointed One

Messiah is Hebrew for anointed one; Christ is the same word in Greek. Every object and every priest in this tent is smeared with oil in anticipation of a person whose title would simply be the anointed — and when a woman broke a flask of costly ointment over his head and the room complained about the waste, he said she had done it to prepare me for burial (Mark 14:8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The recipe was not secret. The restriction was on use, not knowledge.

Now: The smell was to mean one thing only. Anyone in Israel who caught that scent knew instantly what it belonged to, and if people had worn it socially the association would have dissolved inside a generation. Holiness in Scripture is largely a matter of things not being interchangeable.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the finest spices: of liquid myrrh 500 shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, that is, 250, and 250 of aromatic cane, and 500 of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil. And you shall make of these a sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil. With it you shall anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony, and the table and all its utensils, and the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils and the basin and its stand. You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. And you shall say to the people of Israel, 'This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations. It shall not be poured on the body of an ordinary person, and you shall make no other like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever compounds any like it or whoever puts any of it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anointing oil is compounded of myrrh, cinnamon, aromatic cane and cassia in olive oil, and everything in the tent is anointed with it — the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, and Aaron and his sons.

Then the prohibition, with real severity attached: the formula may not be reproduced for ordinary use, and whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people.

It was not that the recipe was secret. It was that the smell was to mean one thing only. Anyone in Israel who caught that scent knew instantly what it belonged to, and if people had been wearing it socially the association would have dissolved within a generation. Holiness in Scripture is largely a matter of things not being interchangeable.

Worth remembering, too, what the word means. Messiah is Hebrew for anointed one; Christ is the same word in Greek. Every object and every priest in this tent is smeared with oil in anticipation of a person whose title would simply be the anointed — and when a woman broke a flask of costly ointment over Jesus' head and the room complained about the waste, he said she had done it to prepare me for burial (Mark 14:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 34-38: The holy incense, compounded the same way and under the same restriction — You shall not make any for yourselves; it shall be for you holy to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Restricted Thing, Given Away

Israel is given a fragrance for prayer and a fragrance for anointing, and forbidden to use either for itself — not because God is stingy with pleasant things but because a sign used for everything stops signifying anything. And then the New Testament does what it characteristically does: Paul says God through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere, and that we are the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2:14-15). The perfume no Israelite was permitted to wear is what the church is now said to smell like.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Reproduce it as a domestic perfume and you are cut off.

Now: Both restrictions guard the same thing — that when these scents were noticed, everyone knew exactly what they meant.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense (of each shall there be an equal part), and make an incense blended as by the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. You shall beat some of it very small, and put part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting where I shall meet with you. It shall be most holy for you. And the incense that you shall make according to its composition, you shall not make for yourselves. It shall be for you holy to the LORD. Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The incense is compounded the same way and carries the same restriction: You shall not make any for yourselves; it shall be for you holy to the LORD. Reproduce it as a domestic perfume and you are cut off.

Take the two together and the chapter has a shape. Israel is given a fragrance for prayer and a fragrance for anointing, and forbidden to use either for itself. What belongs to God is not available for private enjoyment — not because God is stingy with pleasant things, but because a sign that gets used for everything stops signifying anything.

And the New Testament, characteristically, takes the restricted thing and gives it away. Paul tells the Corinthians that God through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere, and that we are the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2:14-15). The perfume that no Israelite was permitted to wear is what the church is now said to smell like.

31.title: The Spirit Equips for God's Work
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah,<sup>3</sup>and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship,<sup>4</sup>to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>5</sup>in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft.<sup>6</sup>And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you:<sup>7</sup>the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent,<sup>8</sup>the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense,<sup>9</sup>and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand,<sup>10</sup>and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests,<sup>11</sup>and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>13</sup>"You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you.<sup>14</sup>You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>15</sup>Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever.<sup>17</sup>It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'"<sup>18</sup>And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
31.overview:
Before the work of building the tabernacle can begin, God provides the workers — and in doing so reveals a glorious truth: God equips by his Spirit those he calls to his work. He names Bezalel and fills him "with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship." This is the first explicit statement in Scripture of someone being filled with the Spirit — and remarkably, it is for the purpose of artistic craftsmanship. God cares about beauty, skill, and excellence in his service, and he himself supplies the ability.

This dignifies all Spirit-empowered work. As Keller has powerfully taught, there is no sacred-secular divide in God's economy: the craftsman working with gold and wood is filled with the same Spirit who would later fill prophets and apostles. Every gift, every skill exercised for God's glory is a Spirit-given grace. God does not merely command the work; he equips the workers. He calls the called and gifts the gifted.

Then God seals the instructions with the Sabbath — "a sign between me and you... that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you." Even the holy work of building the tabernacle must not violate the rhythm of rest. The Sabbath declares that our acceptance rests not on our work but on God's grace; he sanctifies us. As Ferguson notes, the Sabbath is the gospel embedded in the calendar — a weekly testimony that salvation is by grace, not by ceaseless labor. We rest because God has done, and will do, the saving work.

sections.title: Bezalel Filled with the Spirit
sections.commentary:
God calls Bezalel by name and fills him "with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs." This is the first time Scripture describes someone as filled with the Spirit — and it is for the work of skilled craftsmanship: working gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood. God appoints Oholiab alongside him and gives ability to all the skilled craftsmen. The work of building God's dwelling is a Spirit-empowered work from start to finish.

This dignifies all skilled labor done for God's glory and shatters any false divide between sacred and secular work. As Keller taught, the craftsman filled with the Spirit to fashion beautiful things for God's house shows that artistry, excellence, and skill are gifts of God to be exercised in his service. God does not merely issue commands; he equips the workers. Every ability we have for kingdom work is a grace from the Spirit who gifts as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11).

sections.title: The Sign of the Sabbath
sections.commentary:
God seals the tabernacle instructions with the Sabbath command: "You shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you." Even the sacred work of building God's dwelling must not override the Sabbath rest. The Sabbath is a covenant sign, a weekly testimony that the people belong to God and that he, not their labor, sanctifies them.

This is the gospel embedded in the calendar. The Sabbath declares that our standing with God rests not on our ceaseless work but on his grace — "I, the LORD, sanctify you." We rest because God has done and will do the saving work. Hebrews 4 develops this into the eternal rest that remains for the people of God, the rest we enter by faith in Christ, who says, "Come to me, all who labor... and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11:28). The Sabbath sign points to the soul's true rest in the finished work of Christ.

sections.title: The Tablets of Stone
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes as God gives Moses "the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God." The law that will be placed in the Ark, beneath the mercy seat, is written by God's own finger — underscoring its divine origin and authority. These are not human inventions but the very words of God, etched in stone for permanence.

Yet the next chapter will show the people breaking this law almost before the tablets descend the mountain. The tablets written by God's finger, soon to be shattered, set the stage for the great drama of human sin and divine mercy that follows. The law is holy and good, but it cannot make sinful hearts new — it will take a new covenant, written not on stone but on the heart (Jer. 31:33), to accomplish that. The finger of God on stone points forward to the Spirit of God on the heart.

sections.title: Spirit-Empowered Work and Grace-Grounded Rest
sections.commentary:
The chapter holds together two great truths: the Spirit empowers God's people for God's work, and the Sabbath grounds all work in grace. Bezalel is filled with the Spirit to build; the Sabbath sign declares that it is the LORD who sanctifies, not human labor. Work and rest, gift and grace, are woven together in the rhythm of the redeemed life.

This anticipates the New Testament church: a Spirit-gifted body (1 Cor. 12), laboring from rest rather than for it, finding its true Sabbath in Christ, who says, "Come to me, all who labor... and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11:28). The finger of God that wrote on stone tablets points to the Spirit of God who writes the law on the heart in the new covenant (Jer. 31:33; 2 Cor. 3:3).

31.theology:
The Spirit equips for God's work. Bezalel is the first person Scripture describes as filled with the Spirit — for skilled craftsmanship. God gifts those he calls; every ability for kingdom work is grace.

The dignity of skilled labor. There is no sacred-secular divide; artistry and excellence done for God's glory are Spirit-given graces.

The Sabbath as sign of grace. The Sabbath declares that God, not our labor, sanctifies us — the gospel embedded in the calendar, pointing to our rest in Christ's finished work.
31.examples:
Then: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit for skilled craftsmanship to build the tabernacle, and sealed the instructions with the Sabbath — a sign that the LORD, not human labor, sanctifies his people.

Now: God still equips by his Spirit those he calls to his work, dignifying every skill exercised for his glory. And the Sabbath still preaches grace: we rest because God has done the saving work. In Christ we find the soul's true rest — "come to me, and I will give you rest."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — Bezalel and Oholiab, Filled with the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-11: God calls Bezalel by name and fills him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship; appoints Oholiab with him; and grants ability to all able men.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Man Filled With the Spirit Is a Craftsman

Not a prophet, not a priest, not a king. And the filling is described entirely in terms of skill — ability, intelligence, knowledge, and the capacity to design beautiful things and execute them in metal, stone and wood.

That deserves saying plainly, because much Christian thinking has quietly assumed the spiritual gifts are the ones exercised on a platform. The first man in the Bible full of the Spirit of God was good with his hands, and God says so in a list that names specific trades.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tabernacle was not built by two geniuses. I have given to all able men ability takes in every skilled worker in the camp, and credits their competence to God.

Now: Consider where Bezalel learned his trade. He is perhaps eighty, and has spent his life a slave in Egypt — a country of extraordinary metalwork and joinery. Skills acquired in captivity, probably under compulsion, are the skills God now uses to build his house. Nothing learned in the years that felt wasted is necessarily wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft. And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you: the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent, the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand, and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests, and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After seven chapters of specification, God names the man who will build it — and what he says about him is the first statement of its kind in the Bible.

See, I have called by name Bezalel... and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood.

This is the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God. Not a prophet, not a priest, not a king — a craftsman. And the Spirit's filling is described entirely in terms of skill: ability, intelligence, knowledge, and the capacity to design beautiful things and execute them in metal, stone and wood.

That deserves to be said plainly, because a great deal of Christian thinking has quietly assumed that spiritual gifts are the ones exercised on a platform. The first man in the Bible full of the Spirit of God was good with his hands, and God says so in a list that names specific trades.

Oholiab is appointed alongside him, and then a wider provision: And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you. Every skilled worker in the camp is included in that sentence. The tabernacle was not built by two geniuses but by a workforce whose competence is credited to God.

It is also worth noticing where these men learned their trade. Bezalel is perhaps eighty years old and has spent his life as a slave in Egypt, in a country of extraordinary metalwork and joinery. Skills acquired in captivity, probably under compulsion, are the skills God now uses to build his house. Nothing learned in the years that felt wasted is necessarily wasted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — The Sabbath, a Sign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-18: Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, as a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you — and then the two tablets, written with the finger of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Even Work Commanded by God

The placement is the point. Israel has just been handed the most important construction project in its history, with a divine blueprint and an urgent purpose, and the last word before Moses descends is a command to stop one day in seven. The tabernacle could wait. It is a standing rebuke to the idea that sufficiently important work justifies never resting — and the more sacred the project, the more the rebuke applies.

A Sign, Not a Productivity Measure

The sabbath marks out a people who belong to God, and declares that their holiness is something he does to them rather than something they achieve. A nation that downs tools every seventh day is saying, publicly and repeatedly, that the world is not held up by its effort.

The Finger of God

The phrase Egypt's magicians used when they failed (8:19), and the phrase Jesus used of his own authority over demons (Luke 11:20). The same finger that made gnats out of dust and set people free in Galilee wrote the commandments into rock.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses is holding stone tablets inscribed by God himself, containing a covenant Israel has three times sworn to keep.

Now: He turns to carry them down the mountain — and at the bottom of it, at this exact moment, they are dancing round a golden calf.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you. You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'" And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, immediately after all the building instructions, God returns to the sabbath — and the placement is the point. Israel has just been handed the most important construction project in its history, with a divine blueprint and an urgent purpose, and the last word before Moses comes down the mountain is: Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths.

Not even work commanded by God may be used as a reason to skip rest. The tabernacle could wait a day a week. It is a permanent rebuke to the idea that important enough work justifies never stopping, and the more sacred the project the more the rebuke applies.

And the reason given is relational: it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you. The sabbath is not primarily about productivity or even about rest. It is a sign — a visible weekly marker that this people belongs to God, and that their holiness is something he does to them rather than something they achieve. A nation that downs tools every seventh day is saying, publicly and repeatedly, that the world is not held up by its effort.

Then the chapter's last line, and it closes the whole Sinai section: And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.

The finger of God — the phrase Egypt's magicians used when they failed (8:19), and the phrase Jesus used of his own authority over demons (Luke 11:20). The same finger that made gnats out of dust and set people free in Galilee wrote the ten commandments into rock.

Moses is now holding stone tablets inscribed by God himself, containing a covenant Israel has three times sworn to keep. He turns to carry them down the mountain. And at the bottom of that mountain, at this exact moment, they are dancing round a golden calf.

32.title: The Golden Calf and the Intercessor
32.text: <sup>4</sup>...he made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" <sup>11</sup>But Moses implored the LORD his God... <sup>32</sup>"But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written."
32.overview:
While Moses is on the mountain receiving the law, the people commit the great apostasy. They grow impatient, demand gods they can see, and fashion a golden calf, declaring, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" Within weeks of the most stunning revelation of God's glory, they exchange the living God for an idol of gold. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols; we cannot trust ourselves even for a moment.

God's wrath burns, and he threatens to consume the people and start over with Moses. And here the chapter rises to one of the most magnificent portraits of mediation in all Scripture. Moses stands in the breach. He pleads God's own glory and God's own promises. And then, astonishingly, he offers his very life: "if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book." Moses offers to be damned for his people. He cannot actually accomplish it; but his offer points to the One who could and did.

For Jesus is the greater Moses, the true Mediator, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but actually was — who became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), who was forsaken on the cross that we might be forgiven. Moses' intercession is a shadow; Christ's is the substance. As Sproul preached, the golden calf shows us the depth of our sin, and the intercessor shows us the height of God's mercy. The chapter ends with judgment and a plague, but the people are not destroyed — because a mediator stood in the gap.

sections.title: The Great Apostasy
sections.commentary:
While Moses delays on the mountain, the people demand of Aaron, "Make us gods who shall go before us." Aaron collects their gold and fashions a calf, and the people cry, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" They even hold a feast "to the LORD" before it — a horrifying blend of idolatry and the worship of God. Within weeks of hearing God thunder "You shall have no other gods" and "You shall not make a carved image," they break the first two commandments outright.

The speed and depth of the apostasy is staggering. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual idol factory; left to ourselves, we cannot be trusted even for a moment. The golden calf is not merely an ancient sin but the perennial sin of the human heart — preferring a god we can see, control, and shape to our liking over the living God who shapes us. It exposes how desperately we need not only redemption but a new heart.

sections.title: The Wrath of God and the Intercession of Moses
sections.commentary:
God's wrath burns: "Let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, and I will make a great nation of you." The sin is real, the wrath is just. But Moses stands in the breach and implores the LORD, pleading God's glory before the watching Egyptians and God's own covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. "Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster." And the LORD relents from the disaster he had spoken.

Here is mediation in action. Moses does not plead Israel's merit — they have none — but God's glory and God's promises. The intercessor stands between the wrath of God and the people who deserve it. This is a shadow of Christ, our Mediator, who stands between us and the just wrath of God, pleading not our merit but his own finished work. That God "relents" in response to intercession reveals the mysterious power of a mediator's prayer and the heart of a God who delights to show mercy.

sections.title: Judgment and Moses' Offer
sections.commentary:
Moses descends, sees the calf and the revelry, and in righteous anger shatters the tablets — a vivid sign that the covenant has been broken. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, and makes the people drink it. Aaron offers a feeble excuse. The Levites rally to the LORD and execute judgment on the unrepentant, and about three thousand fall. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; the covenant breach brings real and severe consequences.

The shattered tablets preach a sermon: the law is broken, and a broken law brings death. Yet judgment is restrained — the whole nation is not consumed. The tension between God's justice, which cannot ignore sin, and his mercy, which spares a people, builds toward its only possible resolution: a substitute who can satisfy justice and secure mercy at once. The chapter cries out for the cross.

sections.title: Blot Me Out of Your Book
sections.commentary:
The next day Moses returns to the LORD with the most astonishing intercession in the Old Testament: "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. But now, if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." Moses offers his own eternal standing for the sake of his people. He cannot actually accomplish such an exchange — God answers that the one who sins will bear his own guilt — but the offer is a breathtaking foreshadowing of a greater Mediator.

For Jesus is the greater Moses, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but actually was — who became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), who was forsaken by the Father ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?") that we might be forgiven and kept forever in the book of life. Moses' offer was a shadow; Christ's substitution was the substance. Sproul preached that here we see both the depth of human sin and the height of mediatorial love, all pointing to Calvary. A plague follows, but the people are not destroyed — because a mediator stood in the gap. And One greater than Moses would stand in our gap forever.

32.theology:
The idolatry of the human heart. The golden calf, made within weeks of Sinai, reveals that the heart is an idol factory (Calvin). We need not only redemption but a new heart.

The wrath of God against sin. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; the broken law brings real judgment. Justice cannot simply ignore rebellion.

The mediator who stands in the breach. Moses pleads God's glory and offers his own life — a shadow of Christ, who actually became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13) and was forsaken that we might be forgiven.
32.examples:
Then: While Moses received the law, the people made a golden calf, breaking the covenant almost before it was given. God's wrath burned, but Moses stood in the breach, pleading God's glory and offering to be blotted out for his people.

Now: Our hearts are idol factories still, and our sin against a holy God is grievous. But we have a greater Mediator than Moses: Jesus, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but was forsaken on the cross, becoming a curse for us. He stood in our gap so we would never be blotted out of the book of life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the very foot of the mountain still smoking with God's glory, while Moses lingers with God, Israel grows impatient and demands, "make us gods who shall go before us." Aaron collects their gold, casts a calf, and the people cry, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." They rise up to "play" before it. Forty days after vowing "all that the LORD has spoken we will do," the covenant lies shattered in idolatry.
verseByVerse.theology: The golden calf is the archetypal sin: exchanging "the glory of the immortal God" for an image (Rom 1:23; Ps 106:19-20). Note the speed — weeks after Sinai — and the subtlety: they do not renounce the LORD outright but try to worship him under an idol of their own making, on their own terms. That is the perennial temptation, to reshape God into something manageable. The human heart is "a perpetual factory of idols" (Calvin), and only grace can break the mold.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: unwilling to wait, the people traded the invisible God of glory for a golden animal they could see and control, and called it worship.

Now: our idols are rarely metal, but the sin is the same — remaking God to suit us, or giving our heart's worship to money, self, or pleasure. "Little children, keep yourselves from idols" (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, 'Up, make us gods who shall go before us.'... And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The setting makes it almost unbearable. The mountain is still wrapped in fire and cloud; God's voice has barely faded. Only weeks ago the people vowed with one voice, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do" (24:3). And now, because Moses "delayed," they cannot wait, and they demand gods they can see. Aaron — who should have stood firm — melts their gold and makes a calf, and the people commit blasphemy: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt." They credit their rescue to a lump of gold they made that morning. Notice the deadly subtlety: they do not simply abandon the LORD; Aaron even proclaims "a feast to the LORD" (v.5). They try to worship the true God through an idol of their own design, on their own terms — and that is idolatry too. This is the oldest sin of the human heart: to exchange "the glory of the immortal God for images" (Rom 1:23), to remake God into something we can manage. Then they "rose up to play" — the solemn feast collapsing into revelry. How quickly the redeemed forget; how patiently they must be saved by grace alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-14 — Moses Stands in the Breach
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses what is happening below and, testing his servant, says, "let me alone... that I may consume them," offering to make of Moses a great nation instead. But Moses does not seize the offer; he pleads — for God's glory before the watching Egyptians, and on the ground of God's own promises to Abraham. And "the LORD relented from the disaster." Here is intercession at its purest: a mediator standing between a holy God and a guilty people, appealing to grace.
verseByVerse.theology: God's "let me alone" (v.10) is not helplessness but invitation — it opens the door to intercession, as if God were seeking a mediator to plead. Moses pleads not Israel's worth but God's glory and God's promise (vv.11-13), the only ground prayer ever has. That "the LORD relented" (v.14) speaks of God's real responsiveness to prayer, framed in human terms, without any change in his eternal purpose or character (Num 23:19). Moses foreshadows the greater Mediator who "always lives to make intercession" (Heb 7:25) and does not merely plead but bears the wrath himself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: offered personal greatness, Moses refused it and threw himself into the gap for a people who deserved destruction, and God heard him.

Now: we have a Mediator who did infinitely more than plead — he stepped into the breach and took the judgment on himself. "He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him" (Heb 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, in order that I may make a great nation of you.' But Moses implored the LORD his God... 'Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel...' And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.
verseByVerse.commentary: God tells Moses what his people have done, and then says something astonishing: "let me alone... that I may consume them," and offers to start over, making a great nation out of Moses himself. It is at once a righteous verdict on real sin and a test of his servant's heart — for the very words "let me alone" leave a door open, as if God were seeking someone to stand in the gap (cf. Ezek 22:30). And Moses does not grab at greatness. He pleads for the doomed people. Watch the grounds of his prayer, for they are the only grounds any prayer ever has: not Israel's goodness (they have none), but God's glory before the watching Egyptians (v.12) and God's own sworn promise to Abraham (v.13). Moses appeals to God against God's threat, holding God to his grace. "And the LORD relented." We must not imagine God changing his mind like a fickle man (Num 23:19); rather, this is God's real, tender responsiveness to the prayers of his servant, told in the language of the human heart. And it is a shadow — for here stands a mediator between wrath and a guilty people. The true Mediator would do more than plead; he would take the burning into his own body, and quench it there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The Tablets Broken and the Calf Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses descends with the two tablets "written with the finger of God." Seeing the calf and the dancing, his anger burns, and he throws down the tablets, shattering them at the foot of the mountain — a visible sign that the covenant is broken. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes the people drink. Then Aaron gives one of Scripture's feeblest excuses: "I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf."
verseByVerse.theology: The shattered tablets dramatize a broken covenant: Israel has broken the law, so the stone law is broken before their eyes. Sin must be destroyed, not managed — Moses grinds the idol to dust and makes them swallow the bitterness of their folly. Aaron's excuse ("out came this calf," v.24) is the ancient echo of every evasion since Eden: sin that will not own itself, blaming circumstance, the crowd, anything but the self (Gen 3:12-13). Confession, not excuse, is the road back.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the law lay in pieces on the ground, and the idol was ground to powder and swallowed — sin exposed as bitter, ridiculous, and ruinous.

Now: we still meet Aaron's temptation to excuse — "it just happened," "everyone was doing it." But grace meets honesty, not alibis: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful... to forgive" (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain... And Aaron said... 'I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses comes down carrying the tablets "written with the finger of God" — and sees it all: the calf, the dancing, the shame. His anger blazes, and he hurls the tablets down, smashing them at the mountain's foot. It is not a tantrum but a sermon in stone: Israel has shattered God's covenant, so the covenant law is shattered before their eyes. Then Moses deals with the idol as sin must always be dealt with — not managed but destroyed. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes the people drink their own folly, bitter to the last swallow. And then Aaron. Confronted, he offers one of the most pathetic excuses in all Scripture: he collected the gold, "and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf" — as if the idol assembled itself. It is Eden all over again, sin refusing to own itself, blaming the fire, the people, anything but the self (Gen 3:12-13). The way back to God is never paved with excuses. It is paved with confession — and grace waits at the end of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25-29 — The Levites Take Their Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The camp has "broken loose" into chaos. Moses stands in the gate and cries, "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." The sons of Levi rally, and at Moses' command they move through the camp in judgment against the ringleaders of the rebellion. It is a severe day, and a defining one: in the crisis, the Levites chose the LORD over kin and comfort, and were set apart for his service.
verseByVerse.theology: There are moments when neutrality is impossible and a line must be drawn: "Who is on the LORD's side?" (v.26). The Levites' costly loyalty — choosing God above even family ties in a day of judgment — marks them for priestly service (cf. Deut 33:9). The severity is sobering, a real judgment on real apostasy that threatened to destroy the whole nation. It warns that sin tolerated spreads like fire, and that following God sometimes costs everything (Luke 14:26).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: when Moses cried "Who is on the LORD's side?", the Levites stepped forward, and their costly allegiance in the crisis set them apart.

Now: there are still days that demand a clear side, when following Christ means standing against the crowd, even against those closest to us (Matt 10:37). "Choose this day whom you will serve" (Josh 24:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moses saw that the people had broken loose (for Aaron had let them break loose, to the derision of their enemies), then Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, 'Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me.' And all the sons of Levi gathered around him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The scene is chaos — the people "broken loose," Aaron's failure now the mockery of Israel's enemies. Into that anarchy Moses plants himself in the gate and throws down a question that splits the camp in two: "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." There are moments when there is no middle ground, when to stand still is to stand against God. The Levites come. And what follows is a hard day of judgment against the ringleaders of the rebellion — a real and terrible reckoning with a sin that, left to spread, would have consumed the whole nation. The Levites' loyalty cost them dearly; they chose the LORD above even their own kin (Deut 33:9), and for that costly faithfulness they were set apart to his service. It is a sobering passage, and an honest one. Following God is not always gentle; there are hours that demand we choose him over everything and everyone else (Luke 14:26). "Choose this day whom you will serve" (Josh 24:15) — and the Levites chose.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The next day Moses goes back up to God with the most extraordinary prayer. He confesses the people's "great sin," then offers himself: "if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." He would be damned in their place. God will not accept that substitute — each bears his own sin — yet the offer points unmistakably to the One who could and would be blotted out for his people.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses' "blot me out" (v.32) is one of the great foreshadowings of the cross — a mediator willing to be cursed for his people (cf. Rom 9:3, Paul's echo). But Moses cannot be that substitute; God answers, "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book" (v.33). No mere man can bear another's guilt. The offer hangs unfulfilled until Another comes who is sinless, who truly can be "blotted out" in our place — struck by God so that our names might stand forever in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses offered his own soul for his people — but a sinner cannot ransom sinners, and God did not accept the trade.

Now: what Moses could only offer, Christ accomplished. He was "blotted out" — cut off from the land of the living (Isa 53:8) — that our names might never be. "Rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:20).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses returned to the LORD and said, 'Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold. But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written.' But the LORD said to Moses, 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is one of the most breathtaking prayers in the Bible. Moses climbs back up to God, names the sin plainly — "a great sin" — and then makes an offer that stops the heart. He cannot even finish the sentence: "if you will forgive their sin —." The thought is too large; he breaks off. And then: "but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." Moses offers to be damned in their place. Take my name out of your book, he says, but spare them. It is the love of a true shepherd, willing to perish for his sheep — and Paul would one day echo it, wishing himself accursed for his kinsmen (Rom 9:3). But God will not take the trade: "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book." Moses is himself a sinner; he cannot ransom sinners. No mere man can bear another's guilt. And so the offer hangs in the air, aching, unfulfilled — until One comes who is sinless, and who can. Jesus was truly "cut off out of the land of the living" (Isa 53:8), blotted out under the wrath we deserved, so that our names might stand forever in the Lamb's book of life (Rev 21:27). Moses could only offer it. Christ did it.

33.title: If Your Presence Will Not Go
33.text: <sup>14</sup>And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." <sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." <sup>18</sup>Moses said, "Please show me your glory." <sup>20</sup>..."you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live."
33.overview:
After the golden calf, the deepest question is no longer survival but presence. God offers to send Israel to the promised land with an angel — but to withdraw his own presence, lest his holiness consume this stiff-necked people on the way. And here Moses utters one of the most magnificent prayers in all of Scripture: "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. He understands that the land without God's presence is no blessing at all.

This is the very heart of true religion. As Keller has said, the difference between a believer and a moralist is this: the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not want the milk and honey; he wants the God who gives it. "Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" The presence of God is what sets his people apart — it is everything.

Then Moses dares to ask the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." And God answers with infinite grace and infinite reserve: he will cause all his goodness to pass before Moses and proclaim his name, but Moses cannot see his face and live. So God hides him in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and lets him see only his back. Sproul saw here both the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension. We could never bear the full glory — but in Christ, "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6), we behold what Moses longed to see.

sections.title: The Threat of God's Absence
sections.commentary:
God commands Israel to depart for the promised land, flowing with milk and honey, and promises to send an angel before them. But there is a terrible catch: "I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people." The very holiness that makes God's presence the greatest blessing also makes it dangerous to a sinful people. When the people hear this disastrous word, they mourn and strip off their ornaments. The prospect of the land without God's presence is felt as catastrophe.

This is the crisis the golden calf created: the holy God cannot simply dwell among an unholy people without consuming them. The problem demands a solution that chapter 33 cannot yet fully provide — a way for a holy God to dwell with sinful people without destroying them. That way is found only in Christ, in whom God dwells among us in grace, having dealt with our sin at the cross.

sections.title: Moses' Prayer for the Presence
sections.commentary:
Moses pitches the tent of meeting outside the camp, and the LORD speaks with him "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Then Moses prays the great prayer: pleading for God's presence, he says, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" And God grants it: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."

Here is the heart of true faith. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than Canaan without him. As Keller observed, the difference between a true believer and a mere moralist is that the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not crave the milk and honey; he craves the God who gives them. The presence of God is what makes his people distinct — it is everything. To have God's gifts without God himself would be the deepest poverty; to have God's presence in a desert is the greatest wealth.

sections.title: Show Me Your Glory
sections.commentary:
Emboldened, Moses asks the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." God answers with both grace and holy reserve. He will make all his goodness pass before Moses and proclaim his name, the LORD, declaring his sovereign grace and mercy. But "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God hides Moses in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand as his glory passes by, and lets him see only his back.

Here is the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension held together. No sinner can behold the unveiled glory of God and survive; yet God graciously grants Moses a glimpse, sheltering him in the rock. Many have seen the rock that shelters Moses as a picture of Christ, our refuge from the consuming glory. And what Moses could not see — the face of God — is now beheld in Christ: "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). In the incarnate Son, the glory Moses longed for has drawn near, veiled in flesh, so that we may behold it and live.

sections.title: The Crisis and the Cry: A Holy God and a Sinful People
sections.commentary:
The whole chapter turns on a single, unbearable tension: how can a holy God dwell among a sinful people without consuming them? The golden calf created the crisis; Moses' prayer presses it; God's reserve in revealing his glory deepens it. The land without God's presence is no blessing, yet God's presence among the unholy is mortal danger.

This crisis is resolved only in Christ. In him the holy God dwells among sinners in grace, because at the cross our sin was borne and atoned. The glory Moses could not see in full is beheld in "the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). And the deepest cry of faith — "if your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up" — is answered forever in Immanuel, God with us, whose presence will never depart from his people.

33.theology:
The supreme value of God's presence. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. True faith wants God himself, not merely his gifts (Keller).

The problem of a holy God dwelling with sinners. God's presence among an unholy people would consume them — a crisis resolved only in Christ, who deals with our sin so God can dwell with us.

The unseeable glory revealed in Christ. No one can see God's face and live, yet in Christ we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6).
33.examples:
Then: After the calf, God threatened to send Israel onward without his presence, but Moses pleaded, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here," and dared to ask, "Show me your glory."

Now: The mark of true faith is that we want God himself, not merely his blessings. "If your presence will not go, do not send me." And the glory Moses could not fully see has drawn near in Christ, the face of God among us. To have God's presence is everything; in Christ, that presence is ours forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-6 — 'I Will Not Go Up Among You'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Israel to leave Sinai for the promised land — flowing with milk and honey — but adds a devastating word: "I will not go up among you, lest I consume you." He will give them the land but withhold himself. And that, to a people who have tasted his presence, is unbearable news. They mourn, and strip off their ornaments. A land without God is no gift at all.
verseByVerse.theology: God's threat to send Israel on "with an angel" but without his own presence (v.3) exposes the heart of true religion: the gift is nothing without the Giver. A promised land without God would be a golden cage. The people "mourned" (v.4) — a sign of real repentance, for they now grieve God's absence more than any hardship. Moses will refuse to move an inch without the Presence (v.15). The deepest blessing is never God's gifts but God himself (Ps 73:25).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the promise of milk and honey turned to ashes at the words "I will not go up among you." Israel mourned, for they had learned that the land was worthless without its God.

Now: we can want heaven's blessings while forgetting heaven's God. But "whom have I in heaven but you?" (Ps 73:25). Better a wilderness with God than a paradise without him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people.' When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments.
verseByVerse.commentary: God keeps his promise of the land — milk and honey, everything they were journeying toward — and then speaks the most terrible sentence they could hear: "I will not go up among you." He will send an angel, he will give the land, but he will withhold himself, "lest I consume you," for they are a stiff-necked people and his holy presence among sinners is deadly. Here is the crisis the golden calf created: how can a holy God dwell in the midst of an unholy people without destroying them? And notice Israel's response — "when the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned." This is the turning point, the mark of real repentance. They do not grieve over a hard road or a lost comfort; they grieve over the loss of God. The land itself has become worthless to them if he will not be in it. They strip off their ornaments in mourning. A soul that has tasted the presence of God can never again be content with his gifts alone. "Whom have I in heaven but you?" (Ps 73:25). Better the desert with God than Canaan without him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-11 — The Tent of Meeting, and a Friend of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, and there the LORD meets with him. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud descends to the door, and the people rise and worship. And the wonder is stated simply: "the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." In the aftermath of the calf, God still speaks with his mediator — a friendship that keeps hope alive for the whole nation.
verseByVerse.theology: "Face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (v.11) describes an intimacy of communion unmatched under the old covenant (Num 12:8; Deut 34:10) — though even Moses could not see God's face unveiled (v.20). It anticipates the friendship Christ extends: "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends" (John 15:15), and the day when "we shall see face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). The young Joshua lingering in the tent (v.11) is a quiet picture of the next generation learning to seek God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the people watched the cloud come down to the tent door and worshiped from their own doorways, longing for the intimacy their mediator enjoyed.

Now: through Christ that intimacy is opened to us; he calls us friends (John 15:15), and by the Spirit we "behold the glory of the Lord" and are transformed (2 Cor 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting... When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance... Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even after the calf, God does not go silent. Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, and there the LORD comes down to meet him. When Moses enters, the pillar of cloud descends to the doorway, and all the people rise and worship from their own tent doors — watching, longing, worshiping at a distance. And then the line that takes your breath away: "the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Not thunder from a mountaintop now, but conversation — the intimacy of friendship. In a chapter about God threatening to withdraw his presence, here is proof that the door is not shut: God still speaks, still befriends his mediator, and through that friendship keeps hope alive for the whole guilty nation. Yet even this is not the fullness; Moses could not see God's unveiled face and live (v.20). It all leans forward to the One who says, "No longer do I call you servants... but I have called you friends" (John 15:15), and to the day when "we shall see face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). Note too the young Joshua, who "would not depart from the tent" — a new generation already learning to linger in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — 'If Your Presence Will Not Go'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Emboldened by friendship, Moses presses God with holy boldness. He will not settle for an angel; he wants God himself. "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." The very thing that marks Israel out from every other people on earth is not the land, not the law, but this: "Is it not in your going with us?" And God yields: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."
verseByVerse.theology: Moses' argument is the essence of prayer: he holds God to his own words and his own grace, and asks for God himself as the one indispensable gift (vv.13-16). What distinguishes God's people from all others is the presence of God among them (v.16) — not superior virtue, but a Presence given by grace. God's answer, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest" (v.14), is the gospel promise that runs to Christ, "Immanuel" (Matt 1:23), and his word, "I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses staked everything on one request — God's own presence — and would rather stay in the desert with God than march to Canaan without him.

Now: the one thing that makes the church the church is Christ with us: "I am with you always" (Matt 28:20). Seek his presence above every other blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people on the face of the earth?' And the LORD said to Moses, 'This very thing that you have spoken I will do.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Friendship makes Moses bold, and he presses in with the holiest kind of daring. He will not be content with an angel escort; he wants God himself, and he says so plainly: "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." Then he lays bare the deepest truth about God's people: what makes Israel different from every nation on earth is not their land, their law, or their goodness — it is the presence of God in their midst. "Is it not in your going with us?" Strip that away and they are just another tribe wandering the desert. This is the one thing worth asking for, the one gift that contains every other. And God, moved by his servant's plea and his own grace, gives the tender promise: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." Hold those words, for they are the heartbeat of the whole Bible. They run straight to Bethlehem, to "Immanuel, God with us" (Matt 1:23), and to the Savior's invitation, "Come to me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28). The presence that Moses begged for is the presence we are freely given in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having secured God's presence, Moses asks for more still: "Please show me your glory." It is the boldest request in Scripture. God answers by promising to make "all my goodness" pass before him and to proclaim his name — but "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God will hide Moses in a cleft of the rock, cover him with his hand, and let him see only his back as his glory passes by. Grace lets a sinner glimpse God and live — sheltered in the rock.
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory, when unveiled, is unbearable to sinners: "man shall not see me and live" (v.20). Yet grace makes a way — Moses is hidden "in a cleft of the rock" and covered by God's hand while the glory passes (vv.22-23). The rock that shelters from the glory is a picture of Christ, the Rock (1 Cor 10:4), in whom alone we are safe before the holiness of God. And what God shows is chiefly moral glory — "all my goodness," his name and character (v.19) — fully unveiled at last in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6; John 1:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Moses, hidden in the rock and shielded by God's own hand, saw the afterglow of the glory and lived — a sinner sheltered to behold his God.

Now: we behold the glory of God safely, "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), hidden in the true Rock. What Moses glimpsed from behind, we see full-face in the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, 'Please show me your glory.' And he said, 'I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name, The LORD... But,' he said, 'you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live.'... 'Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock... I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses has secured God's presence; now, greatly daring, he asks for the summit of all desire: "Please show me your glory." Who would dare pray such a prayer? And how does God answer? He promises to make "all my goodness" pass by and to proclaim his own name — for the truest glory of God is not raw blazing power but his moral splendor, his goodness and grace and character. But there is a limit even grace cannot cross for now: "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." Unveiled deity would incinerate a sinner. So God devises a way for Moses to see and yet survive: he will hide him "in a cleft of the rock," cover him with his own hand while the glory passes, and let him see only the afterglow, his back. Do not miss the tenderness — God's own hand shielding his servant so that he can bear the unbearable. And do not miss the rock. To behold the glory of God and live, a sinner must be hidden in a rock, sheltered by God himself. That Rock is Christ (1 Cor 10:4). Hidden in him, we are safe before the holiness that would otherwise consume us — and what Moses saw only from behind, we now behold full-face, "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6).

34.title: The LORD, the LORD, a God Merciful and Gracious
34.text: <sup>6</sup>The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, <sup>7</sup>keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty..."
34.overview:
This is the high point of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. Having asked to see God's glory, Moses is given new tablets and meets God on the mountain again. And God reveals his glory not first by sight but by proclamation — by declaring his name, his character: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." This is who God is at the deepest level, the answer to Moses' prayer. The glory of God is supremely the glory of his grace.

This proclamation becomes the most-quoted text in the rest of the Old Testament, echoed again and again (Num. 14, Neh. 9, Pss. 86, 103, 145, Joel 2, Jonah 4, Nah. 1). It is Israel's creed about the heart of God. And notice the perfect balance: God is overflowing with steadfast love and forgiveness, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." His mercy does not cancel his justice; his justice does not quench his mercy. How can both be fully true? The answer comes at the cross, where, as Sproul never tired of saying, God is shown to be "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26) — where guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne.

The covenant is renewed; God's grace triumphs over Israel's sin. And Moses comes down from the mountain with his face shining, radiant from being in God's presence — a glory Paul says is surpassed by the greater glory now shining in the gospel of Christ (2 Cor. 3). The God who is merciful and gracious has, in Christ, drawn infinitely near.

sections.title: The New Tablets
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to cut two new tablets like the first, which he shattered, and to ascend the mountain again. As God's glory passes by, he proclaims his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty." Moses bows and worships, pleading for God to pardon and to go with his stiff-necked people.

This is the climax of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. God answers Moses' request to see his glory not chiefly by sight but by the proclamation of his character — and the heart of that character is grace, mercy, steadfast love (hesed), and faithfulness. Yet held together with mercy is justice: he "will by no means clear the guilty." Here is the great tension of the gospel: how can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? Sproul taught that this tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is shown to be "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being overlooked but by being borne by a substitute.

sections.title: The Covenant Renewed
sections.commentary:
God graciously renews the covenant, promising to do marvels and to drive out the nations before Israel. He warns sternly against idolatry and intermarriage with the surrounding peoples, against making covenants with them or worshiping their gods, for "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." He reaffirms the feasts, the firstborn, the Sabbath, and the firstfruits. The covenant broken by the golden calf is restored — entirely by God's grace, not Israel's merit.

The renewal of the covenant after such a grievous breach is a stunning display of mercy. Israel had forfeited everything; God restores everything. This is the pattern of grace throughout Scripture: not that we keep covenant with God, but that God keeps covenant with us despite our unfaithfulness. The warnings against idolatry remind us that grace is never a license to return to the idols from which we were rescued; the God who forgives is also the God who is jealous for the undivided love of his people.

sections.title: The Shining Face of Moses
sections.commentary:
When Moses comes down from the mountain, his face shines because he has been talking with God — so brightly that the people are afraid to come near, and Moses must veil his face. The radiance is the reflected glory of having been in God's presence. Even a glimpse of God's glory transforms and radiates from the one who beholds it.

Paul takes up this scene in 2 Corinthians 3, showing that the glory on Moses' face — though real — was fading, and was surpassed by the far greater and permanent glory of the new covenant. Under the gospel, "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor. 3:18). The fading glory of Moses gives way to the surpassing, transforming glory of Christ. To behold him is to be changed into his likeness — the radiance Moses reflected is now, by the Spirit, being worked into all who behold the glory of God in the face of Christ.

sections.title: The Name Above All Names: Grace and Justice Meet
sections.commentary:
At the center of the chapter, and of the whole Old Testament's self-revelation of God, stands the proclamation of the divine name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity... but who will by no means clear the guilty." Here grace and justice stand side by side, both absolute, both true.

How can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? The chapter cannot yet say; the cross alone resolves it, where God is shown "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne. And the glory of this name, reflected fadingly on Moses' face, now shines unfading in Christ, transforming all who behold him from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18).

34.theology:
The glory of God is the glory of his grace. God reveals his glory by proclaiming his name: "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love." This is the most-quoted text in the rest of the OT.

Mercy and justice held together. God forgives yet "will by no means clear the guilty." The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26).

Transforming glory. Moses' shining face is surpassed by the greater glory of the gospel; beholding Christ, we are transformed from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18).
34.examples:
Then: God answered Moses' plea to see his glory by proclaiming his name — "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious" — renewing the covenant after the calf and sending Moses down with a face shining from God's presence.

Now: This is the God we worship: merciful and gracious, yet perfectly just. At the cross his mercy and justice meet, for there our guilt was borne, not ignored. And beholding the glory of God in the face of Christ, we are being transformed from one degree of glory to another by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The LORD Proclaims His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls Moses back up with two new stone tablets to replace the ones he shattered. And there, as his goodness passes by, God does the very thing he promised — he proclaims his own name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty." This is God's self-revelation, the most quoted description of God's character in the whole Bible. Moses bows and worships.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the fullest self-portrait God gives in the Old Testament (vv.6-7), echoed again and again across Scripture (Num 14:18; Ps 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Its center is hesed — "steadfast love," God's loyal, covenant-keeping mercy — held together with justice: he forgives iniquity, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." How can both be true at once? The tension is only resolved at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom 3:26) — guilt not cleared but borne, love and justice meeting in the blood of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: at Israel's lowest moment, just after the calf, God reveals himself not chiefly as wrath but as "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love."

Now: this is still who God is toward all who come to him in Christ. His mercy is not reluctant; it is his glory. Yet he does not wink at sin — he laid it on his Son, that mercy and justice might kiss.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, 'The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty...' And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary: God cuts two new tablets of stone — grace rewriting the law Israel had broken — and then keeps the promise he made in the cleft of the rock. As his goodness passes by, God proclaims his own name, and it is the most treasured description of God's character in all of Scripture: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." Feel the timing. This comes not at Israel's best moment but at their worst, days after the golden calf. And God reveals himself first and foremost not as fury but as mercy — patient, gracious, overflowing with hesed, his loyal covenant love. This one verse becomes the church's confession of God, quoted again and again down the Old Testament (Ps 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2). Yet the same breath adds, he "will by no means clear the guilty." God is merciful, and God is just, and he will not pretend sin does not matter. How can both stand together? Not here — only at Calvary, where God proves himself "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom 3:26). The guilt was not waved away; it was carried by the Son, so that mercy and justice could embrace. No wonder Moses "quickly bowed his head... and worshiped."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the ground of his mercy, God renews the covenant, promising to do "marvels" never before seen and to drive out the nations of Canaan. But the warning is urgent: make no covenant with the peoples of the land, tear down their altars, for their idolatry will become a snare. And God tells them his name: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." The God who forgives is also the God who will not share his people's hearts.
verseByVerse.theology: God's "jealousy" (v.14) is not petty envy but the fierce, protective love of a husband for his bride — he will not tolerate rivals for a heart that belongs to him (cf. Deut 4:24; 2 Cor 11:2). The ban on covenants and mixed worship guards against the snare of syncretism, blending the worship of the LORD with idols (as the calf tried to do). The molten gods forbidden in v.17 name the very sin just committed. Grace renews the covenant, but grace also demands undivided loyalty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: forgiven and restored, Israel was warned that peace-treaties with Canaan's idolatry would become a trap — tolerated idols always are.

Now: the God who saved us is jealous for us, in the best sense — he wants all our heart, not a share of it. "You cannot serve God and money" (Matt 6:24). His jealousy is the measure of his love.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth... Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst... for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: On the sheer ground of his mercy, God renews the broken covenant — undeserved, astonishing grace — and promises to do "marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth." But renewal comes with a solemn charge. When they enter Canaan, they must make no covenant with its peoples and must tear down their altars, "lest it become a snare." Why so severe? Because tolerated idolatry never stays contained; make peace with it and you will end up bowing to it. Then God tells them one of his names: "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." We must hear that rightly. This is not the mean jealousy of a small heart, but the burning, protective love of a husband who will not share his bride with another (2 Cor 11:2). God's jealousy is the fire of his love. He forbids the molten gods (v.17) — naming the exact sin they had just committed — because a heart that belongs to him cannot be split. The God who abounds in steadfast love is the same God who says: all of you, not part. And that total claim is not a burden but the truest freedom, for we were made to be wholly his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The renewed covenant restates the rhythms of a life lived before God: keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, redeem every firstborn, rest on the Sabbath even in plowing time and harvest, keep the feasts of Weeks and Ingathering, and bring the best firstfruits. Israel's calendar is re-consecrated. A people brought back from ruin are re-taught how to walk with God through the year.
verseByVerse.theology: These repeated laws (cf. ch. 23) re-establish covenant life after the rupture of the calf: redemption of the firstborn (v.20) confesses that all life is forfeit and must be bought back; the Sabbath even in "plowing time and in harvest" (v.21) tests trust at the busiest, most tempting seasons; the feasts keep the story of grace before the people year by year. Restored people need re-formed rhythms — grace rebuilds a life of ordered worship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even in plowing and harvest — when every hour counted — Israel must rest, trusting God to provide what their labor could not.

Now: the busiest, most pressured seasons are exactly where our trust is tested. Sabbath rest still preaches that our provision comes from God, not from the hours we refuse to stop working (Ps 127:2).

verseByVerse.quote: 'You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread... All that open the womb are mine... Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest... The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: A restored people must relearn how to live, and so God re-establishes the rhythms of covenant life — the same feasts and firstfruits given before (ch. 23), now spoken again after the fall and the forgiveness. Keep Unleavened Bread, remembering the exodus. Redeem every firstborn, for "all that open the womb are mine" — a confession that every life is forfeit to God and must be bought back. Keep the feasts of Weeks and Ingathering. And rest on the Sabbath — with a pointed addition: "in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest." Those are precisely the seasons when a farmer can least afford to stop, when the weather is right and every hour is money. That is the test. Will you trust God enough to lay down your tools when the work screams to be done? The busiest, most pressured moments are where faith is proved. God re-forms his people's calendar because restored hearts need re-ordered lives — a whole year structured to keep the story of grace, and the trust it demands, always before them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27-28 — Forty Days, the Ten Words
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses is with the LORD forty days and forty nights, neither eating bread nor drinking water, and God writes on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.
